phenomena.name: Abada
phenomena.description: The Abada is a two-horned, unicorn-like creature from the folklore of the Kongo language area of Central Africa, said to resemble a small donkey and to have horns that serve as antidotes to poison and disease.
phenomena.origin: Forests and inland regions of the historic Kongo cultural area, including parts of present-day Angola, the Republic of the Congo, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

phenomena.name: Abumi-guchi
phenomena.description: The abumi-guchi is a furry tsukumogami (object spirit) of Japanese folklore that takes the form of a stirrup left behind on a battlefield, said to wait for its dead owner to return. It appears in Toriyama Sekien's late-18th-century yokai compendium Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro.
regions: Historic samurai battlefields of the Japanese archipelago
phenomena.origin: A figure of Japanese yokai art and folklore; geographically associated with old samurai battlefields throughout Japan.

phenomena.name: Adlet
phenomena.description: The Adlet are a race of hybrid beings in Inuit mythology — dog from the waist down, human above — said to be taller than humans, hostile, and the offspring of an Inuit woman and a red dog.
phenomena.origin: Adlet stories are recorded across the eastern Arctic: Greenland (especially Smith Sound), Baffin Island, the Labrador and Hudson Bay coasts, and adjacent inland areas.

phenomena.name: Adze
phenomena.description: The Adze is a vampiric spirit of Ewe folklore (Ghana and Togo) that travels at night in the form of a firefly, drinking blood — especially from children — and causing illness; if caught, it transforms into human shape and is regarded as the spirit possessing a witch.
phenomena.origin: The Ewe-speaking area of West Africa, comprising southeastern Ghana (Volta Region) and southern Togo, with related traditions among neighbouring Gbe-speaking peoples.

phenomena.name: Agropelter
phenomena.description: The Agropelter is a fearsome critter of North American lumberjack folklore: a slender, ape-faced beast that lives in hollow trees and amuses itself by hurling dead branches at unwary woodsmen. It was first catalogued by William T. Cox in his 1910 book Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods.

aliases.name: Anthrocephalus craniofractens
aliases.meaning: the 'man-headed skull-breaker' coined by William T. Cox in 1910

phenomena.origin: According to Cox, the Agropelter ranges through the conifer forests of North America from Maine in the east to Oregon in the west, mirroring the geography of the early-20th-century logging frontier.

phenomena.name: Ahool
phenomena.description: The Ahool is a reported giant bat- or flying-primate-like cryptid said to inhabit the rainforests and river valleys of western Java. It is best known from accounts gathered by the Dutch naturalist Ernest Bartels in the 1920s and popularised in English-language cryptozoology by Ivan T. Sanderson.
phenomena.origin: Reports are concentrated in the rainforests, river valleys, and volcanic uplands of western Java, particularly the Salak and Halimun mountain regions.

phenomena.name: Ahuizotl
phenomena.description: The Ahuizotl is a small, dog-sized water creature of Aztec mythology with monkey-like hands on its limbs and a fifth, hand-tipped tail; it is said to live in deep pools and to drown unwary fishermen, taking their eyes, nails, and teeth.
phenomena.origin: Lakes and waterways of the Valley of Mexico, especially the lake system around the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, with Lake Texcoco as the most-cited locale.

phenomena.name: Aka Manto
phenomena.description: Aka Manto ('Red Cloak') is a Japanese urban legend about a masked, red-cloaked spirit who haunts public and school toilets and asks the occupant to choose between red or blue toilet paper (or red or blue cloak). Either choice ends in death; only refusal lets the victim escape.
phenomena.origin: Originally a Japanese school-yard legend; widely retold across Japan and exported through pop culture to East Asia, North America, and beyond.

phenomena.name: Akaname
phenomena.description: Akaname ('filth-licker') is a small Japanese yokai recorded in Edo-period bestiaries that emerges in dirty, neglected bathrooms and bathhouses to lick the grime off tubs and floors with its long red tongue. It functions in folklore as a moral spur to keep bathrooms clean.
regions: Old urban bathhouses and private bathrooms across Japan
phenomena.origin: A figure of Japanese yokai art and folklore, distributed wherever Edo-period and modern Japanese bathing culture is observed.

phenomena.name: Al-Khidr
phenomena.description: Al-Khidr ('the Green One') is a Quranic figure of Islamic tradition described in Surah al-Kahf 18:65–82 as a righteous servant of God endowed with hidden knowledge. He is variously identified as an angel, prophet, or saint (wali), and is held by many traditions to be still alive, guiding seekers and aiding those in distress.

aliases.name: Khiḍr Elias
aliases.meaning: Khidr-Elijah, paired with the prophet Elijah

phenomena.origin: A pan-Islamic figure with regional inflections across the Arab world, Iran, Turkey, the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Indian subcontinent, and the Malay archipelago; also venerated by Druze and (under different names) by Christian and Yazidi communities.

phenomena.name: Al-Mi'raj
phenomena.description: Al-Mi'raj is a yellow, hare- or rabbit-like creature with a single black horn described in medieval Arabic 'wonders' literature, most famously in Zakariya al-Qazwini's 13th-century Marvels of Things Created. It is said to live on Dragon Island in the Indian Ocean and to drive all other beasts to flight at the sight of it.
regions: Jazīrat al-Tinnīn (Dragon Island) of medieval Arabic cosmography
Indian Ocean of the marvels tradition
phenomena.origin: A creature of Arabic-Persian wonders literature; located in the storyworld of the medieval Indian Ocean, on the unmapped 'Dragon Island'.

phenomena.name: UFOs / UAPs and Alien Encounters
phenomena.description: The cluster of phenomena known as UFOs (unidentified flying objects) or UAPs (unidentified anomalous phenomena) covers reports of unexplained aerial, transmedium, and spaceborne objects, alongside alleged encounters with non-human intelligences. The modern era is conventionally dated to Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting; the US government formally established the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) in 2022.

aliases.name: Flying saucer
aliases.meaning: Popularised after the 1947 Kenneth Arnold sighting

regions: Brazilian Amazon and São Paulo state
phenomena.origin: Worldwide distribution of reports, with reporting density correlated with population, military activity, and the existence of national reporting channels.

phenomena.name: Almas
phenomena.description: A bipedal, human-sized, hair-covered humanoid cryptid reported from the mountainous regions of the Caucasus, Pamir, Tian Shan, and Altai, with deep roots in Mongolian, Turkic, and Caucasian folklore.
phenomena.origin: Reports span a belt of mountain ranges from the Caucasus through the Pamirs and Tian Shan to the Altai and southwestern Mongolia, with isolated accounts from northern Iran and the Hindu Kush.

phenomena.name: Alp
phenomena.description: A male nightmare spirit of German and Austrian folklore that sits on the chests of sleepers, causing oppressive dreams, sleep paralysis, and breathlessness; closely related to the female Mara of broader Germanic tradition.
phenomena.origin: Alp belief is concentrated in German-speaking Europe (Germany, Austria, German-speaking Switzerland) with overlapping traditions in neighbouring regions sharing the broader Mara complex.

phenomena.name: Altamaha-ha
phenomena.description: An aquatic cryptid said to inhabit the lower Altamaha River and Altamaha Sound of coastal Georgia, USA, sometimes called 'Altie'.
phenomena.origin: The lower Altamaha River system in coastal Georgia, USA, including Altamaha Sound and the surrounding salt marsh.

phenomena.name: Alux
phenomena.description: Small, often invisible nature beings of Yucatec Maya tradition, regarded as guardians of the land, forest, and milpa (cornfield), capable of helping or harming humans depending on how they are treated.
phenomena.origin: Yucatec Maya cultural area: the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico, Belize, and northern Guatemala.

phenomena.name: Amarok
phenomena.description: A gigantic, solitary wolf of Inuit oral tradition that hunts at night and is said to stalk hunters foolish enough to travel alone after dark.
phenomena.origin: Inuit oral-tradition range, encompassing Greenland, Arctic Canada (Nunavut, Nunavik), and Alaska.

phenomena.name: Ammit
phenomena.description: An ancient Egyptian funerary demon depicted with the head of a crocodile, the foreparts of a lion, and the hindparts of a hippopotamus, who devours the hearts of the unworthy dead in the Hall of Two Truths.

aliases.name: Eater of Hearts
aliases.meaning: epithet from Book of the Dead

phenomena.origin: Ammit appears in the funerary religion of ancient Egypt, with iconography distributed across tombs, papyri, and temples throughout the Nile Valley and the Egyptian-controlled regions of the New Kingdom.

phenomena.name: Anansi
phenomena.description: A spider trickster of Akan oral tradition, originating among the Ashanti people of present-day Ghana and carried by enslaved West Africans across the Atlantic, where Anansi became one of the central figures of Caribbean and African-American folklore.
phenomena.origin: Originating among the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana and carried through the Atlantic slave trade across West Africa, the Caribbean, and the Americas.

phenomena.name: Ankou
phenomena.description: The Breton personification of Death, traditionally depicted as a tall, gaunt figure in a black robe and wide-brimmed hat, carrying a scythe and driving a creaking cart in which he gathers the souls of the dead.

aliases.name: Labous an Ankou
aliases.meaning: 'bird of the Ankou' (associated with the owl)

phenomena.origin: Brittany (Lower Brittany / Breizh-Izel, the Breton-speaking western part of the region). Cognate figures appear in Cornwall and Wales.

phenomena.name: Antikythera Mechanism
phenomena.description: A Hellenistic Greek hand-powered geared device, recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, that calculated and displayed astronomical positions, eclipse cycles, and the four-year cycle of athletic games.
phenomena.origin: A unique surviving artifact, currently held in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens; recovered from the seafloor off Antikythera, Greece.

phenomena.name: Anubis
phenomena.description: Ancient Egyptian jackal-headed deity associated with mummification, the protection of tombs, and the conduct of souls through the underworld; one of the longest-lived figures in Egyptian religion.
phenomena.origin: Worshipped throughout ancient Egypt, with principal cult centre at Hardai (Cynopolis) in Upper Egypt; cult spread into the wider Greco-Roman world during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods.

phenomena.name: Aokigahara
phenomena.description: A dense forest at the northwestern foot of Mount Fuji in Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, grown on the lava flow of the 864 CE Jōgan eruption and associated in modern reputation with yūrei folklore and a high incidence of suicide.
phenomena.origin: A single contiguous forest at the northwestern base of Mount Fuji.

phenomena.name: Aos Sí
phenomena.description: A supernatural race in Irish (and broader Gaelic) folklore who dwell in fairy mounds and the Otherworld. Traditionally identified with the Tuatha Dé Danann who retreated underground after their defeat by the Milesians.

aliases.name: Sidhe
aliases.meaning: Common English shorthand for the fairy mounds and their inhabitants

aliases.name: The Good Folk
aliases.meaning: Euphemistic name used to avoid attracting their attention

aliases.name: Tuatha Dé Danann
aliases.meaning: 'Peoples of the goddess Danu'; mythological ancestors of the aos sí

regions: Ireland (especially the west: Connacht, Kerry, Donegal)
phenomena.origin: The aos sí tradition is centred on Ireland and extends across the Gaelic-speaking world: Scotland (where the cognate term is sìth), the Isle of Man, and Irish and Scottish diaspora communities. Cognate fairy traditions exist throughout the broader Celtic world (Welsh tylwyth teg, Cornish pobel vean, Breton korrigans).

phenomena.name: Ap (Apas)
phenomena.description: Ap (Vedic Sanskrit áp-, plural āpas) is the Vedic Sanskrit word for water and, in Hindu religious tradition, the personified deification of the waters as a group of female deities celebrated in the Rigveda and Atharvaveda.

aliases.name: Āpaḥ
aliases.meaning: Vocative/nominative plural form of the deified waters

aliases.name: Apām Napāt
aliases.meaning: 'Offspring of the waters' — closely related Vedic deity

aliases.name: Āp
aliases.meaning: Modern descendant of the Vedic word for water

regions: Sapta-Sindhu (the historical Vedic homeland in the northwest Indian subcontinent)
phenomena.origin: The cult of the Apas belongs to the Vedic and broader Hindu religious tradition of the Indian subcontinent. Cognate water-deity traditions exist in the closely related Indo-Iranian (Avestan) religion.

phenomena.name: Area 51
phenomena.description: Highly classified United States Air Force facility in southern Nevada (officially Homey Airport / Groom Lake), used since 1955 for the development and testing of experimental aircraft. The site is the most prominent location in modern UFO and government-cover-up folklore.

aliases.name: Groom Lake
aliases.meaning: Name of the dry lake bed adjacent to the facility

aliases.name: Paradise Ranch
aliases.meaning: Cover name used in the early CIA U-2 program

aliases.name: Watertown Strip
aliases.meaning: Early USAF designation, after CIA director Allen Dulles's birthplace

phenomena.origin: A single fixed installation in southern Nevada, surrounded by the Nevada Test and Training Range and the Nellis Air Force complex. The area is commonly viewed from public vantage points along Nevada State Route 375, the 'Extraterrestrial Highway', and from the small town of Rachel.

phenomena.name: Argopelter
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter of North American lumberjack folklore — a slender, ape-like beast said to dwell in hollow trees of the conifer woods and to hurl branches and wood splinters at passing humans.

aliases.name: Agropelter
aliases.meaning: Original spelling used by William T. Cox (1910)

aliases.name: Anthrocephalus craniofractens
aliases.meaning: Mock-Latin binomial coined by William T. Cox

phenomena.origin: Said by Cox (1910) to inhabit the coniferous forests of North America from Maine to Oregon, with the densest reporting in the Great Lakes / Upper Midwest lumber region.

phenomena.name: Asanbosam
phenomena.description: A vampire-like, tree-dwelling being of Akan (Ashanti) folklore from southern Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, and Togo, said to have iron teeth and iron hooks for feet, and to attack travellers from above by hanging from branches.
regions: Akan-speaking forest belt of West Africa
phenomena.origin: Found in the folklore of the Akan-speaking peoples (Asante, Fante, Akyem, Akwapim, Akuapem) of southern Ghana, with extensions into Côte d'Ivoire and Togo. Asanbosam beliefs were carried to the Caribbean by enslaved Akan-speakers and were recorded among Maroons in 18th-century Jamaica.

phenomena.name: Asmodeus
phenomena.description: A king of the demons in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions, best known as the antagonist of the Book of Tobit, as a builder-figure in Talmudic legends of King Solomon, and as the goetic king Asmoday of the Lesser Key of Solomon.

aliases.name: Asmodaios
aliases.meaning: Form used in the Septuagint Book of Tobit

aliases.name: Ashmedai
aliases.meaning: Talmudic form, king of the demons

aliases.name: Asmoday
aliases.meaning: Form used in the Lesser Key of Solomon (Ars Goetia, no. 32)

aliases.name: Sakhr
aliases.meaning: 'Rock'; demon imprisoned in stone in Islamic legend

regions: Christian Europe (medieval and early-modern grimoiric tradition)
phenomena.origin: A textual phenomenon distributed across the literatures of the Abrahamic world: the Hebrew Bible deuterocanon, Talmud and midrash, Christian demonology, Islamic Quranic commentary and the Arabian Nights, and Western occult grimoires. Veneration / invocation occurs only in marginal occult or magical contexts.

phenomena.name: Astaroth
phenomena.description: A Great Duke of Hell in Christian demonology, derived by demonisation from the Phoenician goddess Astarte / biblical Ashtoreth. Best known as Astaroth, ranked 29th in the Ars Goetia of the Lesser Key of Solomon, where he commands forty legions.

aliases.name: Ashtaroth
aliases.meaning: Plural of the Hebrew form of the goddess name; biblical Hebrew form

aliases.name: Ashtoreth
aliases.meaning: Singular biblical Hebrew form, used as a proper name in the Hebrew Bible

aliases.name: Astarte
aliases.meaning: Underlying ancient Near Eastern goddess from whom the demon name derives

regions: Christian Europe (medieval and early-modern grimoiric tradition)
phenomena.origin: A textual phenomenon of Christian demonology and Western ceremonial magic, with antecedents in the ancient Near Eastern goddess Astarte and the biblical polemic against her cult.

phenomena.name: Aswang
phenomena.description: The aswang is an umbrella term for a complex of shape-shifting evil creatures in Filipino folklore — among the most feared supernatural beings in the Philippines — that live as ordinary humans by day and become predatory monsters by night.

aliases.name: Manananggal
aliases.meaning: That which separates itself — refers to the self-segmenting viscera-sucker variant

aliases.name: Tik-Tik
aliases.meaning: Named for the ticking sound the creature makes; sound grows louder when the creature is far away and softer when close

aliases.name: Wak-Wak
aliases.meaning: Named for a bird-like cry; a variant that appears as a bird at night

aliases.name: Sigbin
aliases.meaning: A nocturnal creature variant said to walk backward

aliases.name: Asuang
aliases.meaning: Variant spelling and regional pronunciation; connected to the evil god Asuang in Bicol origin stories

phenomena.origin: Aswang belief is widespread across the Philippine archipelago, with the highest concentration of tradition in the Visayas region, particularly the province of Capiz in Panay Island (historically called the 'aswang capital'). Variants are also prominent in southern Luzon and parts of Mindanao.

phenomena.name: Atmospheric Beasts
phenomena.description: Atmospheric beasts are hypothetical organisms proposed to inhabit Earth's upper atmosphere permanently, never landing, drifting or flying in air currents — an idea rooted in the writings of Charles Fort and systematized by zoologist Ivan T. Sanderson as an alternative explanation for some UFO reports.

aliases.name: Sky Beasts
aliases.meaning: Alternative term for atmospheric organisms living in the upper atmosphere

aliases.name: Sky Critters
aliases.meaning: Term used by Trevor James Constable for amoeba-like aerial organisms he claimed to photograph

aliases.name: Cloud Beasts
aliases.meaning: Informal term for proposed atmospheric lifeforms resembling drifting cloud formations

aliases.name: Space Critters
aliases.meaning: Broader term encompassing atmospheric or interplanetary proposed lifeforms

aliases.name: Aerial Organisms
aliases.meaning: Neutral scientific-style term for the hypothetical creatures

phenomena.origin: The hypothesis proposes a global atmospheric distribution, with no specific geographic restriction. Reported sightings associated with atmospheric beasts come from multiple continents.

phenomena.name: Aurora Phenomena (Northern and Southern Lights Folklore)
phenomena.description: Aurora phenomena — the Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights) and Aurora Australis (Southern Lights) — are natural light displays in Earth's upper atmosphere caused by charged solar particles interacting with the magnetosphere, and have inspired rich and varied supernatural traditions across polar and sub-polar cultures worldwide.

aliases.name: Aurora Borealis
aliases.meaning: Northern dawn — from Aurora (Roman goddess of dawn) and Boreas (Greek north wind)

aliases.name: Aurora Australis
aliases.meaning: Southern dawn — from Aurora and Auster (Latin south wind)

aliases.name: Guovssahas
aliases.meaning: The light you can hear — reflects Sami belief that the aurora makes a rustling sound

aliases.name: Revontulet
aliases.meaning: Fox fires — from the legend of a cosmic fox running across the sky, its tail brushing sparks

aliases.name: Bifrost
aliases.meaning: Trembling or shimmering road — the bridge connecting the world of the living to Asgard (sometimes identified with the aurora in Norse tradition)

phenomena.origin: Aurora borealis occurs in a ring around the Arctic (auroral oval), centered on the geomagnetic pole. During strong geomagnetic storms it can be seen as far south as the northern United States, central Europe, and occasionally further. Aurora australis similarly occurs around the Antarctic. Both appear year-round but require darkness and clear skies to be visible.

phenomena.name: Automatic Writing
phenomena.description: Automatic writing is the practice of writing without conscious volition, attributed by practitioners to spirit communication, the subconscious mind, or psychic faculties — and explained by scientists through the ideomotor phenomenon of unconscious muscular movement.

aliases.name: Psychography
aliases.meaning: Writing produced by psychic means — from Greek psyche (soul/mind) + graphia (writing)

aliases.name: Trance Writing
aliases.meaning: Writing produced while in a dissociative or trance state

aliases.name: Fuji
aliases.meaning: Planchette writing — Chinese spirit writing tradition dating to the Song dynasty

aliases.name: Spirit Writing
aliases.meaning: Writing attributed to spirit communication, used especially in the Spiritualist tradition

phenomena.origin: Automatic writing has been documented across multiple cultures and continents, with significant traditions in China (fuji/planchette writing), 16th-century European occultism, 19th-century Anglo-American Spiritualism, Brazilian Spiritism (kardecismo), and early 20th-century Surrealism.

phenomena.name: Axehandle Hound
phenomena.description: The Axehandle Hound is a creature from the North American lumberjack tall-tale tradition — the 'fearsome critters' — described as a dog whose head is shaped like an axe blade and whose body resembles an axe handle, said to sneak into logging camps at night to eat wooden axe handles.
phenomena.origin: The Axehandle Hound legend is associated with the logging camps of Wisconsin and Minnesota, the heart of the Great Lakes timber industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Fearsome critter tales spread across North America's logging territories as workers traveled between camps.

phenomena.name: Azazel
phenomena.description: A figure that appears in Leviticus 16 as the destination of the Yom Kippur scapegoat and develops, in Second Temple Jewish literature (especially the Book of Enoch and the Apocalypse of Abraham), into a chief fallen angel who teaches forbidden knowledge to humanity.

aliases.name: ʿAzāʾzēl
aliases.meaning: Hebrew name עֲזָאזֵל; meaning debated (possibly 'rugged cliff', 'the goat that goes away', or proper name of a demon)

aliases.name: Asael
aliases.meaning: Variant spelling used in some manuscripts of the Book of Enoch

phenomena.origin: Azazel is a textual / theological figure rather than a geographically reported entity. The relevant literary traditions originate in the ancient Near East (the Levant and Mesopotamia), especially in Second Temple Judaism; the figure is then transmitted through Jewish, Christian, and Islamic literatures across the wider Mediterranean and Middle East, and into modern Western occultism.

phenomena.name: Baba Yaga
phenomena.description: Baba Yaga is an ambiguous supernatural old woman of Slavic — especially East Slavic — folklore who lives in a forest hut on chicken legs, flies in a wooden mortar steered by a pestle, and acts by turns as villain, donor, and threshold-guardian in fairy tales.

aliases.name: Baba Yaga Bony Leg (Baba Yaga Kostyanaya Noga)

phenomena.origin: Pan-Slavic folkloric figure. Most densely attested in East Slavic (Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian) fairy tales; cognate figures (Ježibaba, Baba Jaga, Baba Roga) appear across West and South Slavic regions.

phenomena.name: The Backrooms
phenomena.description: An internet-born horror concept describing an endless extradimensional maze of empty yellow-walled office space, reached by 'no-clipping' out of reality. Originated as a single anonymous 4chan /x/ post on 12 May 2019 and grew into a sprawling collaborative fictional universe.

aliases.name: Level 0
aliases.meaning: Original / canonical 'first' Backrooms level — yellow-walled empty office space

aliases.name: Noclip realm
aliases.meaning: Internet jargon: a place reached by 'no-clipping out of reality'

aliases.name: The Liminal Space
aliases.region: Online community usage — overlapping with the broader 'liminal spaces' aesthetic

regions: Anglophone internet; English-language imageboard and wiki communities
phenomena.origin: The Backrooms is a digital-era folkloric phenomenon distributed over the global Anglophone internet — primarily through 4chan, Reddit, YouTube, dedicated wikis (backrooms.wikidot.com, backrooms-wiki.fandom.com), and TikTok.

phenomena.name: Bai Ze
phenomena.description: Bai Ze is a wise, white, speaking quadruped of Chinese (and later Japanese) mythology that, according to legend, instructed the Yellow Emperor in the names and natures of all 11,520 supernatural beings — knowledge later reproduced in the lost Bai Ze Tu (Diagram of Bai Ze) and used as a protective talisman.
phenomena.origin: Originating in Chinese mythology and transmitted across the Sinosphere — China, Japan (as Hakutaku), Korea (as Baekttaek), and Vietnam (as Bạch Trạch).

phenomena.name: Bake-kujira
phenomena.description: A yōkai of Japanese coastal folklore most strongly associated with the Shimane Peninsula in former Izumo Province: a colossal, fleshless whale skeleton that surfaces from the sea on rainy nights surrounded by strange birds and fish, and brings curses, fire, and pestilence upon the whaling villages it visits.
regions: former whaling villages of western Japan
phenomena.origin: Strongly associated with the Shimane Peninsula and Oki Islands of former Izumo Province (modern Shimane Prefecture), Japan. Modern depictions, popularised through Mizuki Shigeru's manga, have spread the figure into nation-wide and global popular culture.

phenomena.name: Bakeneko
phenomena.description: A class of yōkai in Japanese folklore: a domestic cat that has developed supernatural powers — shape-shifting, human speech, control of the dead — usually after living to a great age, growing very large, or possessing a long tail. Distinct from but closely related to the two-tailed nekomata.

aliases.name: Kaibyō
aliases.meaning: Generic term for supernatural cats including bakeneko and nekomata

aliases.name: Nabeshima no bakeneko
aliases.meaning: 'The Bakeneko of Nabeshima' — most famous Edo-period bakeneko story

phenomena.origin: Pan-Japanese folklore figure; locally inflected by regional traditions, with the most famous narrative cluster centred on Saga (former Hizen Province), home of the Nabeshima bakeneko tradition.

phenomena.name: Baku
phenomena.description: A composite chimera-like creature originating in Chinese mythology (mò 貘) and adopted into Japanese folklore (baku 獏) by the Muromachi period, traditionally invoked to consume nightmares and protect sleepers. The same Sino-Japanese word now also denotes the tapir.

aliases.name: 獏 / 貘
aliases.meaning: Mythological dream-eating creature; also the modern word for 'tapir'

aliases.name: Mò
aliases.meaning: Original Chinese name of the creature

aliases.name: Dream-eater
aliases.meaning: Common Anglophone gloss for the creature

phenomena.origin: Originating in Chinese mythological tradition (mò 貘) and adopted into Japanese folklore by the Muromachi period; later transmitted across the Sinosphere and globally via popular culture.

phenomena.name: Ball Lightning
phenomena.description: An unexplained atmospheric electrical phenomenon described as a luminous, typically spherical object ranging from a few centimetres to over a metre across, usually associated with thunderstorms and lasting from a fraction of a second to over a minute.
phenomena.origin: Ball lightning has been reported globally, with high concentrations of reports in Europe, Russia, North America, and East Asia. Reports are not strongly geographically constrained but track regions with frequent thunderstorm activity and engaged scientific reporting cultures.

phenomena.name: Banaspati
phenomena.description: A Javanese (and broader Indonesian) supernatural being most commonly described as a hovering ball of phosphorescent flame appearing near graveyards, old trees, and lonely roads at night. The name derives from the Sanskrit Vanaspati, 'Lord of the Forest'.

aliases.name: Vanaspati
aliases.meaning: 'Lord of the forest', literally 'one whose lord is the forest' — Vedic term for a great tree

phenomena.origin: Most strongly attested in Java, with cognate traditions in Bali, Madura, and parts of Sumatra. The architectural Banaspati Raja face is found on Hindu-Buddhist temples across Java, with related Kala-faces across Bali and the wider Southeast Asian Hindu-Buddhist culture sphere.

phenomena.name: Bannik
phenomena.description: A male tutelary spirit of the Russian and East Slavic bathhouse (banya): unpredictable, sometimes helpful and sometimes deadly, who must be propitiated by ritual hospitality. Appears as a small, naked old man covered in soot and birch leaves.

aliases.name: Ба́нник
aliases.meaning: 'The one of the bathhouse', from banya (баня)

phenomena.origin: Documented across the Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian peasant cultural area, with cognate bath-spirit traditions in West Slavic and Baltic regions.

phenomena.name: Banshee
phenomena.description: A female supernatural figure of Irish folklore — the bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound' — whose mourning cry, the keen, foretells the death of a member of certain Irish families.

aliases.name: Bean nighe
aliases.meaning: 'Washerwoman' — Scottish counterpart, a death-omen washing grave-clothes at a ford

aliases.name: Badhbh chaointe
aliases.meaning: 'Keening crow / hag' — variant or related figure

phenomena.origin: Native to Ireland; cognate figures across the Celtic-speaking world (Scotland, Wales, Isle of Man). With the Irish diaspora the banshee tradition has been carried to North America, Australia, and other Anglophone regions.

phenomena.name: Basilisco Chilote
phenomena.description: The Basilisco Chilote is a creature from Chilote mythology of the Chiloé Archipelago in southern Chile — a rooster-serpent hybrid born from an egg laid by an old rooster, which takes up residence beneath a house and slowly drains the life of its inhabitants.

aliases.name: Athrathrao
aliases.meaning: The infant form of the Basilisco Chilote — a small, fuzzy creature hatched from the rooster's egg, before it develops its full serpentine body

aliases.name: El Basilisco
aliases.meaning: The basilisk — the Chilote name combining the European basilisk with local mythological elements

phenomena.origin: The Basilisco Chilote legend is specific to the Chiloé Archipelago in the Los Lagos region of southern Chile. It is embedded in Chilote culture, which developed in relative isolation from the mainland during the colonial period, producing a distinctive mythology that blends Mapuche (Huilliche and Mapuche) indigenous traditions with Spanish Catholic folk belief.

phenomena.name: Basilisk
phenomena.description: A legendary reptile of classical and medieval European tradition, often called the king of serpents, with a lethal gaze, lethal breath, or both. Originally described by Pliny the Elder as a small Cyrenaican snake; later conflated with the cockatrice.

aliases.name: Cockatrice
aliases.meaning: Conflated with the basilisk in late medieval and early modern usage

phenomena.origin: Originally located by Greco-Roman authors in Cyrenaica (modern eastern Libya) and the deserts of North Africa. Medieval European folklore relocated the creature to wells, cellars, and ruins across Europe, with notable later legends in Poland (Warsaw) and Lithuania (Vilnius).

phenomena.name: Basket Woman
phenomena.description: A giant, child-stealing ogress of Pacific Northwest Coast Indigenous folklore, said to carry off careless or disobedient children in a large pack basket on her back. Best known by the Kwakwaka'wakw name Dzunukwa.
phenomena.origin: Coastal and forested regions of the Pacific Northwest, from southeastern Alaska through coastal British Columbia and Washington into Oregon and northern California, in the territories of Northwest Coast nations.

phenomena.name: Batsquatch
phenomena.description: A winged, ape-like cryptid said to inhabit the area around Mount St. Helens and adjacent forests of western Washington. Best known from a 1994 sighting by Brian Canfield in Pierce County.
phenomena.origin: Reports center on the southern Cascades of Washington State, particularly around Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier in Pierce, Skamania, and Lewis counties.

phenomena.name: Batutut
phenomena.description: A reported hominid cryptid of the forests of Vietnam, Laos and adjacent regions, described as a hairy bipedal 'wild man'. Most prominently associated with the Vu Quang region and with Vietnam War-era 'rock ape' encounters.

aliases.name: Rock Ape
aliases.language: English (US military slang, Vietnam War era)

phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the Annamite Range (Trường Sơn) along the Vietnam–Laos border, and in adjacent forested regions of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.

phenomena.name: Beast of Bray Road
phenomena.description: A wolf-like, sometimes-bipedal cryptid reported near Elkhorn, Walworth County, Wisconsin, beginning in the late 1980s. Investigated and popularized by reporter Linda Godfrey, who later argued it is part of a wider 'manwolf' or 'dogman' phenomenon across the Midwest.
phenomena.origin: Reports center on rural Walworth County, Wisconsin (the Elkhorn / Lake Geneva area), with related 'manwolf' or 'dogman' reports across Wisconsin and the broader Upper Midwest.

phenomena.name: Beast of Gévaudan
phenomena.description: An animal or animals that killed roughly 100 people, mostly women and children, in the former French province of Gévaudan between 1764 and 1767. The historical case generated nationwide panic, royal hunts, and centuries of debate over its zoological identity.
phenomena.origin: Former French province of Gévaudan in the Margeride Mountains of south-central France, corresponding mainly to the modern department of Lozère and parts of Haute-Loire.

phenomena.name: Beelzebub
phenomena.description: A major demon in Jewish, Christian and Islamic demonology, originating from the Philistine deity Baʿal Zəvuv ('lord of the flies') of Ekron in the Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 1) and identified in the Synoptic Gospels as 'prince of demons'. Often counted among the seven princes of Hell.
phenomena.origin: Originating in the Philistine cult of Ekron in the southern Levant. Subsequently a figure of Jewish, Christian, and Islamic demonology across the Christian and Muslim worlds.

phenomena.name: Belial
phenomena.description: A major figure of evil in Jewish, Christian and Western occult tradition. Originally a Hebrew Bible noun meaning 'worthlessness' or 'wickedness'; personified in Second Temple literature, especially the Dead Sea Scrolls, as the Angel of Darkness. Later named one of the four crown princes of Hell.
phenomena.origin: Originating in the Hebrew Bible and the Second Temple Jewish literature of the southern Levant, especially the Qumran Dead Sea Scrolls. Subsequently a figure of Christian theology and Western esoteric tradition.

phenomena.name: Belphegor
phenomena.description: A demon in Christian demonology, derived from the Moabite god Baal-Peor of the Hebrew Bible. In Peter Binsfeld's 1589 classification he is the prince of sloth, and one of the seven princes of Hell.
phenomena.origin: Originating in the Moabite cult of Baal-Peor in the Hebrew Bible. Developed as a named demon in medieval and early modern Christian demonology, especially in Latin, French, and Italian sources.

phenomena.name: BEN Drowned
phenomena.description: A multimedia online horror narrative and alternate reality game by Alexander D. Hall ('Jadusable') begun on 4chan's /x/ board on 7 September 2010, framed as a haunted Nintendo 64 cartridge of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask possessed by an entity called BEN.
phenomena.origin: Internet-native phenomenon; primarily distributed via 4chan's /x/ board, YouTube, and Jadusable's hosted website. Audience is global English-speaking internet users.

phenomena.name: Bennington Triangle
phenomena.description: The Bennington Triangle is a term coined by author Joseph A. Citro for an area of southwestern Vermont, centered on Glastenbury Mountain, where five people disappeared under unexplained circumstances between 1945 and 1950.

aliases.name: Vermont's Vanishing Zone
aliases.meaning: Popular press designation for the cluster of disappearances in the Glastenbury Mountain area

phenomena.origin: The Bennington Triangle centers on Glastenbury Mountain in southwestern Vermont, encompassing parts of the towns of Bennington, Woodford, Shaftsbury, and Somerset.

phenomena.name: Berchta
phenomena.description: Berchta (also Perchta) is an Alpine Germanic supernatural figure associated with the Twelve Days of Christmas and Epiphany, manifesting in dual form as a beautiful white-robed woman or a haggard old crone, rewarding industrious households and punishing the idle with gruesome evisceration.

aliases.name: Perchta
aliases.meaning: The bright one / the bearer — from Old High German 'beraht' (bright, shining)

aliases.name: Frau Faste
aliases.meaning: Lady Fasting — connected to the Feast of Epiphany and Shrovetide

aliases.name: Pehta
aliases.meaning: Slovenian name for the same figure

aliases.name: Berchtentag
aliases.meaning: Berchta's Day — the feast of Epiphany (January 6), on which Perchta/Berchta was particularly active

phenomena.origin: Berchta tradition is concentrated in the Alpine Germanic cultural zone: southern Bavaria, Austria (especially Tyrol, Salzburg, Carinthia), Switzerland, and Slovenia. The figure is absent or much diminished in northern Germany.

phenomena.name: Bermuda Triangle
phenomena.description: A loosely defined region in the western North Atlantic Ocean, roughly bounded by Miami, Bermuda, and San Juan, where ships and aircraft are popularly said to have disappeared under mysterious circumstances.

aliases.name: Hurricane Alley
aliases.meaning: Maritime nickname for the same general area

aliases.name: Limbo of the Lost
aliases.meaning: Title of John Wallace Spencer's 1969 book on the area

phenomena.origin: Western North Atlantic Ocean, generally bounded by southern Florida, the island of Bermuda, and Puerto Rico, including the Florida Strait, the Bahamas, and the open Atlantic out to roughly 65°W.

phenomena.name: Berserker
phenomena.description: Old Norse warriors said to fight in a trance-like fury (berserkergang), sometimes ascribed bear-like or wolf-like ferocity. Documented in skaldic poetry and the sagas, and outlawed in early-medieval Scandinavia.
phenomena.origin: Documented across the Viking-Age Norse world: Norway, Iceland, Sweden, Denmark, and the wider areas of Norse settlement and raiding (British Isles, Faroes, North Atlantic).

phenomena.name: Bessie
phenomena.description: A serpentine lake-monster cryptid reported in Lake Erie since the late 18th century, most often described as a 9–12 m grey snake-like creature. Reports cluster along the south shore of the lake, earning the nickname 'South Bay Bessie'.
phenomena.origin: Reports come from across Lake Erie, with the densest cluster on the southern shore in Ohio (Sandusky Bay, Kelleys Island, Put-in-Bay, the Lake Erie Islands) and the Ontario shore near Fort Erie.

phenomena.name: Betobeto-san
phenomena.description: An invisible Japanese yōkai known only by its sound: the patter of straight-following geta (wooden sandal) footsteps that walks behind people on lonely night roads. Harmless, and easily dismissed by stepping aside and politely inviting it to pass.

aliases.name: べとべとさん
aliases.meaning: 'Mr. Sticky-footsteps' — onomatopoeic for the sound of sandals on a road

phenomena.origin: Reports localised to rural Japan, particularly Uda-gun in Nara Prefecture and parts of Shizuoka Prefecture; related Bishakutsu reports in Fukui Prefecture.

phenomena.name: Bhoot
phenomena.description: A bhoot is the restless ghost of a deceased person in South Asian (Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Bengali, Pakistani, Bangladeshi) folklore — typically someone who died violently, prematurely, or without proper funeral rites and so cannot pass to the afterlife.

aliases.name: भूत (bhūta)
aliases.meaning: 'that which has been'; can mean spirit, element, or ghost

aliases.name: churel / chudail
aliases.meaning: Female bhoot of a woman who died in childbirth, with reversed feet

aliases.name: pret
aliases.meaning: Hungry ghost; specific class of bhoot

phenomena.origin: Pan-South Asian: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and the South Asian diaspora (Caribbean, East Africa, UK, North America). Term and beliefs cross Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and Christian South Asian communities.

phenomena.name: Bigfoot
phenomena.description: A large, hairy, bipedal humanoid creature reported throughout North America, particularly in the Pacific Northwest. One of the most extensively reported and culturally entrenched cryptids, with thousands of eyewitness accounts but no specimen accepted by mainstream science.

aliases.name: Skunk Ape
aliases.region: Florida and the Southeastern United States

phenomena.origin: Reports span the contiguous United States, Alaska, and Canada. The densest, most studied clusters are in the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest (northern California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia). Secondary clusters occur in the Ohio River Valley, Appalachia, the Florida Everglades, and the Boreal forests of central Canada.

phenomena.name: Billdad
phenomena.description: A small, kangaroo-legged, hawk-billed amphibious creature of North American lumberjack folklore, said to live only at Boundary Pond in northwestern Maine and to fish by leaping over surface fish and stunning them with a tail-slap.

aliases.name: Saltipiscator falcorostratus
aliases.meaning: 'Leaping fisher with the falcon's beak' — humorous binomial in W. T. Cox (1910)

phenomena.origin: Localised exclusively to Boundary Pond in northwestern Maine, on the Canadian border, per Cox (1910).

phenomena.name: Bilocation
phenomena.description: The alleged psychic or miraculous ability to be — or to appear to be — physically present in two distinct places at the same time. Reported in Catholic hagiography, Hindu and Buddhist siddhi literature, and parapsychology.
phenomena.origin: Globally distributed in religious and folkloric tradition: Catholic Europe and Latin America (Marian apparitions, saintly bilocations), Hindu and Buddhist Asia (yogic siddhis), Norse and Finnish Europe (vardøger, etiäinen), and modern parapsychology.

phenomena.name: Black Dog
phenomena.description: A spectral or phantom black hound of British and Irish folklore, often interpreted as a death-omen or guardian, appearing on lonely roads, churchyards, and bridges throughout the British Isles.

aliases.name: Gurt Dog
aliases.meaning: Protective rather than malevolent black dog

phenomena.origin: Throughout the British Isles, with regionally distinctive names and personalities; closely related figures appear in continental Europe (German Höllenhund, Scandinavian Garmr) and in the African and Caribbean diaspora (Rolling Calf, Cadejo).

phenomena.name: Black-Eyed Children
phenomena.description: A late-1990s internet-born paranormal legend describing encounters with apparently human children or teenagers whose eyes are entirely black, who appear unannounced at doors or vehicles, and who request entry in an unsettlingly insistent way.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrated in the United States (particularly Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and the Midwest), with later international reports in the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere as the legend circulated online.

phenomena.name: Black Knight Satellite
phenomena.description: The Black Knight Satellite is a conspiracy theory alleging that a 13,000-year-old extraterrestrial spacecraft orbits Earth in a polar orbit, with NASA concealing its existence — a narrative assembled by conflating multiple entirely unrelated and separately debunked events spanning 1899 to 1998.

aliases.name: The Black Knight
aliases.meaning: Colloquial short-form name for the alleged extraterrestrial satellite

phenomena.origin: The alleged object is described as being in low Earth polar orbit — a global orbit visible from both hemispheres.

phenomena.name: Black Shuck
phenomena.description: Black Shuck is a spectral black dog from East Anglian folklore, associated with the coastlines and country roads of Norfolk, Suffolk, and neighboring counties, traditionally regarded as a death omen whose sighting presages death within a year.

aliases.name: Old Shuck
aliases.meaning: A familiar/diminutive form; 'Old' as a respectful or fearful intensifier

aliases.name: Shuck
aliases.meaning: Short form; from Old English 'scucca' (devil, fiend)

aliases.name: The Galleytrot
aliases.meaning: A variant black dog of Suffolk tradition

aliases.name: The Hateful Thing
aliases.meaning: Local Norfolk designation for the spectral dog

aliases.name: The Shug Monkey
aliases.meaning: A Cambridgeshire variant — sometimes described as dog-like, sometimes as simian

phenomena.origin: Black Shuck is associated primarily with the East Anglian counties of Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire, and Essex. Related black dog traditions exist across the British Isles, and the phenomenon has been documented from the Highlands to the West Country, but Black Shuck is specifically the East Anglian form.

phenomena.name: Bogeyman
phenomena.description: The Bogeyman is a universal folkloric figure found in virtually every human culture — a deliberately vague, formless monster invoked by caregivers to frighten children into obedience, with its shapelessness allowing each child's imagination to supply the most personally terrifying details.

aliases.name: Bogey
aliases.meaning: Shortened form; general term for a frightening spirit or monster

aliases.name: Bogle
aliases.meaning: Scots form; a phantom or goblin

aliases.name: El Coco
aliases.meaning: The coconut-head monster; used in Spanish lullabies to threaten children who will not sleep

aliases.name: El Cucuy
aliases.meaning: Latin American variant of El Coco; a monster that takes disobedient children

aliases.name: Babau
aliases.meaning: A tall man in a black coat who takes misbehaving children

aliases.name: Butzemann
aliases.meaning: A frightening figure used to discipline children

aliases.name: Sack Man
aliases.meaning: A figure who carries children away in a sack; spreads through Spanish and Portuguese colonization

aliases.name: Madar-i-Al
aliases.meaning: A nocturnal hag figure used to frighten children

aliases.name: Ong ke
aliases.meaning: A creature described with multiple jaws and eyes, used to frighten children

phenomena.origin: The Bogeyman concept is genuinely global — documented on every inhabited continent, in cultures with no historical contact. This universality makes it one of the most widely distributed folkloric entities in human culture.

phenomena.name: Bohemian Grove
phenomena.description: Bohemian Grove is a 2,700-acre (1,100 ha) campground near Monte Rio, California, owned by the private Bohemian Club, which hosts an annual two-week summer encampment attended by political, business, and cultural elites and is the focus of long-running conspiracy theories.

aliases.name: Bohemian Club Encampment
aliases.meaning: Annual two-week summer gathering of the Bohemian Club

phenomena.origin: A single fixed property near Monte Rio, Sonoma County, California, in the redwood country of the Russian River.

phenomena.name: Boto Cor-de-Rosa
phenomena.description: In Amazonian folklore, the Boto Cor-de-Rosa — the pink Amazon river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis) — is said to transform at night into a handsome man who seduces women at riverside parties before returning to the water at dawn.
phenomena.origin: The folklore tracks the natural range of Inia geoffrensis: the Amazon and Orinoco basins of South America. The pink-river-dolphin shapeshifter is most strongly associated with the Brazilian Amazon, with parallel encantado traditions in the Peruvian, Colombian, Bolivian, and Venezuelan Amazon.

phenomena.name: Bridgewater Triangle
phenomena.description: The Bridgewater Triangle is a roughly 200-square-mile (520 km²) area of southeastern Massachusetts, designated by cryptozoologist Loren Coleman in the 1970s, where unusually frequent reports of UFOs, cryptids, ghost lights, and other paranormal phenomena cluster around the Hockomock Swamp.

aliases.name: Hockomock area
aliases.meaning: Refers to the swamp at the heart of the triangle

phenomena.origin: An approximately 200-square-mile region of southeastern Massachusetts in Bristol, Plymouth, and Norfolk counties, including the towns of Abington, Bridgewater, East Bridgewater, West Bridgewater, Brockton, Easton, Freetown, Mansfield, Norton, Raynham, Rehoboth, Seekonk, and Taunton (per Coleman's mapping).

phenomena.name: Brown Mountain Lights
phenomena.description: The Brown Mountain Lights are recurrent unexplained or partially-explained light phenomena observed from overlooks facing Brown Mountain in Burke County, North Carolina, with documented observations dating to the early 20th century and a Cherokee oral tradition that may predate them.
phenomena.origin: A localized ridge phenomenon in Burke County, western North Carolina, observed from overlooks in the Pisgah National Forest and along the Blue Ridge Parkway.

phenomena.name: Brownie
phenomena.description: The brownie is a household tutelary spirit of Scottish and Northern English folklore — typically small, brown-skinned, hairy, and ragged — that performs farm and household labour at night in exchange for small offerings of cream, milk, or porridge, and that famously departs forever if offered new clothes or direct payment.
phenomena.origin: Native to Lowland and Highland Scotland and to Northern England, with regional cognates throughout the British Isles. The figure travelled with Scots and English emigrants to Ulster and to North America.

phenomena.name: Bulgae
phenomena.description: The Bulgae (불개, 'fire dogs') are mythological hounds in Korean folklore sent by the king of the dark realm Gamangnara to steal the sun and the moon, whose biting attempts explain solar and lunar eclipses.
phenomena.origin: The Bulgae legend is a Korean mythological tradition known throughout the Korean peninsula and the Korean diaspora.

phenomena.name: The Bunny Man
phenomena.description: The Bunny Man is an American urban legend from Fairfax County, Virginia, rooted in two confirmed October 1970 incidents in which a man wearing a white rabbit costume threatened people with a hatchet and axe; over decades the legend has grown to centre on the Colchester Road railroad overpass ('Bunny Man Bridge') near Clifton.
phenomena.origin: Localised to Fairfax County, Virginia, with the legend's geographic centre at the Colchester Road overpass near Clifton.

phenomena.name: Bunyip
phenomena.description: The Bunyip is a water-dwelling creature of Australian Aboriginal tradition, said to inhabit waterholes, billabongs, swamps, and creeks; descriptions vary widely between regions, and the figure has played a major role in colonial-era Australian natural-history controversies.

aliases.name: Mulyawonk
aliases.meaning: Water spirit who punishes those who take too much fish

phenomena.origin: Bunyip traditions extend across most of inhabited Australia, with strongest documentation in the Murray–Darling Basin (Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia), Tasmania, and parts of Queensland.

phenomena.name: Al-Burāq
phenomena.description: Al-Burāq is the celestial steed of Islamic tradition that, according to Hadith narrations, carried the Prophet Muhammad on the Isra and Mi'raj — the night journey from the Sacred Mosque in Mecca to the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem and the subsequent ascent through the seven heavens.
phenomena.origin: A single mythological figure of universal scope within Islamic tradition. The narrative geography of the night journey runs from Mecca (al-Masjid al-Haram) to Jerusalem (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) and through the seven heavens.

phenomena.name: Cactus Cat
phenomena.description: The Cactus Cat is a humorous fictional creature of American 'fearsome critters' folklore — a thorn-covered, branched-tailed bobcat-like animal said to slash cacti, drink the fermented sap, and yowl drunkenly through the night canyons of the Southwest.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range covers the deserts of the American Southwest — Arizona, New Mexico, southern Texas — where saguaro and barrel cacti are common.

phenomena.name: Cadborosaurus
phenomena.description: Cadborosaurus, popularly 'Caddy', is a sea-serpent cryptid reported along the Pacific coast from Alaska to California, with the densest cluster of sightings in the inland waters around Vancouver Island, British Columbia, and named after Cadboro Bay near Victoria.

aliases.name: Cadborosaurus willsi
aliases.meaning: Proposed (non-validated) species name applied by Bousfield and LeBlond (1995)

aliases.name: Sisiutl
aliases.meaning: Two-headed sea serpent of Pacific Northwest Coast tradition (a related but distinct figure)

phenomena.origin: The reported range covers the Pacific coast from Alaska to northern California, with the densest cluster of sightings in the inland waters around Vancouver Island, the Strait of Georgia, Puget Sound, and adjacent inlets.

phenomena.name: Caipora
phenomena.description: The Caipora is one of Brazil's most important forest guardian spirits, rooted in Indigenous Tupi-Guarani mythology, who protects wildlife from hunters who violate rules of fair-play and punishes those who disrespect the forest.
phenomena.origin: Found throughout Brazil, with regional variations across the Amazon rainforest, Atlantic Coast, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Minas Gerais, and Ceará. Also present in Argentine and Uruguayan folklore as a fire-breathing ghost variant.

phenomena.name: Candle Cove
phenomena.description: A short horror fiction piece by webcomic author Kris Straub, published in 2009 on the Ichor Falls website. Written in the form of a forum thread in which adults remember a disturbing 1970s children's television program called 'Candle Cove' that turns out never to have existed.
phenomena.origin: An internet phenomenon distributed through the Ichor Falls site, creepypasta wikis, Reddit, YouTube readings, and the Channel Zero television adaptation. The fictional setting is a UHF children's television program in the Huntington–Ashland (West Virginia / Kentucky / Ohio) media market.

phenomena.name: Caoineag
phenomena.description: A female death-portent spirit of the Scottish Highlands, associated particularly with certain clans, who weeps at waterfalls, streams, and lonely places before a death — most famously before the Massacre of Glencoe.

aliases.name: Caointeach
aliases.meaning: regional variant; appears outside the homes of the soon-to-die wearing a green shawl

phenomena.origin: Scottish Highlands and the Hebrides, with strong attestation in Lochaber (Glencoe), Argyll, and Islay.

phenomena.name: Cash–Landrum incident
phenomena.description: A 1980 close-encounter UFO case in southeast Texas in which Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum, and Vickie's seven-year-old grandson Colby reported a diamond-shaped craft emitting flame and heat, escorted by approximately 23 military helicopters. The witnesses subsequently reported severe injuries consistent, in their physicians' view, with radiation exposure.
phenomena.origin: Single-incident case located on FM 1485/2100 between New Caney and Huffman, in Liberty County, Texas, with the encounter terminating near Dayton.

phenomena.name: Ceasg
phenomena.description: A mermaid figure of Scottish Gaelic folklore: the upper body of a woman joined to the tail of a grilse (young salmon). Captured ceasgs are said to grant three wishes in exchange for their freedom.
phenomena.origin: Coastal and riverine Scottish Gàidhealtachd (Highlands and Western Isles).

phenomena.name: Centaur
phenomena.description: A creature of Greek mythology with the upper body of a human and the lower body and legs of a horse. Centaurs inhabited the mountains and forests of Thessaly and feature in some of the foundational stories of Greek myth, including the Centauromachy and the education of heroes by the wise centaur Chiron.

aliases.name: Kéntauros
aliases.meaning: the Greek term, of disputed etymology

phenomena.origin: In Greek myth, centaurs inhabit the mountains of Thessaly (especially Mount Pelion) and the Foloi oak forest of Elis in the western Peloponnese.

phenomena.name: Cerberus
phenomena.description: The multi-headed hound of Greek mythology that guards the gates of Hades, preventing the dead from leaving. Most famously captured by Heracles as his twelfth and final labour.
phenomena.origin: In classical mythology Cerberus is located at the entrance to the Greek underworld; the entrance was traditionally placed at sites such as Cape Tainaron in Laconia and Lake Avernus in Campania.

phenomena.name: Champ
phenomena.description: An aquatic cryptid said to inhabit Lake Champlain on the border of Vermont, New York, and Quebec. Reported as a long-necked, serpentine animal in the loch-monster mould, with several hundred reported sightings since the 19th century.

aliases.name: Onyare'kowa
aliases.region: Iroquois territory; 'great horned serpent' in oral tradition

phenomena.origin: Lake Champlain, a 125-mile-long freshwater lake forming part of the border between Vermont and New York and extending into the Canadian province of Quebec.

phenomena.name: Chaneque
phenomena.description: Small humanoid nature spirits of Mesoamerican (especially Nahua) tradition, regarded as the rightful 'owners' of forests, hills, springs, and other wild places. They guard the land and its animals, and are simultaneously protectors and dangerous tricksters who can lead people astray or steal souls.

aliases.name: Ohuican Chaneque
aliases.meaning: 'those who inhabit dangerous places' / 'owners of the place'

phenomena.origin: Indigenous and rural mestizo communities of central and south-eastern Mexico, with the densest belief in Veracruz, Puebla, Oaxaca, and Tabasco; extension into Mexican diaspora communities.

phenomena.name: Changeling
phenomena.description: A child believed in European folklore to have been substituted by fairies, trolls, or other supernatural beings in place of a stolen human infant. Modern scholarship recognises that the changeling label was historically applied to children with disabilities and developmental conditions, and that 'changeling tests' resulted in real abuse and deaths.
phenomena.origin: Widespread across pre-modern Europe with the strongest documented traditions in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, the Isle of Man, England, Scandinavia (especially Sweden, Norway, Denmark), and German-speaking lands.

phenomena.name: Charlie No-Face
phenomena.description: A western-Pennsylvania urban legend about a faceless or 'green-skinned' figure walking rural roads at night. The legend is rooted in the real life of Raymond Theodore Robinson (1910–1985), severely disfigured by a 1919 electrical accident, who walked the country roads of Beaver County after dark for decades.

aliases.name: Raymond Robinson
aliases.meaning: the historical person whose life inspired the legend

phenomena.origin: Western Pennsylvania, with the legend strongest in Beaver, Butler, and Allegheny counties; Robinson himself lived and walked principally in Beaver County.

phenomena.name: Chemtrails (chemtrail conspiracy theory)
phenomena.description: A conspiracy theory, originating in the late 1990s, claiming that the long-lasting condensation trails (contrails) left by aircraft are in fact 'chemtrails' — chemical or biological agents being deliberately sprayed by governments or other actors for purposes such as population control, weather modification, or covert geoengineering. Atmospheric scientists, public-health agencies, and aviation regulators across many countries have rejected the theory as unsupported.
phenomena.origin: The chemtrail claim is a global Anglophone internet conspiracy theory with strongholds in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and parts of continental Europe.

phenomena.name: Cheollima
phenomena.description: A mythical winged horse of East Asian tradition — Korean cheollima, Chinese qianlima — said to gallop one thousand li in a single day. Long used as a metaphor for exceptional talent in classical Chinese and Korean literature, and adopted in the 20th century as a state symbol in North Korea.
phenomena.origin: Sino-Korean cultural sphere; with strong modern presence in the Korean peninsula, especially North Korea.

phenomena.name: Chimera
phenomena.description: The Chimera is a fire-breathing hybrid monster of Greek mythology, with a lion's body and head, a goat's head rising from its back, and a serpent for a tail. The hero Bellerophon slew it riding the winged horse Pegasus.

aliases.name: Chimaera
aliases.meaning: Latinised form of the Greek name

phenomena.origin: Mythologically located in ancient Lycia in southwestern Anatolia (modern Antalya Province, Turkey). The cultural distribution of the myth covers the entire ancient Greek and Roman world and, through them, all of Western literary tradition.

phenomena.name: Chipekwe
phenomena.description: The Chipekwe is a large, horned, hippo-killing aquatic cryptid reported from the swamps and rivers of Zambia and parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Bemba-language sources describe it as a 'water rhinoceros' with smooth hairless skin and a single white horn.
phenomena.origin: Centred on the wetlands of north-central and northeastern Zambia, particularly Lake Bangweulu and its associated swamps, the Kafue Flats, and the Luapula river system. Reports also extend into adjoining parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and to Lake Tanganyika in some 20th-century retellings.

phenomena.name: Chōchin-obake
phenomena.description: Chōchin-obake is a Japanese yōkai depicted as an old paper lantern (chōchin) that has split open along its bamboo ribs to reveal a single eye, a long protruding tongue, and a wide mouth — a classic example of a tsukumogami, an everyday object brought to life after long use.

aliases.name: Bura-bura
aliases.meaning: literally 'dangle-dangle'; name used by Toriyama Sekien for a hanging lantern yōkai

regions: Edo (modern Tokyo) — primary publishing centre for the imagery
Kyoto and Osaka — kabuki and ukiyo-e production
Nationwide via mass-produced karuta, kusazōshi, and toy prints
phenomena.origin: The chōchin-obake is a creature of the Japanese popular imagination, attested across the Japanese archipelago through printed illustration and stage drama, with no specific regional folk-legend tradition.

phenomena.name: Chullachaqui
phenomena.description: The Chullachaqui (Quechua chulla 'odd / unequal' + chaki 'foot') is a forest spirit of Peruvian and Brazilian Amazonia, depicted as a small humanoid with one mismatched foot — typically one human foot and one animal hoof — who shapeshifts into a familiar person to lead unwary travellers astray.

aliases.name: Curupira
aliases.meaning: Closely related Tupi-Guarani forest spirit, sometimes equated with the Chullachaqui

aliases.name: Shapingo
aliases.meaning: Local variant name in mestizo folklore

phenomena.origin: Western Amazon basin: lowland Peru (especially Loreto, Ucayali, San Martín, and Madre de Dios), eastern Ecuador (Pastaza, Napo), western Brazil (Acre, Amazonas), and the headwaters region of Colombia and Bolivia.

phenomena.name: Chupacabra
phenomena.description: A modern livestock-predator cryptid first widely reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Two distinct forms dominate: an upright, spined, alien-like Puerto Rican type and a hairless, dog-like type reported in Mexico and the southwestern United States.

aliases.name: El Vampiro de Moca
aliases.meaning: 'The vampire of Moca'; 1970s livestock-killing precursor to the modern Chupacabra

phenomena.origin: Reports originated in Puerto Rico in 1995 and within a few years spread across Latin America and into the southwestern and southern United States. Sightings have been reported in Mexico, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Maine, and Russia (rare).

phenomena.name: Ciguapa
phenomena.description: The Ciguapa is a creature of Dominican folklore: a small, beautiful (or in some tellings hideous) woman with smooth, dark or bronze skin, very long flowing hair that covers her body, and feet that point backward, allowing her to leave tracks that mislead anyone who tries to follow her into the mountains.
phenomena.origin: Strongly identified with the Dominican Republic and the wider island of Hispaniola, particularly its mountainous interior. Variants and references occur throughout the Hispanic Caribbean diaspora.

phenomena.name: Clurichaun
phenomena.description: The clurichaun is a solitary fairy of Irish folklore: a small, red-faced, perpetually drunk male sprite who haunts wine cellars, breweries, and pubs, protecting the household's drink if respected and souring it if mistreated.

aliases.name: Cluricaune
aliases.meaning: Variant spelling used by T. Crofton Croker

aliases.name: Naggeneen
aliases.meaning: Pet-name from naigín, 'noggin' (a small drinking measure)

phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the southern half of Ireland — particularly Munster (Cork, Tipperary, Limerick, Waterford) — but regional variants are recorded across Leinster, parts of Ulster, and west into Connacht.

phenomena.name: Cockatrice
phenomena.description: The cockatrice is a legendary medieval European hybrid creature with the head, comb, and wattles of a rooster and the body and tail of a serpent or wyvern, said to kill with its breath, touch, or gaze and hatched from the yolkless egg of a cockerel incubated by a toad or snake.

aliases.name: Calcatrix
aliases.meaning: 'Tracker'; originally the Latin translation of Greek ichneumon

aliases.name: Basiliscus
aliases.meaning: Term for the basilisk often translated as 'cockatrice' in medieval English

aliases.name: Basilisk
aliases.meaning: Closely related and often interchangeable creature in medieval bestiaries

phenomena.origin: A creature of medieval Western and Central European literary and bestiary tradition, with its widest attestation in England, France, the Low Countries, and the Holy Roman Empire. Through colonial-era and modern fantasy literature, the figure has spread to the entire Anglophone world.

phenomena.name: Come-at-a-Body
phenomena.description: The Come-at-a-Body is a fearsome critter of early 20th-century American lumberjack folklore, described by William T. Cox in 1910 as a small, woodchuck-sized animal with soft kitten-like fur that suddenly charges out of the brush at New Hampshire travellers and stops abruptly inches away to startle them.

aliases.name: Apparitio camatabodi
aliases.meaning: Pseudo-scientific binomial supplied by George B. Sudworth in Cox's 1910 book

regions: Maine and Vermont logging country (by extension in later compilations)
phenomena.origin: Strictly localised to the White Mountains of northern New Hampshire in Cox's account, with secondary references in 20th-century compilations covering the wider Northern New England logging country.

phenomena.name: Corpse Candle
phenomena.description: The Corpse Candle (Welsh canwyll corff) is a Welsh death omen: a small, pale, blue or yellow flame seen drifting along country lanes, churchyards, and the route a forthcoming funeral will take, foretelling the death of someone in the household it visits.

aliases.name: Will-o'-the-wisp
aliases.meaning: Generic English term for similar atmospheric ghost lights

aliases.name: Ignis fatuus
aliases.meaning: 'Foolish fire'; learned name for the marsh-light phenomenon

phenomena.origin: Strongly localised to Wales, with secondary occurrences across the Welsh Marches, Cornwall, and parts of Ireland and Scotland; the broader 'death-omen ghost-light' complex extends to most of Northern Europe and to colonial diasporas in the Americas.

phenomena.name: Crawler
phenomena.description: The Crawler (or Pale Crawler) is a 21st-century cryptid of internet folklore: an emaciated, hairless, ghostly-pale humanoid that moves rapidly on all fours with elongated limbs and reverse-bending joints, reported chiefly through anonymous trail-camera photographs, doorbell-camera videos, and YouTube and Reddit testimonies from rural North America.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in the eastern and central United States, particularly forested mountain country (Appalachians, Pennsylvania Wilds, Ozarks), with secondary clusters in rural Canada and isolated Texas and California incidents propagated through viral video. Internet propagation has carried the figure worldwide.

phenomena.name: Crisis Apparition
phenomena.description: A crisis apparition is an apparition of a living person that appears to friends or family at the moment of — or within approximately 12 hours of — that person's death, serious injury, or extreme distress, despite the person being physically distant from the witness.

aliases.name: Veridical apparition
aliases.meaning: An apparition that conveys truthful information about an event at a distance

aliases.name: Death wraith
aliases.meaning: Apparition of a dying person appearing to loved ones

aliases.name: Fetch
aliases.meaning: Double or apparition of a living person, seen at time of crisis or death

phenomena.origin: Crisis apparitions have been reported globally across all cultures and historical periods. Systematic collection has focused heavily on the British Isles and Europe from the 1880s onward, with cases documented in North America, Australia, and other countries.

phenomena.name: Cropsey
phenomena.description: Cropsey is a New York urban legend about a boogeyman figure — originally an escaped mental patient from the abandoned Willowbrook State School — who haunted Staten Island and kidnapped children, later converging with the real crimes of convicted child kidnapper Andre Rand.
phenomena.origin: The Cropsey legend is centered on Staten Island, New York, and is also found in upstate New York summer camp traditions. It is primarily a New York regional legend.

phenomena.name: Crystal Skulls
phenomena.description: Quartz carvings shaped like human skulls long claimed to be pre-Columbian Mesoamerican artifacts. Modern museum analyses have shown the best-known examples are 19th-century European carvings made with rotary tools and abrasives unavailable to ancient craftspeople.

aliases.name: Skull of Doom
aliases.meaning: Sensationalist nickname for the Mitchell-Hedges skull

phenomena.origin: Major specimens are housed in museum and private collections in Europe and North America. Promotional folklore situates their origin in Mesoamerica, but documentary trails trace them to European antiquities markets.

phenomena.name: Cù Sìth
phenomena.description: A large, dark green, shaggy supernatural hound of Scottish Highland folklore, the size of a young bull, said to hunt silently and utter only three baying barks; hearing its third bark before reaching shelter is held to be fatal.
phenomena.origin: Recorded throughout the Scottish Gàidhealtachd, especially the Highlands and Western Isles. Cognate traditions occur across Gaelic Ireland and Wales.

phenomena.name: Curse of the Pharaohs
phenomena.description: The popular belief that those who disturb the tomb of an ancient Egyptian pharaoh, especially Tutankhamun, suffer misfortune or death. The legend coalesced in 1922–1923 around the death of Lord Carnarvon and was sustained by sensational press reporting; statistical study has found no excess mortality.
phenomena.origin: The curse is centred on the Theban necropolis (Valley of the Kings) and on museums holding pharaonic remains, but the legend itself is global through Anglophone press and cinema.

phenomena.name: Curupira
phenomena.description: A forest-protector spirit of Tupi-Guaraní tradition in Brazil and neighbouring countries, depicted as a small, red-haired figure with backward-facing feet that punishes hunters who take more than they need and rewards those who respect the forest.
phenomena.origin: Tupi-Guaraní cultural area: most of Brazil, with strong attestation in the Amazon basin, Atlantic forest, and Cerrado regions; cognate figures in Paraguay and the Guianas.

phenomena.name: Cyclops
phenomena.description: A class of one-eyed giants in Greek mythology. Hesiod's three primordial Cyclopes are divine smiths who forge Zeus' thunderbolts; Homer's Cyclopes are lawless cave-dwelling shepherds, most famously Polyphemus, blinded by Odysseus.
phenomena.origin: Mythologically situated across the Greek world: the island of the Cyclopes in the Odyssey (often identified by ancient and modern commentators with Sicily), the volcanic forges beneath Mount Etna, and the Mycenaean citadels of the Argolid.

phenomena.name: Dames Blanches
phenomena.description: Female fairy beings of French folklore, particularly recorded in Lorraine, Normandy, and the Pyrenees, who haunt liminal places — bridges, fords, ravines, forest paths — and confront travellers with a ritual challenge such as a dance.
phenomena.origin: France, especially Lorraine, Normandy, and the Pyrenees; cognate traditions across the Germanic and Low-Countries area.

phenomena.name: Deer Woman
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting spirit from the traditions of multiple Indigenous nations of North America, appearing as a beautiful woman with deer hooves or a deer's lower body. She enforces social norms — particularly around the treatment of women — and has been embraced as a contemporary symbol in Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women advocacy.
phenomena.origin: Eastern Woodlands and central Plains of North America, with prominent traditions in the territories of nations from the upper Great Lakes to the southeastern United States and the Plains.

phenomena.name: Demons
phenomena.description: A cross-cultural class of supernatural beings, generally malevolent or morally ambivalent, found in nearly every major religious and folkloric tradition. The Christian-Islamic concept of demons as evil spirits or fallen angels developed from older Greek, Hebrew, Mesopotamian, and Zoroastrian categories of intermediate spirits.
phenomena.origin: Demonology is a near-universal feature of human religious systems, with major systematised traditions in West Asia, Europe, North Africa, South and East Asia.

phenomena.name: Denver International Airport Conspiracy Theories
phenomena.description: A cluster of conspiracy theories surrounding Denver International Airport (opened 28 February 1995), including claims of secret underground bunkers, Illuminati or New World Order activity, hidden symbolism in Leo Tanguma's murals, the Blue Mustang sculpture ('Blucifer') by Luis Jiménez, and a dedication capstone inscribed 'New World Airport Commission' (1994).
phenomena.origin: The airport is in Adams County, Colorado, USA. The conspiracy-theory phenomenon itself is global through Internet circulation.

phenomena.name: Div
phenomena.description: A class of demons of Iranian and broader Persianate mythology, descended from the Avestan daēvas demonised under Zoroastrianism. Most famous as the divs of Ferdowsi's Shāhnāmeh — gigantic, horned, monstrous beings, including Div-e Sefid (the White Div) and Akvan Div — who oppose the hero Rostam.

aliases.name: Div-e Sefīd
aliases.meaning: White Div, antagonist of the hero Rostam

phenomena.origin: The Iranian and Persianate cultural sphere, including Iran, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, the Kurdish-speaking areas of Iraq and Turkey, the South Caucasus, and parts of South Asia influenced by Persian literary culture.

phenomena.name: Djinn
phenomena.description: An order of supernatural beings in pre-Islamic Arabian religion and in Islam, created (according to the Quran) from smokeless fire. Jinn possess free will, can be Muslim or non-Muslim, and constitute one of the three created orders alongside humans and angels. Western 'genies' are a literary distortion of the tradition.
phenomena.origin: Belief in jinn is universal across the Islamic world and present in regions of pre-Islamic Arabian religious continuity. The jinn appear in folklore from the Maghreb to Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Dobhar-chú
phenomena.description: The Dobhar-chú is a fearsome Irish cryptid described as a massive otter-like creature approximately 10–15 feet long with a white pelt and a black cross on its back, known for extreme ferocity and territorial aggression toward humans.
phenomena.origin: Found in Irish folklore associated with lakes and rivers throughout Ireland, particularly in the northwest. Most accounts concentrate in County Leitrim. A 2003 sighting report came from Omey Island, Connemara, County Galway.

phenomena.name: Michigan Dogman
phenomena.description: A bipedal, dog-headed humanoid cryptid reported primarily in the northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, popularized by a 1987 radio prank song by disc jockey Steve Cook of WTCM-FM in Traverse City.
phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, particularly around the Manistee River and historically Odawa lands; occasional reports extend into other Great Lakes states.

phenomena.name: Dokkaebi
phenomena.description: Dokkaebi are legendary creatures of Korean folklore, often loosely translated as 'goblins' but distinct from East Asian demons; they arise from the spiritual possession of inanimate objects and are known for mischief, supernatural strength, and the magical club known as the dokkaebi bangmangi.

aliases.name: 도깨비
aliases.meaning: Native Korean term, often loosely translated as 'goblin' or 'ogre'

phenomena.origin: Korean Peninsula, with strong presence across both modern South Korea and North Korea, and within Korean diaspora communities globally.

phenomena.name: Domovoy
phenomena.description: The domovoy is the tutelary household spirit of Slavic folklore — a small old man, often bearded and grey, who lives behind the stove or under the threshold and guards the family, livestock, and prosperity of the home.
phenomena.origin: Across the Slavic world, with the densest tradition in Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus and parallel traditions in Poland, the Czech lands, Slovakia, and the South Slavic regions.

phenomena.name: Doppelgänger
