phenomena.description: The apparitional double of a living person, reported across many cultures and historical periods, sometimes seen by the person themselves and sometimes witnessed by others; modern neuroscience associates some experiences with autoscopy and heautoscopy linked to disturbances of the temporoparietal junction.

aliases.name: Fetch
aliases.meaning: Wraith-like double whose appearance can foretell death

aliases.name: Vardøger
aliases.meaning: Premonitory spirit precursor performing actions before the person

aliases.name: Qarin
aliases.meaning: Spirit double of the same sex and temperament in Islamic tradition

phenomena.origin: Reported worldwide across cultures and historical periods.

phenomena.name: Douen
phenomena.description: In the folklore of Trinidad and Tobago and other parts of the Eastern Caribbean, the douen is the spirit of a child who died before being baptized; depicted as a small, faceless figure with backward-facing feet and a wide straw hat, said to lure other children into the forest.
phenomena.origin: Folklore primarily of Trinidad and Tobago, with the related dwen of Saint Lucia and parallels across the broader Eastern Caribbean.

phenomena.name: Dover Demon
phenomena.description: A small, large-headed humanoid cryptid reportedly seen by three teenage witnesses in Dover, Massachusetts, on the nights of 21–22 April 1977; no further sightings have been recorded.
phenomena.origin: Three reported sightings in the town of Dover, Massachusetts, on Farm Street, Miller Hill Road, and Springdale Avenue, on the nights of 21–22 April 1977.

phenomena.name: Dragon
phenomena.description: A class of large, serpentine or reptilian mythological creatures attested across virtually every culture, ranging from the auspicious water-and-rain dragons of East Asia to the fire-breathing, treasure-hoarding antagonists of European Christian and Norse tradition.

aliases.name: Long / Lóng
aliases.meaning: Chinese long, an auspicious water-and-rain deity

phenomena.origin: Dragon traditions are attested in nearly every culture and on every inhabited continent.

phenomena.name: Draugr
phenomena.description: A corporeal revenant of Old Norse and Icelandic tradition, the draugr is an animated corpse with superhuman strength, magical abilities, and a violent jealousy toward the living, most often encountered as a guardian of treasure in a burial mound or as a re-walking neighbour terrorizing a farmstead.

aliases.name: Haugbúi
aliases.meaning: Mound-dweller — draugr who remains in the burial mound

phenomena.origin: Old Norse and post-Norse Scandinavia: Iceland, Norway, the Faroe Islands, with related traditions in Sweden, Denmark, and the Northern Isles of Britain (Orkney, Shetland).

phenomena.name: Drop Bear
phenomena.description: A wholly fictional Australian creature: an oversized, predatory koala that supposedly drops from eucalyptus trees onto unsuspecting passers-by, used as a long-standing in-joke to prank tourists.

aliases.name: Thylarctos plummetus
aliases.meaning: Pseudo-binomial coined by the Australian Museum for the drop bear

regions: All Australian states and territories (within the joke)
phenomena.origin: Joke localised to Australia, particularly its eucalyptus forests; told primarily to international tourists.

phenomena.name: Drude
phenomena.description: A malevolent nocturnal spirit of Southern German and Austrian folklore, the drude was held to press upon sleepers and cause nightmares; the term later became a generic word for 'witch' and gives its name to the Drudenfuss (pentagram) and Drudenstein (holed-pebble) protective charms.
phenomena.origin: Primarily Southern Germany, Bavaria, Austria, and Tyrol, with parallels in wider Germanic-speaking Europe.

phenomena.name: Duende
phenomena.description: Duendes are small humanoid folkloric beings of Iberian, Latin American, and Filipino tradition, ranging from helpful or mischievous house-sprites to dangerous forest dwellers said to lure children astray; in 1933 Federico García Lorca repurposed the word as an aesthetic concept for the dark vital force of art.
phenomena.origin: Iberian Peninsula, Latin America (especially Mexico, Central America, and Andean countries), the Philippines, and the Mariana Islands; with parallels and overlaps with regional Indigenous traditions.

phenomena.name: Dulce Base
phenomena.description: An alleged secret underground facility beneath Archuleta Mesa near Dulce, New Mexico, said by conspiracy proponents to be a joint US-government / extraterrestrial laboratory. The story originated with the disinformation campaign that the US Air Force Office of Special Investigations directed against Albuquerque businessman Paul Bennewitz from 1980 onwards.
phenomena.origin: Alleged location: Archuleta Mesa, near the town of Dulce in northwestern New Mexico, USA, on the Jicarilla Apache Nation.

phenomena.name: Dullahan
phenomena.description: A headless rider of Irish folklore who appears as a harbinger of death, riding a black horse and carrying his own severed head.

aliases.name: Coiste Bodhar
aliases.meaning: deaf or silent coach (the death coach)

phenomena.origin: Folkloric range across the island of Ireland, with the densest narrative tradition in the southern counties documented by Crofton Croker and the western counties documented by Yeats and later folklorists.

phenomena.name: Dungavenhooter
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter of North American lumberjack folklore: a mouthless, alligator-like swamp creature that pounds its victims to vapor with its tail and inhales them through its enormous nostrils.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range across the swampy lumberwoods of the northeastern United States and the upper Great Lakes, broadly between Maine and Michigan as recorded in Tryon's 1939 catalogue.

phenomena.name: Duppy
phenomena.description: A spirit of the dead in Jamaican and wider Caribbean folklore, of West African (especially Ga and Akan) origin, generally regarded as malevolent and haunting at night.

aliases.name: Rolling Calf
aliases.meaning: specific malevolent duppy in the form of a chained calf

phenomena.origin: Jamaican folklore is the densest locus of duppy tradition; cognate beliefs span the Anglophone Caribbean (Bahamas, Barbados, the Caymans, Belize, Guyana) and the wider Caribbean diaspora in the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada. The tradition has antecedents in the Ga and Akan cosmologies of present-day Ghana.

phenomena.name: Dyatlov Pass Incident
phenomena.description: The 1959 deaths of nine experienced Soviet ski-hikers on the eastern slope of Kholat Syakhl in the northern Urals, long unexplained and now most plausibly attributed to a small delayed slab avalanche.

aliases.name: Death Mountain incident
aliases.meaning: after Kholat Syakhl, glossed locally as 'Dead Mountain'

phenomena.origin: The incident occurred on the eastern shoulder of Kholat Syakhl in the Northern Urals, in what was then Sverdlovsk Oblast (RSFSR, Soviet Union); now in Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russian Federation.

phenomena.name: Each-uisge
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting Celtic water horse of Scottish and Irish folklore, considered the fiercest of all water horses; lures riders into sea lochs and freshwater lochs and devours all but their livers.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range across the Scottish Highlands and Hebrides, with cognates in Ireland (each-uisce / aughisky) and the Isle of Man (cabyll-ushtey).

phenomena.name: Earthquake Lights
phenomena.description: Luminous optical phenomena reported in the sky or near the ground before, during, or shortly after seismic activity, with reports spanning more than a millennium.
phenomena.origin: Global; reported wherever earthquakes occur, with relatively higher report frequency in South America, China, southern Europe (Greece, Italy, France, Germany), and Japan; lower in North America.

phenomena.name: Easter Island
phenomena.description: A Chilean Polynesian island in the southeastern Pacific, world-famous for its 887 monumental moai statues and as one of archaeology's most-studied cases of cultural development and ecological change.

aliases.name: Rapa Nui
aliases.meaning: literally 'Big Rapa'; the modern Polynesian name for the island and its people

aliases.name: Te Pito o Te Henua
aliases.meaning: 'The navel of the world' (a traditional name)

phenomena.origin: A single island in the southeastern Pacific, 3,512 km west of continental Chile and ~2,075 km east of the Pitcairn Islands.

phenomena.name: Ebu Gogo
phenomena.description: A small, hairy, humanoid creature in the oral traditions of the Nage people of central Flores, Indonesia, often discussed in connection with the discovery of Homo floresiensis at Liang Bua in 2003.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range confined to central Flores Island, Indonesia, particularly the area around the Nage village of Boawae and the volcanic massif of Ebulobo.

phenomena.name: Eilean Mòr Lighthouse Mystery
phenomena.description: The 1900 disappearance of three lighthouse keepers from the Flannan Isles Lighthouse on Eilean Mòr in the Outer Hebrides, Scotland — most plausibly attributable to a rogue wave during a severe storm.

aliases.name: Disappearance of the Flannan Isles keepers

phenomena.origin: Single location: Eilean Mòr (the largest of the Flannan Isles), about 32 km west of the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland.

phenomena.name: El Cadejo
phenomena.description: A Central American spirit that takes the form of a large dog, appearing in two opposing variants: a benevolent white cadejo that protects nocturnal travellers and a malevolent black cadejo (sometimes identified with the Devil) that harms them.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range across Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama) with extensions into several Mexican states.

phenomena.name: El Silbón
phenomena.description: A cursed wandering spirit of the Venezuelan and Colombian Llanos who carries his murdered father's bones in a sack and whose whistle reverses with distance: close-sounding when far, distant-sounding when very near.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric range across the Llanos savanna of Venezuela and the Eastern Llanos of Colombia, with the densest tradition in the Venezuelan state of Portuguesa.

phenomena.name: Sisimite
phenomena.description: The Sisimite is a large, bipedal, ape-like humanoid from Central American folklore — particularly Belize and Honduras — described as covered in black or dark brown fur with four-fingered hands and backward-facing feet, known for its ferocity and alleged abduction of humans.
phenomena.origin: Found in the folklore of Belize, Honduras, Guatemala, and Nicaragua. Related reports extend into southern Mexico (Campeche, Chiapas, Quintana Roo) and reportedly as far south as Colombia, where it is called the 'Darien Monster.'

phenomena.name: Electronic Voice Phenomena (EVP)
phenomena.description: Sounds present on electronic recordings that are interpreted as the voices of the dead or other discarnate entities; mainstream science treats EVP as auditory pareidolia and radio/equipment artifact, while paranormal investigators continue to record and catalogue alleged messages.

aliases.name: Raudive Voices
aliases.meaning: Named after Konstantin Raudive, who popularized the practice

aliases.name: Instrumental Trans-Communication (ITC)
aliases.meaning: Broader term coined by Ernst Senkowski covering EVP and other electronic 'spirit communication' methods

phenomena.origin: EVP recording is a global phenomenon practiced across Europe, the Americas, and Asia, originating in mid-20th-century Sweden, Latvia, and the United States and spreading widely with consumer audio recorders and the internet.

phenomena.name: Elemental Spirits
phenomena.description: The four classes of nature spirits — gnomes (earth), undines (water), sylphs (air), and salamanders (fire) — codified in the 16th-century writings of Paracelsus and elaborated through Rosicrucian, Theosophical, and modern occult traditions.

aliases.name: Sagani
aliases.meaning: Paracelsus's collective term for the four elementals (De Meteoris)

phenomena.origin: Conceptually global — wherever earth, water, air, or fire is found — but the systematic classification originates in Western European Renaissance occultism and has spread globally through Rosicrucian, Theosophical, and modern esoteric currents.

phenomena.name: Eloko
phenomena.description: A dangerous dwarf-like forest spirit of the Mongo-Nkundo peoples of the Congo Basin, said to dwell in hollow trees, dressed in leaves with a beard of grass, carrying enchanting bells and possessing claws and a wide-opening mouth. Often understood as the spirit of an ancestor who died in the forest under unjust circumstances.
phenomena.origin: Confined to the rainforests of the central Congo Basin, particularly the territory of the Mongo-Nkundo peoples of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

phenomena.name: Emela-ntouka
phenomena.description: An elephant-sized, single-horned, semi-aquatic cryptid reported from the Likouala swamps of the Republic of the Congo and elsewhere in the Congo Basin; its Lingala name means 'killer of elephants'.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in the Likouala swamp region of the Republic of the Congo, with adjacent reports from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Cameroon, and (under different names) Zambia and east-central Africa.

phenomena.name: Empusa
phenomena.description: A shape-shifting female phantom of Greek mythology, associated with the goddess Hecate, said to possess one leg of bronze and one of donkey-form, and to seduce and devour young men.

aliases.name: Empousai
aliases.meaning: Plural form, attested as a class of phantoms in late antiquity

phenomena.origin: Ancient Greek mythological geography: encountered in Greece (Attica) and the broader Hellenistic world; transmitted through Greek and Roman literary culture.

phenomena.name: Encantado
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting being of Amazonian Brazilian folklore that lives by day as a pink river dolphin (boto cor-de-rosa) and emerges at night, especially during festivals, in the form of a tall, handsome, white-clad man who seduces women and lures the unwary into the underwater realm of Encante.

aliases.name: Boto cor-de-rosa
aliases.meaning: 'Pink boto'; the Amazon river dolphin in its mythical aspect

aliases.name: Boto
aliases.meaning: Common name for Inia geoffrensis, the Amazon river dolphin

phenomena.origin: Concentrated in the Brazilian Amazon basin (states of Amazonas, Pará, Acre, Rondônia, Roraima, Amapá), with parallel traditions in adjacent Amazonian regions of Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Venezuela, and the Guianas.

phenomena.name: Enenra
phenomena.description: A Japanese yōkai composed of smoke, said to dwell in bonfires and to be visible only to the pure of heart; first illustrated by Toriyama Sekien in the 1781 yōkai compendium Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.
phenomena.origin: Japanese folklore; the figure originates in Edo-period yōkai literature and is part of the contemporary national Japanese supernatural canon.

phenomena.name: Enfield Horror
phenomena.description: An unidentified creature reported in and around Enfield, Illinois during a brief sighting cluster in late April and early May 1973, described as a roughly four-and-a-half-foot-tall, gray, three-legged entity with two short arms and pink eyes.
phenomena.origin: Reports limited to a small area in and around Enfield, Illinois, during a six-week window in 1973; no documented reports outside this geographic and temporal cluster.

phenomena.name: Erlking
phenomena.description: A malevolent fairy-king of Germanic Romanticism, derived via Herder's 1778 mistranslation from the Danish 'ellekonge' ('king of the elves'); famously portrayed in Goethe's 1782 ballad 'Erlkönig' as a supernatural being who lures a child to its death, set to music by Franz Schubert (D. 328, 1815).

aliases.name: Ellekonge
aliases.meaning: 'King of the elves'; the original Scandinavian root

aliases.name: The Erl-King
aliases.meaning: Standard English rendering, popularized through Goethe and Schubert

phenomena.origin: Originating in Danish ballad tradition and codified in late-18th-century German literature; spread globally through Goethe's poem and Schubert's lied.

phenomena.name: Exorcism
phenomena.description: A religious or spiritual practice for evicting demons, jinn, or other malevolent entities from a person, place, or object; recognized in Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism, with the Catholic 'Roman Ritual' (1614, revised 1999) being the best-known formal rite.

aliases.name: exorkismós
aliases.meaning: 'binding by oath'; etymological root of the modern term

aliases.name: Major exorcism
aliases.meaning: Catholic formal rite according to the Roman Ritual

aliases.name: Minor exorcism
aliases.meaning: Lesser exorcisms in Catholic baptismal and other liturgies

aliases.name: Deliverance ministry
aliases.meaning: Charismatic and Pentecostal practice analogous to exorcism

phenomena.origin: Exorcism is practiced globally, in every major religious tradition, with regional and confessional variations.

phenomena.name: Eyeless Jack
phenomena.description: Eyeless Jack is a fictional character from internet creepypasta fiction, depicted as a figure in a black hoodie and blue mask with empty, black-fluid-leaking eye sockets who breaks into homes to harvest and eat human organs — particularly kidneys.
phenomena.origin: As an internet-based fictional character, Eyeless Jack has no geographic distribution in the traditional sense. The character circulates globally through English-language and translated creepypasta communities.

phenomena.name: Fairies / Fae Folk
phenomena.description: Fairies are a class of supernatural beings in European folklore, particularly Celtic, Germanic and English traditions, dwelling in an Otherworld that overlaps with our own and capable of magic, abduction, and exchange of changelings.

aliases.name: The Good Neighbours
aliases.meaning: euphemism to avoid offending the Fae

phenomena.origin: Fairy belief is centred in the Celtic-speaking regions of Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales, Cornwall, and Brittany, with extensive parallel traditions across Germanic and Scandinavian Europe and surviving Anglo-American folk belief in Newfoundland and Appalachia.

phenomena.name: Fearsome Critters
phenomena.description: Fearsome critters are a body of legendary tall-tale animals from the oral tradition of late-19th and early-20th century North American logging camps, ranging from the Hodag to the Hidebehind, the Squonk, the Hugag, and the Splintercat.

aliases.name: Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods
aliases.meaning: title of W. T. Cox's 1910 book that anchors the genre

phenomena.origin: Fearsome critters are concentrated in the historical North American lumber regions: the Great Lakes pinewoods (Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota), New England, the Pacific Northwest, the Appalachians (especially Maryland and West Virginia), the Ozarks, and the Canadian boreal forest.

phenomena.name: Fenrir
phenomena.description: Fenrir is a monstrous wolf in Norse mythology, son of Loki and the jötunn Angrboða, bound by the gods with the magical fetter Gleipnir and prophesied to break free at Ragnarök and slay Odin.

aliases.name: Fenrisúlfr
aliases.meaning: Fenrir's wolf / the wolf of Fenrir

regions: Jötunheimr (place of his upbringing in some accounts)
phenomena.origin: Fenrir is a figure of the cosmological geography of Old Norse mythology rather than a being of the historical world. He is bound on the island of Lyngvi in the lake Ámsvartnir, and reaches Vígríðr at Ragnarök.

phenomena.name: Flat Earth
phenomena.description: Flat Earth is a modern conspiracy belief that the Earth is a flat plane (typically a disc with the Arctic at the centre and Antarctica as a perimeter ice wall) rather than the oblate spheroid established by more than two millennia of observational and physical evidence.

aliases.name: Zetetic Astronomy
aliases.meaning: the 19th-century system of Samuel Rowbotham, from Greek zetein 'to seek'

phenomena.origin: The modern Flat Earth movement is a global, primarily English-speaking online community with concentrations in the United States, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and parts of Africa and South Asia, and with significant enclaves in Russian and Spanish-speaking communities.

phenomena.name: Flatwoods Monster
phenomena.description: The Flatwoods Monster is a 10-foot-tall, spade-headed entity allegedly encountered by a group of seven witnesses in Flatwoods, West Virginia, on the night of 12 September 1952, in connection with a fireball that crossed the eastern United States.
phenomena.origin: A single localized incident in central West Virginia. Subsequent regional folklore and tourism are concentrated in Braxton County and the town of Sutton.

phenomena.name: Foo Fighters
phenomena.description: Foo fighters were luminous aerial objects reported pacing Allied (and some Axis) aircraft over Europe and the Pacific in the final years of World War II, particularly in 1944–45, and treated by the postwar Robertson Panel as the first major case-set of military UAP.

aliases.name: Foo-fighter
aliases.meaning: from the Smokey Stover comic strip catchphrase 'where there's foo, there's fire'

phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the European Theater of Operations (Western Front airspace 1944–45) and the Pacific Theater (Mariana Islands, Japanese home islands airspace 1944–45), with isolated 1941–43 antecedents in the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean.

phenomena.name: Fox Sister (여우 누이)
phenomena.description: The Fox Sister is a figure of Korean folklore in which a kumiho (nine-tailed fox spirit) takes the form of a young girl and infiltrates a family as their long-lost daughter, secretly devouring livestock and family members until exposed by an older brother.
phenomena.origin: Korean folktale tradition (Korean peninsula and the wider Korean diaspora). The kumiho is part of the East Asian fox-spirit complex but the specific 'fox sister' motif is distinctively Korean.

phenomena.name: Fresno Nightcrawlers
phenomena.description: The Fresno Nightcrawlers are small bipedal entities famous from a brief 2007 home-security video filmed in a Fresno, California front yard, depicting two pale figures consisting almost entirely of legs and a small head with no visible torso or arms.
phenomena.origin: All canonical Nightcrawler footage originates within California's Central Valley and adjacent Sierra Nevada foothills.

phenomena.name: Fur-Bearing Trout
phenomena.description: The fur-bearing trout is a legendary fish, North American and Icelandic in origin, said to grow a thick coat of fur to survive cold northern waters; in practice it is a long-running tall tale and taxidermy hoax in which a real trout is mounted with rabbit fur attached.
phenomena.origin: The fur-bearing trout is a folkloric and tourist tradition of North America (especially the northern Rockies, the Great Lakes region, and Canada) and a folktale tradition of Iceland. There is no real biological range.

phenomena.name: Futakuchi-onna
phenomena.description: Futakuchi-onna is a Japanese yokai — a two-mouthed woman — whose hair moves like serpents to feed a second, fully functional mouth on the back of her head that screams demands for food and causes excruciating pain if unfed.
phenomena.origin: A creature of Japanese folklore; associated with rural Japan in the Edo period and earlier. No specific geographic region within Japan is particularly associated with the futakuchi-onna.

phenomena.name: Garuda
phenomena.description: Garuda is a divine eagle-like bird in Hindu and Buddhist mythology, the mount (vahana) of Vishnu, king of birds, and eternal enemy of the nagas (serpents); it serves as the national symbol of Indonesia and Thailand.

aliases.name: Garuḍa
aliases.meaning: Possibly from verb gri (to speak); also associated with the sun

phenomena.origin: Garuda is a central figure in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, giving him cultural presence across South Asia (India, Nepal), Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, Myanmar), and anywhere these religions have spread.

phenomena.name: Gashadokuro
phenomena.description: Gashadokuro is a colossal skeletal Japanese yokai standing 10 or more meters tall, formed from the accumulated bones and rage of those who died of starvation, that prowls at night hunting travelers to devour.
phenomena.origin: A creature of Japanese mythology associated with the Kanto region and with sites of historical mass starvation or battlefield death. Most strongly associated with events in the Kanto area related to Taira no Masakado.

phenomena.name: Gello
phenomena.description: A female demon of Greek and Byzantine tradition, attested as early as Sappho (6th century BC), said to attack pregnant women, newborns, and the unmarried, and the central target of a long-running corpus of apotropaic charms and exorcisms in the Greek-speaking world.

aliases.name: Gelloudes
aliases.meaning: plural form denoting a class of demons

aliases.name: Abyzou
aliases.meaning: from abyssos, 'the deep'; identified with Gello in late antiquity and Byzantine literature

phenomena.origin: Originally a localized Greek tradition (attested for Sappho on Lesbos), the Gello / gelloudes complex spread throughout the Greek-speaking Byzantine world and, through the 'Legend of Saint Sisinnios', into Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Romanian, Slavonic, Arabic, Syriac, and Hebrew manuscript traditions across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East.

phenomena.name: Gettysburg Battlefield
phenomena.description: Site of the July 1–3, 1863 Battle of Gettysburg, the bloodiest engagement of the American Civil War. The battlefield and adjacent town are among the most extensively reported haunted locations in the United States, with ghost lore dating back to the immediate aftermath of the battle and a major commercial ghost-tour industry from the 1990s onward.

aliases.name: Ghosts of Gettysburg
aliases.meaning: popular name for the cluster of paranormal traditions associated with the battlefield

phenomena.origin: Reports are concentrated within the roughly 6,000-acre Gettysburg National Military Park, the borough of Gettysburg, and immediately surrounding farmland in Adams County, Pennsylvania.

phenomena.name: Ghosts and Hauntings
phenomena.description: Ghosts are alleged manifestations of the dead — visual apparitions, voices, sounds, and physical effects — reported across virtually every human culture from Mesopotamia to the present. Mainstream science treats them as folklore and misperception; parapsychology and Spiritualism continue to study them as a possible class of phenomena.
phenomena.origin: Ghost beliefs are virtually universal across human cultures, attested from at least the third millennium BC (Mesopotamian texts) to the present. Reports occur worldwide; concentrations of widely-publicized cases exist in the British Isles, the United States, Japan, China, and Latin America.

phenomena.name: Ghul
phenomena.description: A demonic, shape-shifting being of pre-Islamic Arabian and Islamic folklore, classed as a type of jinn, said to dwell in graveyards, deserts, and ruined places, lure travelers from their path, and consume corpses and human flesh.

aliases.name: Ghoul
aliases.meaning: Anglicization of ghul; first attested in English in William Beckford's Vathek (1786)

aliases.name: Si'lat / Si'la
aliases.meaning: shape-shifting female demon often paired with the ghul

phenomena.origin: The ghul belongs to Arab, Persian, and broader Islamic folklore. Reports and traditions extend across the Arabian Peninsula, the Levant, Mesopotamia, North Africa, the Maghreb, Iran, Afghanistan, and Central and South Asia, with regional cognates and equivalents elsewhere in the Islamic world.

phenomena.name: Gillygaloo
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter from North American lumberjack tall-tale tradition: a hillside-dwelling bird famous for laying square or cubic eggs that will not roll downhill. Documented as a piece of camp folklore rather than a claimed real animal.
phenomena.origin: A folkloric creature 'reported' across the geography of the North American lumberjack tradition: the Great Lakes states (Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota), New England (Maine), the Pacific Northwest, and Canada.

phenomena.name: Glastonbury Tor
phenomena.description: A 158-metre (518-foot) conical hill near Glastonbury, Somerset, England, topped by the roofless 14th-century tower of St Michael's Church. Long associated with Arthurian Avalon, with Celtic Otherworld traditions, and with modern earth-mysteries and pilgrimage culture; now a National Trust property.

aliases.name: Avalon
aliases.meaning: associated by Gerald of Wales (12th century) with Glastonbury and the Tor

phenomena.origin: A single, fixed location near Glastonbury, Somerset, southwestern England. Cultural and pilgrimage 'distribution' extends across the British Isles and to international neopagan, Goddess-movement, and New Age communities.

phenomena.name: Glitch in the Matrix
phenomena.description: An umbrella term, popularized by the 1999 film 'The Matrix', for first-person experiences in which reality appears momentarily to malfunction — déjà vu, objects appearing or disappearing, duplicate strangers, sudden timeline mismatches — and which the experiencer interprets as evidence that the world is a computer simulation.

aliases.name: Simulation glitch
aliases.meaning: framed in terms of the simulation hypothesis

phenomena.origin: A globally distributed, internet-mediated phenomenon, most heavily reported in English-speaking online communities (United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia) but with active counterparts in many languages.

phenomena.name: Globster
phenomena.description: An unidentified, often large, fibrous organic mass washed up on a shoreline. Once a staple of cryptozoological speculation, almost every well-studied globster has been identified by DNA or histology as the decomposed remains of a whale or other large vertebrate.
phenomena.origin: Globsters have been reported on coastlines globally — Atlantic, Pacific, Indian Oceans, and adjacent seas. The phenomenon is not regional in any meaningful sense; it tracks the geography of large cetacean populations and shipping/observer density.

phenomena.name: Goatman
phenomena.description: An umbrella name for several American urban-legend creatures described as half-man, half-goat. The best-attested versions are the Maryland Goatman of Prince George's County (popularized 1971), the Lake Worth Monster of Fort Worth, Texas (sightings July 1969), and the Pope Lick Monster of Fisherville, Kentucky.
phenomena.origin: The Goatman complex is concentrated in the United States, with three major regional clusters in Maryland (Prince George's County), Texas (Fort Worth / Lake Worth), and Kentucky (Fisherville / Pope Lick).

phenomena.name: Goblin
phenomena.description: Goblins are small, grotesque, mischievous or malevolent supernatural beings from European folklore, first attested in the 12th century, ranging from household pranksters (brownies) to murderous territorial spirits (redcaps), and now archetypal monsters in modern fantasy.
phenomena.origin: Goblin traditions are found across Europe, with the oldest documented examples from Norman France and England (12th century). Cognate traditions exist globally in Korea (dokkaebi), Africa (Zulu tokoloshe), and among Indigenous North American peoples (Wampanoag pukwudgie). The modern fantasy goblin has achieved global distribution through literature and gaming.

phenomena.name: Golem
phenomena.description: The golem is an animated anthropomorphic being of Jewish folklore, created from inanimate matter such as clay or mud through Kabbalistic ritual use of sacred Hebrew names, most famously the Golem of Prague attributed to Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel in the 16th century.

aliases.name: גולם
aliases.meaning: Raw material; unfinished human being; also 'dumb' or 'helpless' in Modern Hebrew

aliases.name: Goylem
aliases.meaning: Lethargic or stuporous person; the Yiddish borrowing from Hebrew golem

aliases.name: Golem of Prague
aliases.meaning: The most famous specific golem, attributed to Rabbi Loew

aliases.name: Yossele
aliases.meaning: Diminutive of Josef; the name given to the Golem of Prague in some traditions

phenomena.origin: Golem legends are rooted in Jewish communities of medieval and early modern Europe, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe (Poland, Czech Republic, Germany). The Prague legend is the most geographically specific. The concept has since spread globally through popular culture.

phenomena.name: Goofang
phenomena.description: The Goofang is a fictional fish from North American lumberjack tall tale folklore, described as swimming exclusively backward to keep water out of its eyes, and listed in the Paul Bunyan Natural History tradition.
phenomena.origin: Associated with the Great Lakes lumberjack camp tradition, particularly Minnesota and Wisconsin. As a fictional tall tale creature, it has no real geographic distribution.

phenomena.name: Gorgon
phenomena.description: The Gorgons are three monstrous sisters of Greek myth — Medusa, Stheno, and Euryale — daughters of the primordial sea-deities Phorcys and Ceto, whose gaze turned mortals to stone.

aliases.name: Gorgoneion
aliases.meaning: apotropaic image of a Gorgon's head

phenomena.origin: A creature of Ancient Greek and broader Mediterranean myth. Literary references locate the Gorgons at the edges of the known world; iconographically, gorgoneia were used across the Greek, Etruscan, and Roman worlds and into Roman Britain.

phenomena.name: Gozu (Cow Head)
phenomena.description: Gozu ('Cow Head') is a Japanese urban legend about a story so terrifying that anyone who hears it is said to die or fall gravely ill. The full text of the story is itself never told.
phenomena.origin: Originated and primarily circulated in Japan; now diffused globally through internet 'creepypasta' and horror communities.

phenomena.name: Grafton Monster
phenomena.description: A pale, headless humanoid creature reportedly seen by a local journalist near Grafton, West Virginia, on the night of 16 June 1964. The legend rests on this single newspaper-published account.
phenomena.origin: Restricted to a single sighting near Grafton, Taylor County, West Virginia.

phenomena.name: Gremlin
phenomena.description: Gremlins are mischievous fairy-like creatures of 20th-century aviation folklore, blamed by Royal Air Force pilots from the 1920s onward for unexplained mechanical faults in aircraft.

aliases.name: Fifinella
aliases.meaning: female gremlin in Roald Dahl's 1943 book

phenomena.origin: Originated in the British Royal Air Force in the 1920s and spread through Allied air forces during World War II; subsequently a global pop-culture motif.

phenomena.name: Grey Lady
phenomena.description: 'Grey Lady' is a recurring archetype in British, North American, and broader anglophone ghost-lore: a female apparition dressed in grey, usually associated with a specific historic building and a tragic backstory.
regions: New England and the Midwest US
phenomena.origin: Anglophone world, with concentrations in the British Isles and North America. The Wikipedia disambiguation page lists Grey Lady ghosts in England, Northern Ireland, Malta, New Zealand, and the United States.

phenomena.name: Grey Aliens (Greys)
phenomena.description: Greys are the most commonly reported alleged extraterrestrial entity in modern UFO and abduction literature: small, hairless humanoids with disproportionately large heads and large black eyes, central to the Betty and Barney Hill case (1961) and Whitley Strieber's Communion (1987).

aliases.name: Zeta Reticulans
aliases.meaning: after the 'Zeta Reticuli star map' from the Hill case

aliases.name: The Visitors
aliases.meaning: term used by Whitley Strieber in Communion (1987)

phenomena.origin: Reports concentrated in the United States, with significant numbers in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and continental Europe. Per C. D. B. Bryan's review, Greys account for ~73% of US alien-encounter reports, ~50% in Australia, ~48% in continental Europe, and ~12% in the UK.

phenomena.name: Griffin
phenomena.description: The Griffin is a legendary hybrid creature with the body of a lion and the head, wings, and forelimb-talons of an eagle. Attested from Bronze Age Near Eastern art and central to Greek and medieval European heraldry.
phenomena.origin: A creature of myth and iconography. Imagery extends from Predynastic Egypt and Mesopotamia through Bronze Age Crete, the wider Mediterranean, the medieval Christian West, and into modern heraldry.

phenomena.name: Grootslang
phenomena.description: The Grootslang is a giant serpent of South African folklore, said to inhabit a deep cave (the 'Wonder Hole') in the Richtersveld and to guard a hoard of diamonds.
phenomena.origin: South African folklore confined to the Richtersveld region of the Northern Cape, especially the cave called the Wonder Hole.

phenomena.name: Gumberoo
phenomena.description: The Gumberoo is a fearsome critter of Pacific Northwest lumberjack folklore — a hairless bear-shaped creature with a hide so tough that bullets bounce off, but which explodes when set on fire.

aliases.name: Megalogaster repercussus
aliases.meaning: fanciful Latin classification given by William T. Cox (1910)

phenomena.origin: Confined in folklore to the Pacific Northwest of North America — the heavy-timber districts of Oregon, Washington, northern California, and coastal British Columbia.

phenomena.name: Gumiho
phenomena.description: The gumiho is a nine-tailed fox spirit of Korean folklore, typically depicted as a shapeshifting woman who feeds on humans — particularly their livers or hearts — to sustain or transform her supernatural existence.
phenomena.origin: Korean cultural sphere — Korean Peninsula and the Korean diaspora.

phenomena.name: HAARP Conspiracy Theories
phenomena.description: HAARP is a real ionospheric research facility near Gakona, Alaska, but it has become the focus of a long-running set of conspiracy theories that allege it is a secret weather-modification, mind-control, or earthquake-generation weapon.
phenomena.origin: Conspiracy theory primarily anglophone with substantial Latin American (Spanish), Russian, and Chinese-language uptake. Real facility is in Alaska.

phenomena.name: Haetae
phenomena.description: The Haetae (also Haechi) is a legendary guardian beast from Korean and Chinese mythology, depicted as a muscular lion-like creature with scales and a single horn, revered as a symbol of justice, law, and protection against fire.

aliases.name: Haechi
aliases.meaning: Variant romanization of the same creature

aliases.name: Xiezhi
aliases.meaning: 獬豸; the Chinese source figure

aliases.name: Unicorn-lion
aliases.meaning: Descriptive English name referencing its single horn and leonine body

phenomena.origin: Originating in Chinese mythology and adopted throughout East Asia. Most prominent in Korea, where haetae statues guard palace complexes. Also found in China, Japan, and Vietnam.

phenomena.name: Hanako-san
phenomena.description: Hanako-san is a Japanese school ghost said to inhabit the third stall of the third-floor girls' bathroom and to answer when summoned with a specific knocking ritual. She is one of the most widely circulated school-based urban legends in modern Japan.
phenomena.origin: Japan-wide schoolyard urban legend, with regional variants in nearly every prefecture. The legend has been exported through anime, manga, films, and the global creepypasta and J-horror communities.

phenomena.name: Hantu Air
phenomena.description: Hantu Air ('water ghost') is the Malay/Indonesian name for an unseen inhabitant of rivers, lakes, swamps, and the sea in the animist traditions of Maritime Southeast Asia. It can be benevolent or malevolent depending on how humans treat the body of water it occupies.

aliases.name: Water Ghost / Spirit of the Water

phenomena.origin: Maritime Southeast Asia, especially the Malay-speaking world: peninsular Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Singapore, southern Thailand, and the broader Malay diaspora.

phenomena.name: Hantu Bungkus
phenomena.description: Hantu Bungkus (Malay 'wrapped ghost'), known in Indonesian as Pocong, is the restless spirit of a deceased Muslim whose burial shroud (kain kafan) was not properly untied at burial. It is depicted as a body still wrapped in white cloth that hops or floats at night.

aliases.name: Kafan ghost
aliases.meaning: After kain kafan, the Islamic burial shroud

phenomena.origin: Predominantly the Malay-Indonesian Muslim cultural sphere: Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, southern Thailand, and the Malay diaspora.

phenomena.name: Hantu Jerangan
phenomena.description: Hantu Jerangan is a regional Malay fishing-community spirit said to be associated with fishing nets and unexplained drownings at sea. It is a relatively obscure figure within the broader hantu taxonomy and is documented mainly in coastal Malaysian oral tradition rather than in major published ethnographies.
phenomena.origin: Coastal Malaysian fishing communities; not well documented in academic sources outside this region.

phenomena.name: Pontianak
phenomena.description: Pontianak is the ghost of a woman who died during pregnancy or childbirth in Malay-Indonesian folklore. She appears as a beautiful long-haired woman in white whose form changes into a fanged, bloody monster when she attacks, and she primarily preys on men.

aliases.name: Langsuir
aliases.meaning: Closely related female ghost; in some traditions Pontianak is the stillborn child of Langsuir

phenomena.origin: Throughout the Malay-Indonesian world: Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, southern Thailand, and the Malay diaspora.

phenomena.name: Hantu Raya
phenomena.description: Hantu Raya ('Great Ghost') is a powerful Malay familiar spirit said to be bound to a human master — typically a bomoh (shaman) or pawang — for whom it serves as a strength-augmenting double. It demands strict ritual offerings and is inherited within families as hantu pusaka.

aliases.name: Hantu Pusaka
aliases.meaning: Heirloom spirit, when inherited within a family lineage

phenomena.origin: Malay-Islamic cultural sphere of Maritime Southeast Asia: peninsular Malaysia in particular, with belief extending into Singapore, Brunei, southern Thailand, and parts of Indonesia.

phenomena.name: Hantu Tetek
phenomena.description: Hantu Tetek (Malay 'breast ghost'), also known as Hantu Kopek, is a female ghost in Malay folklore depicted as an old woman with grotesquely enlarged, pendulous breasts. She is said to smother victims, especially disobedient children who wander out at night, and is mainly invoked as a cautionary figure.
phenomena.origin: Predominantly Malaysia, with comparable variants in Indonesia and Brunei among Malay-language communities.

phenomena.name: Harpy
phenomena.description: The Harpies are winged spirits in Greek mythology, originally personifications of stormy winds and divine snatchers. They appear in early sources as fair-haired winged maidens and in later literature as bird-bodied, women-faced monsters who steal food and abduct people as agents of divine punishment.

aliases.name: Aello
aliases.meaning: 'Storm-swift' — an individual harpy named in Hesiod

aliases.name: Ocypete
aliases.meaning: 'Swift-wing' — an individual harpy named in Hesiod

aliases.name: Celaeno
aliases.meaning: 'Dark, dusky' — an individual harpy added by Virgil

aliases.name: Podarge
aliases.meaning: 'Fleet-foot' — a harpy named in Homer; mother of Achilles' horses Balius and Xanthus

phenomena.origin: Mythologically, the wider Greek and Mediterranean world: Thrace (Phineus), the Strophades (Aeneid), the cave of Zephyrus, and stormy maritime regions in general. Culturally, harpies have been received throughout the Greco-Roman, medieval European, and modern global imaginary.

phenomena.name: Hasshaku-sama
phenomena.description: Hasshaku-sama is a Japanese internet-era urban legend originating on 2channel describing an unnaturally tall female ghost roughly 2.4 metres in height who, having become fixated on a child, pursues them with a deep masculine 'po, po, po' laugh and an ability to imitate family members' voices.
phenomena.origin: Japanese internet folklore originating on 2channel; the canonical story is set in rural Japan but the legend itself is now globally circulated through creepypasta communities.

phenomena.name: Haunted Places
phenomena.description: Haunted places are locations across the world where paranormal activity — apparitions, unexplained sounds, sensations, or anomalies — is repeatedly reported by independent witnesses over time. They are studied as a form of ghostlore (a sub-genre of folklore) and underpin a substantial global ghost-tourism industry.
phenomena.origin: Global. Wikipedia's List of reportedly haunted locations covers more than 47 countries across every inhabited continent.

phenomena.name: Headless Horseman
phenomena.description: The Headless Horseman is a transcultural folk figure of a decapitated rider on horseback. The most famous American version is Washington Irving's Galloping Hessian of the Hollow in 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (1820), but headless horseman figures appear in earlier Irish, Scottish, German, and Welsh folklore.

aliases.name: Galloping Hessian of the Hollow
aliases.meaning: Washington Irving's name for the figure

aliases.name: El Muerto
aliases.meaning: 'The Dead One' — South Texas headless rider

phenomena.origin: Pan-European folk traditions (Irish, Scottish, English, Welsh, German) and their North American descendants. The most famous geographic locus is Sleepy Hollow (Tarrytown), New York.

phenomena.name: Helltown, Ohio
phenomena.description: Helltown is an informal name for the abandoned village of Boston Mills in Boston Township, Summit County, Ohio, depopulated after a 1974 federal land acquisition for the Cuyahoga Valley National Recreation Area (now Cuyahoga Valley National Park). Empty homes, boarded-up structures, and a real toxic-waste cleanup at the Krejci Dump fed a cluster of urban legends from the 1980s onward.
phenomena.origin: Boston Township, Summit County, Ohio, within Cuyahoga Valley National Park, between Akron and Cleveland.

phenomena.name: Hessdalen Lights
phenomena.description: Recurring unexplained luminous phenomena observed in the Hessdalen valley of central Norway, instrumentally recorded since the early 1980s and the subject of a long-running scientific monitoring programme.
phenomena.origin: The phenomenon is concentrated almost entirely within the Hessdalen valley (Holtålen municipality) in Sør-Trøndelag, central Norway, with occasional reports from neighbouring valleys.

phenomena.name: Hidebehind
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter from American lumberjack folklore that always hides behind the nearest object, making it impossible to observe directly; used to explain unexplained disappearances of loggers in the deep woods.
phenomena.origin: Reported throughout the lumber-camp belt of North America: the upper Midwest (Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota), the Pacific Northwest, New England, and adjacent parts of Canada.

phenomena.name: Hitotsume-kozō
phenomena.description: A Japanese yōkai depicted as a bald child-monk with a single large eye in the centre of its face; widely treated in folklore as comparatively harmless, surprising rather than injuring those who encounter it.
phenomena.origin: Reported across Japan in classical and regional folklore, with the densest tradition in the Kantō region. Notable strands of tradition link the figure to Mount Hiei (Shiga / Kyōto) and to local folklore in eastern and central Japan.

phenomena.name: Hobgoblin
phenomena.description: A small, hairy household sprite of English and broader British folklore, originally helpful or merely mischievous and only later conflated with malevolent goblins.

aliases.name: Hob
aliases.meaning: A familiar diminutive of 'Robert', used for household sprites

aliases.name: Robin Goodfellow
aliases.meaning: Most famous individual hobgoblin; identified with Puck

aliases.name: Puck
aliases.meaning: Mischievous sprite of English folklore identified by Shakespeare with the hobgoblin

phenomena.origin: Hobgoblin and hob traditions are concentrated in England — particularly the north and Midlands — and in adjacent parts of the British Isles. Closely related figures appear in Scottish, Welsh, and Manx folklore.

phenomena.name: Hodag
phenomena.description: A horned, spiked, scaly creature from northern Wisconsin lumberjack folklore, made famous by surveyor Eugene Shepard's 1893 hoax in Rhinelander; now the official symbol of the city.

aliases.name: Bovine spiritualis
aliases.meaning: Mock-scientific name used in Eugene Shepard's 1893 publicity material

phenomena.origin: Strongly localised to northern Wisconsin, especially Oneida County and the area around Rhinelander.

phenomena.name: Hoia-Baciu Forest
phenomena.description: An oak forest west of Cluj-Napoca in Transylvania, Romania, internationally known as a hotspot of paranormal claims — UFO sightings, ghost reports, missing-person legends, and an alleged 'dead zone' clearing — and the subject of paranormal-tourism interest.
phenomena.origin: A specific location: an oak forest of approximately 250–295 hectares on the western outskirts of Cluj-Napoca, Cluj County, Transylvania, Romania.

phenomena.name: Hollow Earth
phenomena.description: The proposition that the Earth is partly or entirely hollow, with one or more habitable inner surfaces and openings (often at the poles) — historically a serious scientific hypothesis, now firmly debunked but persistent as a conspiracy and esoteric tradition.

aliases.name: Shambhala
aliases.meaning: Buddhist mythical kingdom often associated in modern Western occultism with an inner Earth

phenomena.origin: A theoretical claim about the entire Earth; major proponents and movements have been concentrated in the United Kingdom (Halley), the United States (Symmes, Teed, Gardner, modern conspiracists), and Russia / continental Europe (Ossendowski, Theosophy).

phenomena.name: The Hookman
phenomena.description: A classic American urban legend in which a couple parked at a lovers' lane flee from a radio-warned escaped killer with a hook for a hand and find his hook torn off and dangling from the car door handle.
phenomena.origin: American urban legend with countless local variants throughout the contiguous United States; the legend has also circulated in Canada and the United Kingdom.

phenomena.name: Hoop snake
phenomena.description: A legendary serpent of North American (and Australian) folklore that grasps its tail in its mouth and rolls like a wheel to chase prey, striking with a venomous stinger on its tail.
phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the eastern and midwestern United States and parts of Canada, with Australian parallels.

phenomena.name: Hopkinsville Goblins
phenomena.description: A 1955 close-encounter case in which the Sutton family and visitor Billy Ray Taylor reported, near Kelly, Kentucky, a landed object and small humanoid creatures who besieged a farmhouse for several hours, in one of the most-investigated UFO incidents of the period.
phenomena.origin: A single, geographically localised incident at the Sutton/Lankford farm between Kelly and Hopkinsville in Christian County, Kentucky.

phenomena.name: Hugag
phenomena.description: The Hugag is a large moose-like creature from American lumberjack tall-tale tradition, distinguished by jointless legs that prevent it from lying down, forcing it to sleep standing up while leaning against trees.
phenomena.origin: Northern Minnesota, western Wisconsin, and the Canadian wilderness toward Hudson Bay, according to lumberjack tall-tale tradition.

phenomena.name: Hulder
phenomena.description: The Hulder (Huldra) is a seductive and beautiful supernatural woman from Scandinavian folklore who conceals her true nature — a hollow back like a rotted tree and an animal's tail — beneath her alluring appearance.

aliases.name: Ulda
aliases.meaning: Sámi cognate of the same hidden folk

phenomena.origin: Scandinavian Peninsula and Sámi territories. Documented primarily in Norway, Sweden, and Sápmi. Regional naming variants reflect local linguistic traditions.

phenomena.name: Huli jing
phenomena.description: Huli jing are supernatural fox spirits in Chinese mythology and folklore capable of shapeshifting into human form, ranging from benevolent fox immortals (huxian) to malevolent fox demons (huyao) that drain life essence from human victims.
phenomena.origin: Fox spirit traditions are distributed across the Sinosphere. The core tradition is Han Chinese, with strong fox-cult belief historically concentrated in northern China (Hebei, Shandong, Shanxi, Manchuria). Cognate traditions extend to Korea (kumiho), Japan (kitsune), and Vietnam (hồ ly tinh).

phenomena.name: Hungry ghost
phenomena.description: Hungry ghosts (Sanskrit preta; Chinese e gui; Japanese gaki) are beings of one of the six Buddhist realms of rebirth, characterized by insatiable hunger and thirst caused by past karma of greed and attachment.
phenomena.origin: Hungry-ghost belief follows the geographic spread of Buddhism. Doctrinally rooted in South Asia (India, Nepal, Sri Lanka), it became a major popular tradition across China, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Tibet, Mongolia, and Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos).

phenomena.name: Lernaean Hydra
phenomena.description: The Lernaean Hydra is a many-headed serpentine drakōn of Greek mythology, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, slain by Heracles as his second labor; its defining trait is the regrowth of two heads for each one severed.
phenomena.origin: Mythological habitat is the marsh of Lerna, in the Argolid region of the Peloponnese, southern Greece, near a reputed entrance to the Underworld.

phenomena.name: Iara
phenomena.description: The Iara is a beautiful freshwater siren of Brazilian folklore, especially associated with the Amazon basin, who lures men into rivers to drown them or condemn them to lasting madness.
phenomena.origin: The Iara figure is distributed across the freshwater systems of Brazil, particularly the Amazon basin and the rivers of the north and central regions. It is largely a Brazilian phenomenon with diffusion through Lusophone South America.

phenomena.name: Ibaraki-dōji
phenomena.description: Ibaraki-dōji is a celebrated oni (demon) of Heian-period Japanese legend, the chief retainer of the demon king Shuten-dōji and the antagonist of the famous Rashōmon / Modori-bashi episode in which the warrior Watanabe no Tsuna severs its arm.
phenomena.origin: The Ibaraki-dōji legend is centered on Heian-period Kyoto and on the surrounding regions of Settsu (modern Osaka, Hyōgo) and Echigo (modern Niigata).

phenomena.name: Ifrit
phenomena.description: An ifrit is a powerful, often malevolent class of jinn in Arabic and Islamic tradition, frequently associated with fire, the underworld, and the spirits of the violently slain.
phenomena.origin: Ifrit belief is distributed across the Arabic-speaking world and the broader Islamic cultural sphere, including the Mashriq, Egypt, North Africa, the Persian world, and parts of South and Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Ijiraq
phenomena.description: The ijiraq is a shapeshifting being of Inuit religion and oral tradition, said to live between the worlds of the living and the dead, glimpsed only at the edge of vision and known to take and hide away children.
phenomena.origin: The ijiraq is part of Inuit religion and folklore, especially among the Inuit of the eastern Canadian Arctic, the central Arctic islands, and the high Arctic. The term is well-attested in North Baffin Inuktitut.

phenomena.name: Illuminati
phenomena.description: The Illuminati refers both to a real secret society founded in Bavaria in 1776 (suppressed by 1785) and to the enduring conspiracy theory claiming that organization secretly survived to control world governments, finance, and media.

aliases.name: Bavarian Illuminati
aliases.meaning: Historical secret society founded in Bavaria in 1776

phenomena.origin: The historical society operated in Bavaria and spread to central Europe. The conspiracy theory is globally distributed.

phenomena.name: Imp
phenomena.description: An imp is a small, mischievous supernatural creature from European folklore — originally a fairy-like trickster spirit that was later reinterpreted by Christianity as a minor demon or witch's familiar.

aliases.name: Familiar spirit
aliases.meaning: When bound to a witch or sorcerer

aliases.name: Impa
aliases.meaning: Original form; meaning 'young shoot or scion'

phenomena.origin: European folklore tradition, primarily Germanic and British. Most documented specific accounts originate in England.

phenomena.name: Impundulu
phenomena.description: The Impundulu (Lightning Bird) is a supernatural creature from Zulu, Xhosa, and Pondo folklore in South Africa that serves as a witch's familiar, summons lightning, and is said to possess vampiric qualities and the ability to take human form.
regions: South African coastal and interior regions
phenomena.origin: South Africa; primarily associated with Zulu, Xhosa, and Pondo peoples of the eastern and southeastern regions.

phenomena.name: Inugami
phenomena.description: Inugami ('dog god') is a powerful and dangerous spirit familiar from Japanese folklore, created through a ritual sacrifice of a dog and bound to serve a sorcerer or family line across generations, capable of possession, curse, illness, and divination.
phenomena.origin: Concentrated in western Japan, particularly Kyushu, Shikoku, and associated island chains. Belief strongest in eastern Ōita, Shimane, northern Shikoku (Kōchi), Yamaguchi, all of Kyushu, and the Satsunan Islands through Okinawa.

phenomena.name: Ittan-momen
phenomena.description: Ittan-momen (一反木綿, 'one bolt of cotton') is a dangerous yokai from Kagoshima Prefecture in southern Japan, appearing as a long white strip of cotton cloth that flies through the night sky and kills humans by wrapping around their heads and necks.

aliases.name: 一反木綿
aliases.meaning: One bolt of cotton / one tan of cotton cloth

phenomena.origin: Originating in Kōyama, Kimotsuki District, Kagoshima Prefecture, southern Kyushu. Modern sightings reported more broadly across Kyushu, Tokyo, and Shizuoka.

phenomena.name: Jackalope
phenomena.description: The jackalope is a mythical North American hare with antelope or deer antlers, originating as a 1930s taxidermy creation by the Herrick brothers in Douglas, Wyoming. It is the most famous American example of an old global folkloric tradition of horned hares.

aliases.name: Lepus cornutus
aliases.meaning: Horned hare; pre-modern European cryptozoological label for horned rabbits

aliases.name: Wolpertinger
aliases.meaning: Bavarian taxidermy chimera analogous to the jackalope

aliases.name: Al-mi'raj
aliases.meaning: Single-horned hare from medieval Islamic bestiaries

phenomena.origin: Folklore range covers the American West, especially Wyoming, with secondary tall-tale presence across Nebraska, South Dakota, Montana, and Colorado. The wider 'horned hare' tradition is global, with European (wolpertinger, lepus cornutus) and Middle Eastern (al-mi'raj) analogues.

phenomena.name: Jeff the Killer
phenomena.description: Jeff the Killer is a creepypasta character who became one of the most widely spread internet horror figures, depicted as a disfigured pale-skinned young man with a permanent grin who sneaks into homes at night to kill, whispering 'Go to sleep.'

aliases.name: Jeffrey Woods
aliases.meaning: Character's canonical given name in the story

phenomena.origin: An internet-born character with no geographic origin; the story is set in a generic American suburban context. The character's spread is global via internet platforms.

phenomena.name: Jengu
phenomena.description: The Jengu (plural Miengu) are beautiful, mermaid-like water spirits from the folklore of the Sawa peoples of Cameroon's coastal and riverine regions, venerated for healing, protection, and mediation between the living and the ancestral world.

aliases.name: Bisima
aliases.meaning: Alternative name used among Sawa-speaking peoples

phenomena.origin: Cameroonian coast and river regions, particularly the Wouri River, its tributaries, the Wouri estuary, and nearby islands. Veneration persists in Cameroon's Littoral and Southwest Provinces.

phenomena.name: Jersey Devil
phenomena.description: The Jersey Devil is a legendary winged, bipedal creature of the New Jersey Pine Barrens, traditionally said to be the cursed thirteenth child of 'Mother Leeds' born in 1735. Its most famous burst of activity was a week of mass sightings across South Jersey and Philadelphia in January 1909.

aliases.name: Leeds Devil
aliases.meaning: Earlier name connecting the legend to the Leeds family of colonial New Jersey

phenomena.origin: The Jersey Devil is a distinctly regional cryptid associated with the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey and adjacent areas of southeastern Pennsylvania and the Delaware Valley.

phenomena.name: Jiangshi
phenomena.description: The jiangshi (僵尸, 'stiff corpse') is a reanimated corpse from Chinese folklore, depicted in modern popular culture in Qing dynasty official garb, hopping with arms outstretched, and draining the qi (life force) of the living. It is repelled by Taoist talismans, mirrors, and other ritual implements.

aliases.name: Hopping vampire
aliases.meaning: Western popular term for the jiangshi

phenomena.origin: Native to Han Chinese folklore, with strong regional roots in southern China (especially Western Hunan / Xiangxi). The jiangshi spread throughout the Sinosphere — Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, Korea, and Japan — primarily through Hong Kong cinema in the 1980s.

phenomena.name: Jinn
phenomena.description: The jinn are sapient, invisible beings of pre-Islamic Arabian religion and Islamic theology, said to be created by God from smokeless fire. The Quran devotes Surah 72 (Al-Jinn) to them; belief in jinn remains widespread across the Muslim world.

aliases.name: Genie
aliases.meaning: Anglicization, popularized by 18th-century French translations of the One Thousand and One Nights

aliases.name: Ifrit (عفريت)
aliases.meaning: Class of powerful, often malevolent jinn

aliases.name: Marid (مارد)
aliases.meaning: Class of especially powerful jinn, often associated with the sea

aliases.name: Ghul (غول)
aliases.meaning: Cannibalistic, shape-shifting jinn of desolate places

aliases.name: Shaytan (شيطان)
aliases.meaning: Satan; in Islamic theology the rebellious jinn Iblis and his progeny

aliases.name: Pari (پری)
aliases.meaning: Beautiful winged spirit, often paralleled with jinn

phenomena.origin: Conceptually present throughout the Islamic world, with strong continuity with pre-Islamic Arabian religion and parallels in Persian, Turkic, Berber, Swahili, and Malay cultures.

phenomena.name: Joint Snake
phenomena.description: The Joint Snake is a creature from Southern US folklore said to shatter into pieces when struck, then reassemble itself; the legend is rooted in misidentification of legless lizards (glass lizards) that can autotomize their tails.

aliases.name: Glass snake
aliases.meaning: Named for the 'glassy' skin texture described in folklore; also the common name for actual legless lizards (Ophisaurus spp.) that inspired the legend

aliases.name: Hoop snake
aliases.meaning: Related legend of a snake that grasps its tail and rolls like a wheel; overlaps with joint-snake tradition

phenomena.origin: Southern United States from southern Virginia to Texas; range extends north to Wisconsin and Iowa in western areas. Hoop snake tradition extends to Canada and Australia.

phenomena.name: Jörmungandr
phenomena.description: Jörmungandr is the colossal sea serpent of Norse mythology, son of Loki and Angrboða, sibling of Fenrir and Hel, who encircles the world (Midgard) biting his own tail. He is the cosmic adversary of the thunder god Thor, whom he kills and is killed by at Ragnarök.

aliases.name: Jǫrmungandr
aliases.meaning: 'Huge monster' / 'mighty wand'; from jǫrmun- ('huge, vast') + gandr ('staff / monster / magic')

phenomena.origin: Mythological. Within Norse cosmology, Jörmungandr inhabits the world-ocean encircling Midgard. Cultural distribution covers the Viking Age and post-Viking Norse-speaking world (Scandinavia, Iceland, the British Isles, parts of the North Atlantic).
phenomena.first_reported: Pre-Viking oral tradition; Eddic poetry compiled 13th century

phenomena.name: Jorōgumo
phenomena.description: The Jorōgumo is a spider yōkai of Japanese folklore, traditionally said to be a Trichonephila clavata that has lived for centuries and gained the power to take the form of a beautiful woman, luring men to ensnare and devour. Famous as the haunt of Jōren Falls in the Izu Peninsula.

aliases.name: 女郎蜘蛛
aliases.meaning: 'Whore spider' or 'woman spider', the entomological / vernacular spelling

aliases.name: Jorō spider
aliases.meaning: Trichonephila clavata, the golden silk orb-weaver — the real spider lending its name to the yokai

phenomena.origin: Native to Japanese folklore, with regional legends concentrated in central and western Honshu, especially the Izu Peninsula (Shizuoka), Kashikobuchi (Sendai, Miyagi), and the mountain forests of Kyoto and Kii.

phenomena.name: Jumbie
phenomena.description: Jumbie (also jumbee) is a broad term from Caribbean folklore for supernatural entities — primarily spirits of the dead but also nature spirits, shapeshifters, and other beings — rooted in West and Central African traditions carried to the Caribbean through the transatlantic slave trade.

aliases.name: Duppy
aliases.meaning: Cognate term used in Jamaica and Barbados for ancestral ghost spirits

aliases.name: Mendo
aliases.meaning: Alternative name in Colombia and Venezuela

aliases.name: Chongo
aliases.meaning: Additional alternative name in Colombia and Venezuela

aliases.name: Mocko Jumbie
aliases.meaning: Stilt-dancer figure associated with carnival; protective spirit embodiment

phenomena.origin: English-speaking Caribbean territories, primarily those with British colonial history. Also present in Guyana and some South American territories. Related traditions in French Caribbean (zombi) and Jamaica/Barbados (duppy).

phenomena.name: Kappa
phenomena.description: The kappa (河童, 'river child') is one of the most famous yōkai in Japanese folklore: a child-sized amphibious water-spirit with a turtle-like shell, beaked face, and a water-filled dish (sara) on its head whose drying or spilling renders it powerless.
phenomena.origin: Found throughout Japanese folklore, with strong regional concentrations in Kyushu (garappa, hyōsube) and Tōhoku (Tōno).

phenomena.name: Kapre
phenomena.description: The Kapre is a giant, dark-skinned, tobacco-smoking tree-dwelling spirit of Philippine folklore, traditionally associated with large balete, acacia, and mango trees. Generally non-hostile but mischievous and territorial, the kapre is regarded as a guardian of its tree.

aliases.name: Kapre
aliases.language: Tagalog (loanword from Spanish cafre / Arabic kāfir)
aliases.meaning: From Spanish cafre, ultimately Arabic kāfir ('non-believer'); colonial-era pejorative reapplied to a folkloric giant

aliases.name: Agta
aliases.meaning: 'Black one' / dark-skinned forest giant; regional analogue of the kapre

aliases.name: Chapri
aliases.meaning: Earliest Spanish-language attestation, recorded by Antonio Pigafetta during the Magellan expedition

phenomena.origin: Found throughout the Philippine archipelago, especially in lowland forests, rural barangays, and old agricultural land where balete and other large trees survive.

phenomena.name: Kasa-obake
phenomena.description: A whimsical Japanese yōkai depicted as an old paper umbrella that has come to life, characteristically bearing a single eye, a long lolling tongue, and a single sandaled leg on which it hops about.
phenomena.origin: Kasa-obake is a creature of Japanese popular folklore and art; it is not localized to a particular region but is associated broadly with Edo-period urban culture and tsukumogami traditions.

phenomena.name: Kawa-no-Kami
phenomena.description: Kawa-no-Kami is the generic Shinto designation for a river deity in Japanese mythology — the spirit or god (kami) of a river, sometimes treated as a single 'king of the river gods' and at other times as a class of localized spirits resident in specific rivers.

aliases.name: Kahaku
aliases.meaning: river earl / river lord (河伯), borrowed from Chinese Hebo

aliases.name: Suijin
aliases.meaning: water deity (broader category encompassing river kami)

phenomena.origin: Throughout the Japanese archipelago wherever rivers are venerated; the figure is part of the broader East Asian river-deity complex (Chinese Hebo, Korean Habaek).

phenomena.name: Kecksburg UFO Incident
phenomena.description: On 9 December 1965 a brilliant fireball was observed across at least six U.S. states and parts of Canada; eyewitnesses near Kecksburg, Pennsylvania reported a metallic, acorn-shaped object coming to rest in the woods, where U.S. military personnel are said to have cordoned the area before removing something on a flatbed truck.

aliases.name: Pennsylvania's Roswell
aliases.meaning: popular nickname comparing it to the 1947 Roswell incident

aliases.name: The Kecksburg Acorn
aliases.meaning: from the acorn-shaped object reportedly recovered

aliases.name: December 9, 1965 Great Lakes fireball
aliases.meaning: scientific framing as a wide-area fireball event

phenomena.origin: The fireball was visible from Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Indiana, New York, and parts of Canada. The recovery and military activity reports center on Kecksburg, Pennsylvania.

phenomena.name: Kelpie
phenomena.description: A shape-shifting water spirit of Scottish folklore, most often appearing as a horse near rivers and lochs, that lures victims onto its back and drags them underwater to drown.

aliases.name: Each-uisge
aliases.meaning: 'water horse' — the loch-dwelling cousin of the river kelpie

phenomena.origin: Scotland, particularly the Highlands and the major river systems and lochs; cognate water-horse traditions across Ireland, the Isle of Man, Wales, the Hebrides, Orkney, and Shetland.

phenomena.name: Kidney Thieves Urban Legend
phenomena.description: A widely circulated late-20th-century urban legend in which a traveler, often male, is drugged by a stranger and wakes in a bathtub of ice with a fresh surgical incision and a note instructing them to call 911 because their kidney has been removed for the black market.

aliases.name: Bathtub of Ice
aliases.meaning: from the central image of the legend

regions: United States (esp. New Orleans, Las Vegas, New York)
phenomena.origin: Originated in the United States and spread worldwide via email and social media; localized variants exist in many countries.

phenomena.name: Kikimora
phenomena.description: A female house spirit of Slavic — especially Russian — folklore, often paired with the male domovoi, who keeps the household clean and reasonable when respected but punishes lazy or neglectful families with broken dishes, tangled yarn, sleepless nights, and the tickling of children.

aliases.name: Kikimora bolotnaya
aliases.meaning: swamp kikimora — the wetland-dwelling variant married to the leshy

phenomena.origin: Concentrated in East Slavic territory — Russia, Belarus, parts of Ukraine and Poland — with related figures across the wider Slavic world.

phenomena.name: Kirin (Qilin)
phenomena.description: An auspicious chimerical creature of East Asian mythology — qilin in Chinese, kirin in Japanese, girin in Korean, kỳ lân in Vietnamese — said to appear at the birth or death of a sage or just ruler, and so gentle that it will not tread on living grass or eat living things.

aliases.name: Qilin
aliases.meaning: 麒麟; the original Chinese name

phenomena.origin: Throughout the East Asian cultural sphere — China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam — and in adjacent traditions of Mongolia, Tibet, and Thailand.

phenomena.name: Kitsune
phenomena.description: A Japanese fox spirit possessing intelligence, longevity, magical powers, and the ability to shapeshift — most often into a beautiful woman — and serving in folklore as either a benevolent messenger of the Shinto deity Inari or as a tricksterous, sometimes dangerous wild fox.

aliases.name: Zenko
aliases.meaning: 善狐, benevolent foxes serving Inari

aliases.name: Húli jīng
aliases.meaning: 狐狸精 — Chinese fox spirit, the cultural ancestor

phenomena.origin: Throughout Japan, with particularly dense lore in central Honshū around Kyoto and Inari shrines; cognate fox-spirit traditions extend across China (huli jing), Korea (kumiho), and Vietnam.

phenomena.name: Knocker
phenomena.description: A small, wrinkled, miner-clad subterranean fairy of Cornish and Devon folklore, said to inhabit mines and to make knocking sounds in the rock — sometimes guiding miners toward rich tin or copper veins, sometimes warning of imminent collapse, and sometimes maliciously punishing whistlers or thieves.

aliases.name: Bucca
aliases.meaning: related Cornish folk spirit sometimes equated with the knocker

aliases.name: Tommyknocker
aliases.meaning: American adaptation of the Cornish knocker by Cornish miners in Colorado, Nevada, California, and Pennsylvania

aliases.name: Berggeist / Bergmännlein
aliases.meaning: 'mountain spirit / little mountain man' — German mining-spirit counterpart

aliases.name: Kobold (mining sense)
aliases.meaning: specifically the underground/mine kobold, parallel to the knocker

phenomena.origin: Concentrated in Cornwall and Devon (England) and Wales, with diaspora presence in mining communities of Pennsylvania, Colorado, Nevada, California, Wisconsin, and Michigan, USA — wherever Cornish 'Cousin Jack' miners settled.

phenomena.name: Kongamato
phenomena.description: A reported flying creature of the swamps of north-western Zambia, eastern Angola, and the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, said by Kaonde and Lunda informants to attack boats and inflict severe wounds, and frequently described in cryptozoological literature as resembling a pterosaur — a long-beaked, leathery-winged, toothed flying reptile.

aliases.name: Olitiau
aliases.meaning: another African pterosaur-like cryptid sometimes grouped with the kongamato in cryptozoological literature

phenomena.origin: North-western Zambia (Mwinilunga District and adjacent swamps), the Bangweulu wetlands of north-eastern Zambia, eastern Angola, and the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, with secondary reports from Zimbabwe and Cameroon (where similar cryptids are reported under other names).

phenomena.name: Kraken
phenomena.description: A legendary sea monster of enormous size from Scandinavian folklore, traditionally described as a giant cephalopod dwelling off the coasts of Norway and Greenland, capable of dragging entire ships beneath the waves.

aliases.name: Hafgufa
aliases.meaning: Sea reeker; a medieval sea monster often equated with the Kraken

aliases.name: Sciu-crak
aliases.meaning: Variant name recorded by Francesco Negri in 1700

aliases.name: Krake
aliases.meaning: Indefinite form of the Norwegian word from which Kraken derives

regions: Waters off the coast of Nordland, Norway
phenomena.origin: Legendary range centered on the Norwegian Sea off the coast of Norway, extending to Greenland, Iceland, and in some accounts as far as the waters off Baffin Island, Canada.

phenomena.name: Krampus
phenomena.description: A horned, anthropomorphic figure from Central Alpine folklore who accompanies Saint Nicholas on December 5th (Krampusnacht), punishing misbehaving children with birch rods and threatening to carry the worst offenders away in a sack.
phenomena.origin: Traditional range covers the Central and Eastern Alpine region. Active celebrations are found across Austria, Bavaria, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Northern Italy, and parts of the Low Countries. Since the late 20th century, Krampus traditions have spread to North America and globally.

phenomena.name: Krasue
phenomena.description: A female nocturnal spirit of mainland Southeast Asian folklore, manifesting as a floating disembodied woman's head from which the heart, stomach and other internal organs trail. Belief in the Krasue remains active in rural Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

aliases.name: Ahp
aliases.meaning: from Sanskrit āpyati, 'to cause to suffer'

phenomena.origin: Belief in the Krasue and its cognates spans mainland Southeast Asia and the Malay Archipelago, with the strongest contemporary tradition in rural Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Closely related figures are reported throughout Malaysia, Indonesia (including Bali), the Philippines and parts of Vietnam.

phenomena.name: Kuchisake-onna
phenomena.description: A malevolent female figure of Japanese urban legend who covers her mouth with a surgical mask and asks 'Am I beautiful?' before revealing a mouth slit ear-to-ear. The modern legend caused a documented school-route panic across Japan in 1979.
phenomena.origin: Originated in Gifu Prefecture, Japan, in late 1978 and spread nationally through Japan in 1979. Subsequent transmission carried the legend to South Korea and into the worldwide horror-media imaginary.

phenomena.name: Kunekune
phenomena.description: Kunekune is an internet-born Japanese urban legend describing a slender, white humanoid figure said to appear at midday in summer rice fields, writhing in the wind. Looking at it closely is said to drive the observer insane.
phenomena.origin: A Japanese internet-born legend; locations are narrative rather than mapped, but the canonical setting is the rural Japanese rice paddy.

phenomena.name: La Diablesse
phenomena.description: La Diablesse ('the She-Devil') is a Caribbean folkloric demoness, especially associated with Trinidad and Tobago, who appears as a beautiful woman in old-fashioned dress with one human leg and one cloven cow-hoof, luring men into the forest where they become lost and die.

aliases.name: She-Devil
aliases.meaning: literal English gloss of la diablesse

phenomena.origin: Trinidad and Tobago is the heartland of the La Diablesse tradition, with cognate figures in Grenada, Saint Lucia, Dominica and other French-Creole Caribbean islands.

phenomena.name: La Llorona
phenomena.description: A weeping female ghost said to haunt rivers, lakes, and irrigation channels across Mexico, Central America, parts of South America, and the southwestern United States, mourning the children she drowned. Among the most widespread and durable legends in the Spanish-speaking Americas.

aliases.name: La Malinche (folkloric conflation)
aliases.meaning: Some Mexican variants conflate La Llorona with the historical Doña Marina (La Malinche)

aliases.name: Cihuacóatl
aliases.meaning: 'Serpent woman'; pre-Columbian Aztec mother-goddess identified by Sahagún with a weeping female omen

phenomena.origin: La Llorona is widespread across the Spanish-speaking Americas. Core regions are Mexico (especially central Mexico and the Mexico City basin), the U.S.-Mexico border, and the southwestern United States, with strong variants throughout Central America, in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and as far south as Uruguay.
