Significant regional names include María Pardo and Tarumama in Colombia and La Sayona in Venezuela.

phenomena.name: Lagahoo
phenomena.description: The Lagahoo is a shapeshifting monster of Trinidad and Tobago folklore, drawn from French-Creole loup-garou and West African shapeshifter traditions, who appears at night as a headless man dragging a coffin and chains and can transform into many animals.
phenomena.origin: Trinidad and Tobago, especially rural Trinidad. The figure overlaps in tradition with French-Caribbean loup-garou belief on neighbouring islands.

phenomena.name: Lamassu
phenomena.description: The Lamassu is a Mesopotamian protective deity depicted as a colossal hybrid figure with a human head, the body of a bull or lion and the wings of an eagle. Monumental Assyrian lamassu pairs were placed at city and palace gates from the Neo-Assyrian period.

aliases.name: Lamma
aliases.meaning: early-period name of the protective female deity

aliases.name: Aladlammû
aliases.meaning: winged-bull / guardian spirit, used interchangeably with lamassu in Assyrian contexts

phenomena.origin: Originally an artistic and religious tradition of southern Mesopotamia (Sumer / Akkad); reaches its monumental culmination in the Neo-Assyrian Empire of the 9th–7th centuries BC, with examples from Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh in present-day Iraq. The form was subsequently absorbed by the Achaemenid Persian Empire (Persepolis).

phenomena.name: Langsuir
phenomena.description: The Langsuir is a female revenant of Malay folklore, the ghost of a woman who died in or shortly after childbirth, who flies as a beautiful long-haired woman or as a floating head trailing entrails and feeds on the blood of newborns through a hole in the back of her neck.
phenomena.origin: Belief in the Langsuir is found throughout the Malay world: peninsular Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, parts of southern Thailand and the southern Philippines.

phenomena.name: Lavender Town Syndrome
phenomena.description: Lavender Town Syndrome is a creepypasta — an explicitly fictional internet horror story — first posted in February 2010 alleging that the music of Lavender Town in 1996's Pokémon Red and Green caused suicides and illness in Japanese children. No newspaper records or epidemiological evidence support the claim.
phenomena.origin: Internet-native phenomenon distributed through English- and Japanese-language creepypasta and Pokémon fan communities, with in-game setting in fictional Kanto, Japan.

phenomena.name: Leak
phenomena.description: The Leak (Balinese: Leyak) is a flying-head witch-spirit of Balinese folklore: a practitioner of black magic whose head detaches at night from her body, trailing entrails, to hunt blood — particularly that of pregnant women and newborns. The Leyak serve the witch-queen Rangda.
phenomena.origin: Centred in Bali, Indonesia, with extension to Lombok and Java; the wider Southeast Asian female-vampire complex (Krasue, Penanggalan, Manananggal) shares the detached-head motif.

phenomena.name: Leprechaun
phenomena.description: The leprechaun is a diminutive male solitary fairy of Irish folklore, traditionally portrayed as a shoemaker who guards a hidden hoard of gold. He is descended from Old Irish luchorpán, first attested in the 8th-century saga Echtra Fergusa maic Léti.

aliases.name: luchorpán
aliases.meaning: supposed early form of the name; Old Irish lexicon term

phenomena.origin: Native to the folklore of Ireland; the figure is a defining feature of Irish national folklore and has been transmitted globally through the Irish diaspora and through 20th- and 21st-century popular media.

phenomena.name: Leshy
phenomena.description: A male woodland spirit from Slavic folklore who serves as supernatural guardian and ruler of the forest, capable of changing size and shape, leading travelers astray, and abducting children who venture too deep into the woods.
phenomena.origin: Slavic forest regions of Eastern Europe. Leshy beliefs are most densely documented in the northern forest zones of Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine, extending into Poland and other Slavic territories wherever dense old-growth forest was central to peasant economy.

phenomena.name: Ley Lines
phenomena.description: A claim, originating with Alfred Watkins in the 1920s, that prehistoric sites across Britain are aligned in straight lines. Later mystical reinterpretations proposed invisible energy conduits running through the Earth. The concept has been comprehensively rejected by archaeology and physics.

aliases.name: Heilige Linien
aliases.meaning: Holy lines — term used by Wilhelm Teudt (1909)

aliases.name: Leys
aliases.meaning: Old English for cleared space; adopted by Alfred Watkins as the name for aligned ancient trackways

aliases.name: Lung mei
aliases.meaning: Dragon veins — Chinese geomantic concept incorrectly equated with ley lines by John Michell

phenomena.origin: Claimed in the British Isles (primary focus), Germany, France, and globally in New Age tradition. Watkins's original claims centered on Herefordshire and the wider British Isles. John Michell's later work focused particularly on West Penwith, Cornwall, and Wiltshire.

phenomena.name: Likho
phenomena.description: Likho is the Slavic personification of bad luck and evil fate, most often depicted as a one-eyed gaunt old woman in black or, more rarely, as a male forest goblin. It is a fairy-tale figure rather than a major mythological deity, woven into proverbs warning against tempting fate.

aliases.name: One-eyed Likho
aliases.meaning: Лихо одноглазое — single-eyed personification of misfortune

phenomena.origin: Likho is a figure of East and West Slavic folklore, most prominent in Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Polish tradition. The figure is woven into proverbs and fairy tales rather than tied to a specific landscape.

phenomena.name: Liminal Spaces
phenomena.description: Liminal spaces are an internet-born aesthetic of empty, transitional or transitionary built environments — corridors, hotel hallways, abandoned malls, stairwells — photographed without people, where the absence of human presence makes a familiar place feel uncanny, eerie, and dreamlike.

aliases.name: Weirdcore
aliases.meaning: Adjacent low-fidelity online aesthetic often paired with liminal imagery

phenomena.origin: Global, networked phenomenon: imagery is sourced from buildings worldwide but circulates almost entirely online via Anglophone social-media platforms.

phenomena.name: Lindworm
phenomena.description: A lindworm is a serpentine dragon of Germanic, Norse and Central European folklore — typically wingless, with two clawed forelimbs in continental traditions and entirely limbless in much Swedish lore. Unlike fire-breathing medieval dragons, lindworms emphasise venom, constriction, and treasure-hoarding.

aliases.name: Hjulorm
aliases.meaning: 'wheel-worm' — variant that bites its tail to roll

phenomena.origin: Lindworm folklore is concentrated in the Germanic-speaking and North European world: Scandinavia, the German-speaking lands, the Low Countries, and the British Isles, with regional offshoots reaching into Slavic and Baltic dragon imagery.

phenomena.name: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp
phenomena.description: The Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp is a reptilian humanoid cryptid reported around Bishopville, Lee County, South Carolina, after a 1988 encounter by a 17-year-old motorist named Christopher Davis. Subsequent reports of vehicle damage, footprints and brief follow-up sightings made it a national news story that summer.

aliases.name: Scape Ore Lizard Man
aliases.region: Scape Ore Swamp, South Carolina, USA

phenomena.origin: Reports are tightly concentrated around Scape Ore Swamp and Browntown in Lee County, South Carolina, particularly along rural roads north of Bishopville.

phenomena.name: Loch Ness Monster
phenomena.description: A large aquatic cryptid said to inhabit Loch Ness, a deep freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands. The most reported lake monster in the world, with a continuous record of sightings since the 1930s and a distant precursor in the 6th-century Life of St. Columba.

aliases.name: Nessie
aliases.meaning: Affectionate diminutive in widespread use from the 1940s onwards

phenomena.origin: Reports are confined to Loch Ness in the Scottish Highlands, with a minor secondary tradition (the Morag) in the nearby Loch Morar.

phenomena.name: Loup-Garou
phenomena.description: The Loup-Garou is the French-language werewolf, transplanted by French settlers into Louisiana (where it became the Rougarou of the bayous), into Haitian and Caribbean Creole cultures (Lougarou, Loogaroo), and into French Canadian / Métis tradition. It is typically a human cursed to transform into a wolf-like or hybrid form by breaking Catholic Lenten observance.
phenomena.origin: The loup-garou tradition is found wherever French and French-Creole communities settled: continental France (especially rural Catholic regions), French Canada, Louisiana (Acadiana and Greater New Orleans), Haiti, and the wider Francophone Caribbean. Métis and Ojibwe communities of the Great Lakes have a related rugaru figure.

phenomena.name: Loveland Frog
phenomena.description: The Loveland Frog (or Frogman) is a roughly four-foot-tall bipedal humanoid with leathery skin and a frog- or lizard-like face, reported around Loveland, Ohio along the Little Miami River. It is most famous for two 1972 sightings by Loveland police officers — one of whom later identified the creature as a tailless escaped iguana.
phenomena.origin: Reports are tightly localised to Loveland, Ohio and the Little Miami River corridor in Hamilton, Clermont, and Warren counties.

phenomena.name: Luferlang
phenomena.description: The Luferlang is a 'fearsome critter' of North American logging-camp tall tales, recorded in Henry H. Tryon's 1939 Fearsome Critters as a hideous equine beast with triple-jointed legs that allow it to run equally fast in any direction, a dark blue dorsal stripe, a swivel-jointed tail set in the middle of its back, and a single deadly bite delivered only once a year.
phenomena.origin: A creature of the oral tradition of North American logging camps, with no fixed real-world range. Tryon (1939) places fearsome critters generally in the forests of the northern United States and Canada.

phenomena.name: Lusca
phenomena.description: The Lusca is a marine cryptid of Bahamian and Caribbean folklore, said to inhabit the blue holes of Andros Island and surrounding waters. It is most often described as a gigantic octopus or a half-octopus, half-shark or half-dragon hybrid, and is blamed locally for the deaths of swimmers, divers and small craft drawn into blue-hole tidal currents.
phenomena.origin: Lusca legends are concentrated on Andros Island, Bahamas, and extend through the Bahamas and the wider Caribbean wherever blue holes and cave systems exist.

phenomena.name: Madremonte
phenomena.description: Madremonte (Madre Monte, 'Mother Mountain' or 'Mother of the Forest') is a powerful female nature-spirit in Colombian folklore — protector of forests, rivers, and animals — who punishes those who damage the environment and is recognised across Andean Colombia and parts of the Caribbean coast.
phenomena.origin: Madremonte is most prominent in the Andean regions of Colombia — including Antioquia, the central and western Andes, the Eje Cafetero coffee-growing zones, and the Magdalena and Valle del Cauca river basins. Closely related figures (Fantasma del Monte, Madre Selva, Madre de los Cerros) appear in Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay.

phenomena.name: Mae Nak Phra Khanong
phenomena.description: Mae Nak Phra Khanong ('Lady Nak of Phra Khanong') is the most popular ghost of Thai folklore: a young woman of the Phra Khanong canal who died with her child in childbirth and returned as a phi tai thang klom to live with her unsuspecting husband Mak. Her shrine at Wat Mahabut in Bangkok remains a major pilgrimage site.

aliases.name: Amdaeng Nak
aliases.meaning: Earlier Thai title used in 19th-century newspaper accounts

phenomena.origin: Mae Nak's narrative and devotional practice are concentrated in Bangkok, particularly in the Phra Khanong / Suan Luang area, but her cultural reach extends throughout Thailand and across the Thai-speaking diaspora.

phenomena.name: Mahaha
phenomena.description: The Mahaha is a malevolent spirit of Inuit oral tradition: a thin, blue-skinned, perpetually grinning demon of the Arctic that ambushes lone travellers and tickles them to death with long, sharp-clawed fingers, leaving its victims with a frozen smile.
phenomena.origin: Mahaha stories are part of Inuit oral tradition across the Canadian Arctic (Inuit Nunangat); they are best documented in popular folklore writing rather than in tightly-localised regional accounts.

phenomena.name: Mahr
phenomena.description: A malicious entity in Germanic and Slavic folklore that sits on sleepers' chests during the night, causing nightmares, chest pressure, cold sweats, and sleep paralysis — the supernatural explanation for a cluster of experiences now understood as sleep paralysis.
phenomena.origin: Germanic and Slavic Europe, with the broadest distribution across Northern and Central Europe and Scandinavia. Related traditions with the same sleep-paralysis substrate exist globally.

phenomena.name: Mama Dlo
phenomena.description: A Caribbean water guardian spirit, particularly prominent in Trinidad and Tobago, depicted as a beautiful woman from the waist up with the lower body of a great snake. She protects rivers, streams, and the animals that live in them.
phenomena.origin: Folkloric tradition of the southern Caribbean, particularly Trinidad and Tobago, with related figures in Saint Lucia and Dominica.

phenomena.name: Mamlambo
phenomena.description: A river goddess and serpent water spirit of South African (especially Zulu and Xhosa) tradition, said to grant wealth to those who keep her — and to take a heavy toll from those who do.

aliases.name: Brain Sucker
aliases.meaning: Local nickname coined during the 1997 Mzintlava River reports

phenomena.origin: Eastern and southern South Africa, particularly within Zulu and Xhosa cultural areas; the most widely reported modern episode centred on the Mzintlava River near Mount Ayliff in the Eastern Cape (1997).

phenomena.name: Mammon
phenomena.description: A biblical and later Christian personification of wealth and greed. Originally an Aramaic word for 'riches' used in the Gospels, Mammon was later treated in Christian thought as a false god and, in medieval and Renaissance literature, as a fallen angel and demon of avarice.
phenomena.origin: A figure of Christian theology and Western literature; not tied to a specific geographic locale.

phenomena.name: Man-Monkey
phenomena.description: A black, ape-like figure with large white eyes reported on the Shropshire Union Canal at Bridge 39, near Norbury Junction on the Staffordshire–Shropshire border. The original 1879 encounter was recorded by folklorist Charlotte Sophia Burne in 1883.

aliases.name: Man-Monkey of the Shropshire Union Canal

phenomena.origin: Reports are localized to the Shropshire Union Canal corridor near the Staffordshire–Shropshire border, especially the area around Norbury Junction and the canal bridge identified as Bridge 39.

phenomena.name: Manananggal
phenomena.description: A creature of Filipino folklore, especially in the Visayan regions, that appears as a woman by day and at night separates her upper torso from her lower body, sprouting bat-like wings and flying in search of pregnant women, infants, and lovers, on whom she preys with an elongated proboscis-like tongue.
phenomena.origin: Throughout the Philippines, but most strongly associated with the Visayan region — particularly the provinces of Capiz, Iloilo, Antique, and Bohol — which is also the cultural heartland of the broader aswang tradition.

phenomena.name: Mandela Effect
phenomena.description: A phenomenon in which large numbers of people share a confidently held but factually incorrect memory. Named by Fiona Broome in 2009 after the widespread false memory of Nelson Mandela having died in prison in the 1980s — Mandela was in fact released in 1990 and died in 2013.
phenomena.origin: Reported globally wherever there is a shared culture and a strong online discussion community; most documentation is in English-language media.

phenomena.name: Manticore
phenomena.description: A man-eating creature of Persian origin, first described in Greek by the physician-historian Ctesias in the 5th century BCE. The manticore has the body of a lion, the face of a man with three rows of teeth, and a tail tipped with venomous spines or a scorpion's sting.

aliases.name: Martichora
aliases.meaning: transliteration of the Old Persian name

phenomena.origin: Originally placed in 'India' by Ctesias and his Greek and Latin successors. In medieval bestiaries and heraldry the creature is generic to far-eastern and exotic landscapes.

phenomena.name: Mapinguari
phenomena.description: A large, foul-smelling, hair-covered cryptid of the Brazilian and Peruvian Amazon, reported across multiple Indigenous traditions. Some cryptozoologists, notably ornithologist David Oren, have proposed that Mapinguari reports may reflect a surviving population of giant ground sloth.
phenomena.origin: Reported throughout the Amazon basin, particularly in the Brazilian states of Acre, Rondônia, Pará, and Amazonas, as well as in adjacent Peru and Bolivia. Especially strong in Karitiana, Machiguenga, and Mura territories.

phenomena.name: Mara
phenomena.description: A female nightmare spirit of Germanic and Slavic folklore who 'rides' sleepers and presses on their chests, producing the experience that gave English the word 'nightmare' (literally 'night-mara').
phenomena.origin: Germanic-, Scandinavian-, and Slavic-speaking Europe, with strong continuity from medieval to modern times.

phenomena.name: Mare
phenomena.description: The pan-European nightmare spirit — the 'mare' from which English 'nightmare' (literally 'night-mare') is derived. A malicious entity, typically female, in Germanic and Slavic folklore that 'rides' people's chests at night.
phenomena.origin: Across Germanic-, Scandinavian-, and Slavic-speaking Europe, with cognates and continuations into modern French (cauchemar) and many other languages.

phenomena.name: Marfa Lights
phenomena.description: Anomalous nocturnal lights observed on Mitchell Flat east of Marfa, Texas, since at least 1883. The lights typically appear as glowing, drifting orbs that hover, split, merge, and move erratically; a 2004 University of Texas at Dallas physics study attributed many modern observations to refracted headlights from U.S. Highway 67 between Marfa and Presidio.
phenomena.origin: Mitchell Flat, east of Marfa, Texas, in the Trans-Pecos region.

phenomena.name: Marid
phenomena.description: A category of powerful, rebellious jinn in Islamic theology and Arabian folklore. The Quran (37:7) speaks of stars guarding the lowest heaven against the 'rebellious devils' (shayṭānin māridin), and later Arabic literature, including the Thousand and One Nights, treats the Marid as among the strongest classes of jinn.
phenomena.origin: Pan-Islamic — present wherever Islamic theology and Arabic folklore are transmitted; especially prominent in classical Arabic literature.

phenomena.name: Marozi
phenomena.description: A reported small, highland-dwelling lion of East Africa with retained leopard-like spots into adulthood and a reduced or absent mane. Two specimens were shot in the Kenyan Aberdares in 1931 but no living example or accepted subspecies has been confirmed.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrated in the Kenyan central highlands — particularly the Aberdare Range, the Mau Escarpment edge, and the Kinangop Plateau — with neighbouring reports from highland Tanzania, Uganda, and the Virunga / Rwanda border (sometimes treated as the related ikimizi and ntararago).

phenomena.name: Mary Celeste
phenomena.description: An American brigantine found drifting in good order but completely abandoned in the Atlantic east of the Azores on 4 December 1872; her ten-person company — Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife and infant daughter, and seven crew — were never seen again.

aliases.name: Marie Celeste
aliases.meaning: Misspelling popularised by Arthur Conan Doyle's 1884 short story 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement'

aliases.name: Amazon
aliases.meaning: Original name of the brigantine before her 1868 sale and renaming

phenomena.origin: The events occurred in the central North Atlantic, with the abandonment somewhere east of the Azores. The ship was found at approximately 38°20′N 17°15′W, midway between the Azores and the Portuguese coast.

phenomena.name: Māui
phenomena.description: Māui is the great culture-hero and trickster of Polynesian mythology, credited across the Pacific with snaring the sun, fishing up islands, securing fire for humanity, and ultimately dying in his attempt to defeat death.
phenomena.origin: The Māui cycle is told across virtually all of Polynesia. Wikipedia notes the tradition can be traced 'as far west as islands off New Guinea' and is found in Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa, Tonga, Sāmoa, Tahiti, Mangareva, the Marquesas, the New Hebrides (Vanuatu), and beyond.

phenomena.name: Medusa
phenomena.description: In Greek mythology, the only mortal of the three Gorgon sisters, whose gaze turned onlookers to stone and who was beheaded by the hero Perseus; her severed head, the Gorgoneion, became Athena's apotropaic symbol set on the Aegis.

aliases.name: Gorgo / Gorgon
aliases.meaning: 'Dreadful one'; used for all three Gorgon sisters

regions: Mythic 'far west' beyond Ocean (in archaic geography)
phenomena.origin: Medusa is a figure of ancient Greek mythology, transmitted across the Greek and Roman Mediterranean and into the broader European tradition through Latin sources (notably Ovid).

phenomena.name: Melon Heads
phenomena.description: Regional American urban legends — concentrated in Michigan, Ohio and Connecticut — describing small humanoid beings with grossly enlarged heads who emerge at night from forested back roads, asylum sites, or rural mansions to attack trespassers.
phenomena.origin: Three principal regional clusters in the United States: Michigan (especially the Felt Mansion area in Saugatuck Township, Allegan County), Ohio (Kirtland in Lake County and Chardon Township in Geauga County), and Connecticut (southern Litchfield County, central/eastern Fairfield County, western New Haven County).

phenomena.name: Men in Black
phenomena.description: Mysterious figures in dark suits who, in modern UFO lore beginning with Albert K. Bender (1953), allegedly visit witnesses of UFO sightings to intimidate them into silence; the tradition was popularised in print by Gray Barker and John Keel and has since become deeply embedded in popular culture.

aliases.name: Three Men in Black
aliases.meaning: Phrasing used by Albert K. Bender in his 1962 account

phenomena.origin: Reports are concentrated in the United States, with secondary reports in the United Kingdom, continental Europe, and Latin America.

phenomena.name: Menehune
phenomena.description: A legendary race of small, industrious people in Hawaiian tradition, said to have inhabited the islands before Polynesian settlers and to have built stonework, fishponds, and heiau by night — most famously the Menehune (Alekoko) Fishpond and the Kīkīaola ditch on Kauaʻi.

aliases.name: Manahune
aliases.meaning: 'Lowly people' or 'commoner' — proposed root by Katharine Luomala

phenomena.origin: The Menehune are a tradition of the Hawaiian Islands, with the densest cycle of stories on the island of Kauaʻi and adjacent Oʻahu.

phenomena.name: Min Min Light
phenomena.description: An anomalous light phenomenon reported across the Australian outback — most famously near Boulia in Queensland's Channel Country — and now widely attributed by physicist Jack Pettigrew (2003) to an inferior-mirage Fata Morgana effect over cool, still inland air.
phenomena.origin: Reports range across outback Australia from western New South Wales (Brewarrina) north to Boulia in northern Queensland, with additional sightings in Yunta (South Australia) and the Pilbara (Western Australia). The classic location is the Channel Country of western Queensland.
phenomena.first_reported: Pre-contact (Aboriginal traditions); reported in European-language sources from the late 19th c.

phenomena.name: Minhocão
phenomena.description: A 19th-century Brazilian cryptid reported chiefly in southern Brazil — described as a vast subterranean black-scaled worm or eel-like creature blamed for tunnels, trenches, and toppled trees — investigated by Auguste de Saint-Hilaire (1846) and Fritz Müller (1877–1878) and now generally treated as a folkloric explanation of soil-erosion and slumping events.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in southern Brazil (especially Santa Catarina and Paraná around Curitibanos), with secondary reports in Goiás and São Paulo; Saint-Hilaire's accounts also included locations such as Padre Aranda and Lake Feia.

phenomena.name: Minotaur
phenomena.description: In Greek mythology, the bull-headed son of Pasiphaë and the Cretan Bull, kept by King Minos in Daedalus's Labyrinth at Knossos and slain by the Athenian hero Theseus with the help of Ariadne and her thread.

aliases.name: Asterion
aliases.meaning: 'Starry one' — the creature's true name in Pseudo-Apollodorus

aliases.name: Minotauros
aliases.meaning: 'Bull of Minos' — Μῑνώταυρος, from Μίνως (Minos) + ταῦρος (bull)

phenomena.origin: The Minotaur is a figure of ancient Cretan and pan-Hellenic Greek mythology, transmitted across the Greek and Roman Mediterranean and into the wider European tradition.

phenomena.name: Mngwa
phenomena.description: A large, grey-brindled mystery cat reported from the coastal regions of Tanzania and Zanzibar, East Africa, described as significantly larger than a lion with tabby-like markings and held responsible for a series of human fatalities investigated by British officials in the 1920s.

aliases.name: Nunda
aliases.meaning: Fierce animal; cruel man; something heavy

aliases.name: Nunda, Eater of People
aliases.meaning: Fierce man-eating creature (from the fairy tale collected by Steere, 1870)

phenomena.origin: Reported from the coastal regions of mainland Tanzania and the island of Zanzibar; tradition associated with Swahili-speaking peoples of the East African coast.

phenomena.name: Mo'o
phenomena.description: Shapeshifting lizard spirits in Hawaiian mythology who serve as powerful ancestral guardians (ʻaumākua) of freshwater sources, manifesting as monstrous reptiles, tiny geckos, or humans, and revered as sacred protectors of the land and water.

aliases.name: Moʻo
aliases.meaning: Lizard; also used for succession or continuity — the name carries multiple layered meanings

regions: Oʻahu — particularly Kawainui Marsh (windward) and Waialua
Hawaii Island — various streams and pools
phenomena.origin: All major Hawaiian islands. Moʻo are associated with specific named water bodies throughout the archipelago. Comparable water guardian traditions exist across Polynesia.

phenomena.name: Moehau Man
phenomena.description: A large, hairy bipedal cryptid said to inhabit the rugged Moehau Range and other forested ranges of New Zealand, often linked by Maori tradition to the maeroero, a wild bush-dwelling people.

aliases.name: Moehau
aliases.region: Coromandel Peninsula, North Island, New Zealand

phenomena.origin: Primarily the Moehau Range and broader Coromandel Peninsula of the North Island, New Zealand. In Maori tradition the maeroero are spoken of in remote bush regions across both the North and South Islands.

phenomena.name: Mogwai
phenomena.description: Mogwai (魔鬼, Cantonese mō gwái) is a Chinese term for demons, devils, or evil spirits, denoting a category of malevolent supernatural beings in Chinese folk and religious traditions.
regions: Sinosphere (Vietnam, Korea, Japan via Buddhist transmission)
phenomena.origin: Mogwai are part of the broad Chinese demonological tradition and appear throughout Chinese-speaking cultures and the Sinosphere (where Chinese Buddhism and Daoism shaped local folklore).

phenomena.name: El Mohán
phenomena.description: El Mohán is a Colombian folk figure — a hairy, long-bearded river spirit and shamanic ancestor associated with the Magdalena River and the rivers of Tolima and Huila — said to seduce young women, harass fishermen, and guard hidden treasures.

aliases.name: Mohanes
aliases.region: Colombia and parts of South and Central America

phenomena.origin: Strongest in the Magdalena River basin and the central Andean Colombian departments of Tolima and Huila. Variants of the figure (Muan, Moan, Poira, Mohanes) appear across Colombia and into other parts of South and Central America.

phenomena.name: Mokele-mbembe
phenomena.description: Mokele-mbembe is a legendary water-dwelling creature of Congo Basin folklore, sometimes described in modern cryptozoology as a surviving sauropod-like animal of the Likouala swamps and Lake Tele.

aliases.name: Mokèlé-mbèmbé
aliases.meaning: commonly translated as 'one who stops the flow of rivers'

phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the Likouala region and around Lake Tele in the Republic of the Congo, with adjacent reports from Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

phenomena.name: Momo the Missouri Monster
phenomena.description: Momo (the Missouri Monster) is a Bigfoot-type cryptid reportedly seen near Louisiana, Missouri in the early 1970s, most famously during a brief 'monster flap' in July 1972.
phenomena.origin: Highly localised to the area around Louisiana, Missouri, in Pike County, Missouri, along the Mississippi River.

phenomena.name: Momo Challenge hoax
phenomena.description: The 'Momo Challenge' was a 2018-2019 internet hoax and media-driven moral panic alleging that a sinister character named 'Momo' contacted children via WhatsApp and YouTube and instructed them to perform self-harm; investigators, platforms and child-safety organisations found no evidence of any such challenge.

aliases.name: Momo
aliases.region: Used as the avatar image of the hoax

phenomena.origin: Global, on the English-language internet, with substantial coverage in Latin America, India, Europe and North America.

phenomena.name: Mongolian Death Worm
phenomena.description: The Mongolian Death Worm (olgoi-khorkhoi, 'large intestine worm') is a cryptid said to inhabit the Gobi Desert of Mongolia, described by Mongolian herders as a thick, dark-red, intestine-like worm credited with the ability to kill at a distance.
phenomena.origin: The most desolate parts of the Gobi Desert, principally in southern and western Mongolia, with adjacent ranges sometimes mentioned in folklore.

phenomena.name: Montauk Project
phenomena.description: The Montauk Project is a conspiracy theory alleging that secret U.S. government experiments in time travel, teleportation, mind control and contact with extraterrestrials were conducted at Camp Hero / Montauk Air Force Station on Long Island, New York; the claims, originating with Preston Nichols and Peter Moon in the early 1990s, are widely characterised as fiction.
phenomena.origin: Allegedly centred at Camp Hero / Montauk Air Force Station on the eastern tip of Long Island, New York. As a conspiracy theory it has spread globally through Nichols' and Moon's books and subsequent media adaptations.

phenomena.name: Moon landing conspiracy theories
phenomena.description: Moon landing conspiracy theories claim that NASA's six crewed Apollo lunar landings between 1969 and 1972 were faked; the claims have been examined and rebutted by scientists, engineers, multiple independent national space agencies, and physical evidence on the Moon itself.

aliases.name: We Never Went to the Moon

phenomena.origin: Originated in the United States, with significant followings in Russia, the United Kingdom and elsewhere; the conspiracy theory circulates globally on the internet.

phenomena.name: Mothman
phenomena.description: A large winged humanoid creature with glowing red eyes reported in and around Point Pleasant, West Virginia from November 1966 through December 1967. Sightings clustered near the abandoned 'TNT area' of a former World War II munitions plant. The phenomenon culminated, in popular culture, in the December 15, 1967 collapse of the Silver Bridge.

aliases.name: Bird
aliases.region: Point Pleasant, West Virginia (early 1966 newspaper headlines)
aliases.meaning: How witnesses initially described it before 'Mothman' was coined

aliases.name: Cornstalk's Curse (folkloric framing)
aliases.meaning: Local folklore tying the entity to a curse on Point Pleasant attributed to the Shawnee chief Cornstalk after his 1777 murder

phenomena.origin: Sightings centered on Point Pleasant, West Virginia and the immediate Ohio River Valley (Mason County, WV; Gallia County, OH; Meigs County, OH). A small number of contemporaneous reports came from elsewhere in the eastern United States but the canonical wave is local.

phenomena.name: The Mothman Prophecies
phenomena.description: The Mothman Prophecies is a 1975 nonfiction book by John Keel investigating the Mothman sightings around Point Pleasant, West Virginia (1966-1967), the December 1967 Silver Bridge collapse, and associated UFO and 'ultraterrestrial' phenomena, later adapted into a 2002 film directed by Mark Pellington.
phenomena.origin: Published worldwide as paranormal nonfiction; the 2002 film had global theatrical and home-media distribution.

phenomena.name: Mount Shasta
phenomena.description: Mount Shasta is a 14,179-foot (4,322 m) stratovolcano in the southern Cascade Range of Siskiyou County, California, sacred to multiple Indigenous nations (Shasta, Karuk, Modoc, Wintu, Klamath) and a focal point of modern paranormal traditions including the legend of the hidden Lemurian city of Telos and Guy Ballard's 'I AM' Activity.
phenomena.origin: Single mountain in Siskiyou County, northern California, with cultural and paranormal influence felt across the western United States and globally through New Age and UFO-religion networks.

phenomena.name: Mystery Airships (1896-1897)
phenomena.description: The 'Mystery Airships' wave of 1896-1897 was a major pre-aviation mass sighting episode in which thousands of Americans reported large cigar-shaped craft with searchlights and propellers crossing the night sky, beginning over Sacramento, California in November 1896 and spreading across much of the United States by April 1897.
phenomena.origin: Reports spread across California beginning in November 1896, reached Arizona Territory, Nevada, Oregon, Washington and British Columbia, and then jumped to the Midwest (Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota) in February-April 1897, with thousands of reported sightings.

phenomena.name: Nachtkrapp
phenomena.description: A folkloric nocturnal bird-like creature of Germanic and Central European tradition, invoked chiefly to frighten children into obedience and bed. Reports cluster in southern Germany and Austria, with related figures across northern Germany, Hungary, Poland, and Sweden.

aliases.name: Nattramn
aliases.meaning: night raven; ghost of an unbaptized child or unholy burial

phenomena.origin: Primarily attested in southern Germany and Austria, with cognate figures across northern Germany, Central Europe (Hungary, Poland), and Sweden.

phenomena.name: Nachzehrer
phenomena.description: A revenant of northern Germanic folklore believed to remain in its grave chewing its burial shroud and its own flesh, draining the life of surviving relatives at a distance. Distinct from the more familiar bloodsucking vampire of Slavic and English-language tradition.

aliases.name: Nachzehrer
aliases.meaning: after-consumer; one who consumes after death

phenomena.origin: Folklore of the Nachzehrer is concentrated in northern Germany, Silesia, Bavaria, and Kashubia (northern Poland).

phenomena.name: Naga
phenomena.description: A divine, semi-divine race of serpent beings central to Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology and to the religious life of South and Southeast Asia. Nagas are guardians of waters and treasures, capable of taking serpent, human, or hybrid form.

aliases.name: Nāga
aliases.meaning: snake; in particular the Indian cobra (Naja naja)

phenomena.origin: Veneration and folklore of nagas extend across South Asia and mainland and maritime Southeast Asia, with significant Tibetan and Himalayan traditions.

phenomena.name: Nandi Bear
phenomena.description: An East African cryptid reported chiefly from western Kenya during the 19th and early 20th centuries, described as a powerful, bipedally-rearing carnivore with high front shoulders and a sloping back. No specimen has ever been collected; mainstream zoologists attribute reports to misidentification of known animals.
phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in western Kenya and adjacent parts of East Africa.

phenomena.name: Nang Kwak
phenomena.description: A benevolent female household deity of Thai folk religion, regarded as the patron of merchants and a bringer of customers and prosperity. Depicted as a beautiful woman in red Thai dress, kneeling, with her right hand raised in a beckoning gesture.

aliases.name: Nang Supawadee
aliases.meaning: name in the Buddhist origin legend

phenomena.origin: Veneration is centered in Thailand and extends to ethnic-Thai and Chinese-Thai communities across Southeast Asia, with documented presence in Hong Kong.

phenomena.name: Nang Mai
phenomena.description: A general Thai folkloric category of female spirits that inhabit large trees. Specific named tree spirits — including Nang Tani and Nang Ta-khian — are types of Nang Mai. The male equivalent is the Rukkhadeva.

aliases.name: นางไม้
aliases.meaning: Lady of the Tree / Wood Lady

phenomena.origin: Nang Mai veneration is found throughout Thailand and in adjacent Theravada-Buddhist Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Nang Tani
phenomena.description: A female tree spirit of Thai (and Lao and Cambodian) folklore, believed to inhabit clumps of the wild banana Musa acuminata (kluai tani). She is one of the best-known Nang Mai (tree spirits) and is generally benevolent, though said to harm men who have wronged women.

aliases.name: Phi Tani
aliases.meaning: Ghost of Tani (ผีตานี)

aliases.name: Phrai Tani
aliases.meaning: Nymph of Tani (พรายตานี)

phenomena.origin: Folklore of Nang Tani is concentrated in Thailand and extends to neighboring Laos and Cambodia.

phenomena.name: Nazca Lines
phenomena.description: An extensive group of pre-Columbian geoglyphs scratched into the desert pampa between the towns of Nazca and Palpa in southern Peru, created by the Paracas and Nazca cultures roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.
phenomena.origin: Concentrated in the arid Pampas de Jumana plateau between Nazca and Palpa in southern Peru, approximately 400 km south of Lima.

phenomena.name: Near-Death Experiences
phenomena.description: Profound personal experiences associated with death or impending death, often reported by survivors of cardiac arrest and other life-threatening events. Common features include out-of-body sensations, passage through a tunnel, encounters with light and deceased relatives, and life review.

aliases.name: Recalled Experience of Death (RED)
aliases.meaning: 2022 terminology proposed by NDE researchers for rigorous distinction

phenomena.origin: NDEs are reported worldwide and cross-culturally, with documented research in North America, Europe, and Asia.

phenomena.name: Nekomata
phenomena.description: A class of supernatural cat (yōkai) of Japanese folklore, distinguished by a forked tail and powers of necromancy and shapeshifting. Two principal subtypes are recognized: large mountain nekomata that prey on humans, and household cats that transform into nekomata with great age.

aliases.name: 猫また / 猫又 / 猫股 / 猫胯

phenomena.origin: The nekomata is a Japanese folkloric figure attested across the Japanese archipelago, with particular regional associations including Mount Nekomata (Nekomatayama) in Etchū Province (modern Toyama Prefecture).

phenomena.name: New World Order
phenomena.description: A family of conspiracy theories alleging that a secretive power-elite is conspiring to establish an authoritarian one-world government, displacing democratic nation-states. Mainstream scholarship treats it as an unfounded conspiracy narrative rather than as a description of any actual coordinated plot.
phenomena.origin: Belief in the New World Order is concentrated in Anglophone right-wing political subcultures, especially in the United States, with significant uptake in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and across the European far right; online distribution has globalized the discourse.

phenomena.name: Người Rừng
phenomena.description: A proposed Indochinese hominid cryptid reported from the dense forests of Vietnam and Laos, broadly analogous to the North American Bigfoot. Reports cluster in the Vu Quang region of Vietnam and on the Vietnam-Laos border; no specimen has been collected.
regions: Vu Quang National Park (Hà Tĩnh Province)
phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the forested mountains of central Vietnam (notably the Vu Quang region) and along the Vietnam-Laos border, with related Batutut/Ujit accounts extending into Laos and reportedly into northern Borneo.

phenomena.name: Nguruvilu
phenomena.description: A serpentine water creature of Mapuche folklore in Chile and Argentina with a fox-like head and snake-like body, blamed for drownings in lakes, rivers, and treacherous fords.

aliases.name: Ngarrafilu
aliases.region: Neuquén Province, Argentina (Limay River, Aluminé Lake)

aliases.name: Lord of the water
aliases.meaning: Euphemism used to avoid speaking the creature's true name

phenomena.origin: Lakes, rivers, and water crossings in Mapuche cultural territory across southern Chile and southwestern Argentina.

phenomena.name: Nian
phenomena.description: A beast of Chinese folklore said to emerge at the end of each lunar year to attack villages, scared off by the colour red, fire, and loud noises — the etiological story for many Chinese New Year traditions.
phenomena.origin: Greater China and the global Chinese diaspora; the Nian is a pan-Chinese folkloric figure attached to Lunar New Year customs.

phenomena.name: Night Hag
phenomena.description: A supernatural figure reported in folk traditions worldwide as the cause of sleep paralysis: a malevolent presence that sits, presses, or 'rides' on the chest of a paralyzed sleeper.
phenomena.origin: Reports of night-hag-type sleep paralysis encounters are documented in nearly every studied human culture.

phenomena.name: Night Marchers
phenomena.description: Spectral processions of ancient Hawaiian warriors said to march along ancient trails in the islands at night, escorting deceased aliʻi and dangerous to mortals who look upon them.
phenomena.origin: Reports are concentrated on the Hawaiian Islands, particularly along ancient trails, near heiau, and at recorded battlefields.

phenomena.name: Nightmare
phenomena.description: The mare — a female demon of Germanic and Slavic folklore that rides sleepers' chests, causing sleep paralysis and bad dreams. The original referent of the modern English word 'nightmare'.

aliases.name: Mare
aliases.language: Old English / Old Norse / Common Germanic

phenomena.origin: Germanic and Slavic Europe; the mare and her cognates are documented across Scandinavia, the Low Countries, German-speaking Europe, the British Isles, and Slavic lands.

phenomena.name: Nine-Tailed Fox
phenomena.description: A powerful fox spirit of East Asian mythology, distinguished by nine tails. It can live for centuries, accumulate spiritual power, and shapeshift into a beautiful human — beneficent in early Chinese tradition, often seductive and dangerous in later accounts.
phenomena.origin: East Asia: China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

phenomena.name: Ninki Nanka
phenomena.description: A dragon-like cryptid of West African folklore, particularly in the Gambia and Senegal, said to inhabit swamps and rivers and feared as a deadly omen. Investigated in 2006 by the Centre for Fortean Zoology.

aliases.name: Dragon
aliases.meaning: Per Mandinka tradition the name simply translates as 'dragon' or 'great serpent'

phenomena.origin: West Africa, with the strongest concentration of accounts in the Gambia, Senegal, and surrounding Mandinka-speaking areas.

phenomena.name: Nix
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting water spirit of Germanic and Scandinavian folklore that lures victims with enchanting music — often violin — and drowns them, with regional male and female forms.
phenomena.origin: Germanic and Nordic Europe, including England (as the Old English nicor and its descendants), Germany, the Low Countries, Scandinavia, Finland, and Estonia.

phenomena.name: Not Deer
phenomena.description: An internet-era cryptid that emerged in 2019 — a deer-shaped creature that strikes observers as fundamentally 'wrong'. Strongly associated with Appalachia and propagated through Tumblr and TikTok.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in the Appalachian region of the eastern United States, with online accounts also from elsewhere in North America.

phenomena.name: Nuckelavee
phenomena.description: A skinless horse-and-rider demon of Orkney folklore, described as the most malevolent being in Orcadian tradition. Blamed for droughts, epidemics, and mortasheen, and repelled by fresh water.

aliases.name: Knoggelvi
aliases.meaning: 'Devil of the Sea' (per Walter Traill Dennison)

phenomena.origin: Orkney Islands, off the north coast of Scotland.

phenomena.name: Nue
phenomena.description: A chimeric yokai of Japanese legend with a monkey's head, a tanuki's body, a tiger's limbs, and a snake-tail; famous for the Heian-period account of the warrior Minamoto no Yorimasa shooting it down to cure Emperor Konoe.
phenomena.origin: Japan; the canonical narrative is set at the imperial palace in Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto). Sites associated with the Nuezuka (Nue burial mounds) and Yorimasa relics are scattered across Japan, including Hyōgo and Osaka prefectures.

phenomena.name: Nuppeppō
phenomena.description: A blob-like Japanese yokai resembling a soft, wrinkled mass of flesh, said to wander abandoned temples and graveyards. Depicted in classic Edo-period yokai scrolls including Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776).

aliases.name: Nikujin (肉人)
aliases.meaning: 'Meat-person'; related figure recorded in 1609 at Sunpu Castle

phenomena.origin: Japan; an Edo-period yokai documented in classical Japanese yokai scrolls.

phenomena.name: Nurarihyon
phenomena.description: An Edo-period Japanese yōkai depicted as an old man with an elongated, gourd-shaped head, originally an obscure figure in yōkai picture scrolls, later popularised in twentieth-century media as a refined intruder and supreme commander of yōkai.

aliases.name: Nurarihyon
aliases.meaning: From 'nurari' (to slip away) + 'hyon' (onomatopoeia for floating upward); written 滑瓢 ('slippery gourd')

aliases.name: Sea-monster nurarihyon
aliases.meaning: Globe-shaped umibōzu-like creature in the Seto Inland Sea

regions: Edo (modern Tokyo) — origin of the principal scrolls
phenomena.origin: A pan-Japanese folklore figure; specific regional traditions in Akita Prefecture (as a member of the night parade) and Okayama Prefecture (sea-creature variant). Modern media-driven popularity is national.

phenomena.name: Nurikabe
phenomena.description: A Japanese yōkai of folklore from northern Kyushu that manifests as an invisible barrier blocking the path of nighttime travelers. Defeating it traditionally requires sweeping a stick along its base.

aliases.name: Nurikabe
aliases.meaning: From nuru ('to plaster, paint') + kabe ('wall'); 'plastered wall'

phenomena.origin: Indigenous folk tradition is concentrated in northern Kyushu, especially Fukuoka Prefecture (former Chikuzen Province) and Ōita Prefecture. The figure is now nationally and internationally recognised through Mizuki Shigeru's manga.

phenomena.name: Oak Island Money Pit
phenomena.description: Oak Island is a 57-hectare (140-acre) tree-covered island in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, the focus of one of the longest-running treasure hunts in history. Since 1795, expeditions have excavated the so-called 'Money Pit' in search of buried treasure, with multiple deaths but no verified treasure recovered.
phenomena.origin: A single island in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, Canada, accessed from the village of Western Shore by a causeway constructed in 1965.

phenomena.name: Ogopogo
phenomena.description: A serpentine lake creature reported in Okanagan Lake, British Columbia, Canada. Rooted in the long-standing Nx̌ax̌aitkʷ tradition of the Syilx (Okanagan) people, it became a settler-era cryptid in the late 19th century and one of Canada's most famous lake monsters under the name 'Ogopogo' from 1926 onward.

aliases.name: Nx̌ax̌aitkʷ
aliases.meaning: Approximately 'sacred creature/spirit of the water', often translated 'water demon' or 'water god'

aliases.name: Ogopogo
aliases.meaning: Coined from a 1924 English music-hall song 'The Ogo-Pogo: The Funny Foxtrot'

phenomena.origin: Reports are confined to Okanagan Lake (a 127-km-long fjord lake reaching 232 m / 762 ft depth) and immediately adjacent waters in the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia.

phenomena.name: Oni
phenomena.description: Oni are demons or ogres of Japanese folklore and Buddhist mythology, typically depicted as horned, fanged, brightly-coloured humanoids in tiger-skin loincloths who carry iron clubs (kanabō). They guard the Buddhist hells, punish the wicked, and are warded off by the Setsubun bean-throwing ritual.

aliases.name: Oni (鬼)
aliases.meaning: Demon, ogre; from on/onu (隠), 'to hide, conceal'

aliases.name: Ki / Gui (鬼)
aliases.meaning: Spirit of the dead; the kanji adopted into Japanese

aliases.name: Namahage
aliases.meaning: New Year ritual figures with oni-like masks

regions: Mount Ōe (Tango Province, modern Kyoto Prefecture) — Shuten-dōji legend
Mount Iozan / Beppu — onsen demon imagery
phenomena.origin: A pan-Japanese supernatural figure with regional concentrations of legend (Mount Ōe, Akita's Oga Peninsula). Imagery has spread internationally through manga and anime.

phenomena.name: Orang Bati
phenomena.description: A reported winged humanoid creature from Seram Island in the Maluku (Molucca) Islands of eastern Indonesia, described as approximately five feet tall with bat-like black wings and red skin, said to emerge from caves on Mount Kairatu to abduct children from remote villages at night.
phenomena.origin: Reported exclusively from Seram Island (Ceram), Maluku (Molucca) Islands, eastern Indonesia. The creature is specifically associated with the interior mountains, particularly Mount Kairatu (Gunung Binaiya).

phenomena.name: Orang Dalam
phenomena.description: A large, bipedal, black-furred humanoid creature reported from the jungles of Johor, Malaysia, and sometimes Singapore, described as standing 2.4–3 meters tall and known by the alternative name Orang Mawas.

aliases.name: Orang Mawas
aliases.meaning: Person of the forest / forest orangutan-person; 'mawas' is a regional name for orangutan

aliases.name: Johor Bigfoot
aliases.meaning: Media term for the creature following 2005–2006 media coverage

phenomena.origin: Reported from the jungles of Johor, Malaysia's southernmost state, and occasionally from Singapore. Related creature (Muwa) reported from the Philippines; a related tradition (Butnak) from southern Thailand. In Sumatra, 'mawas' is used as a name for orangutans.

phenomena.name: Orang Gadang
phenomena.description: A giant humanoid cryptid reported from the forests of Sumatra, Indonesia, described as standing 7.5–12 feet tall, covered in dark bushy hair, and leaving very large footprints; sometimes called the Sumatran Bigfoot.
phenomena.origin: Reported from Sumatra, Indonesia, particularly the Rokan area of Riau province. May extend into other forested mountainous areas of Sumatra.

phenomena.name: Orang Minyak
phenomena.description: A figure from Malay folklore and urban legend described as a naked man covered entirely in black oil who breaks into homes to assault women, associated with a 1950s–1970s moral panic in Malaysia and Singapore and depicted in multiple films.
phenomena.origin: Reported from Malaysia and Singapore, with the legend originating in the Malay-speaking communities of both countries. Specific modern incident reports from Gombak, Selangor, Malaysia (2012).

phenomena.name: Orang Pendek
phenomena.description: A small, ground-dwelling, bipedal primate reported from the mountainous rainforests of Sumatra, Indonesia, particularly Kerinci Seblat National Park, described as 80–150 cm tall with dark fur and considered one of the more credible cryptid primate reports due to consistent descriptions and physical evidence.

aliases.name: Sedapa
aliases.meaning: Regional name used in Dutch colonial-era accounts

aliases.name: Hantu Pendek
aliases.meaning: Short ghost — Suku Anak Dalam (Orang Rimba) term, framing the creature as supernatural rather than biological

phenomena.origin: Remote mountainous forests of Sumatra, Indonesia, with sightings concentrated in the Kerinci Regency of central Sumatra, particularly within Kerinci Seblat National Park (TNKS). Historical reports suggest the creature's range may extend more broadly across Sumatra.

phenomena.name: Out-of-Body Experiences
phenomena.description: Out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are sensations in which a person perceives their consciousness to have separated from the physical body, allowing perception from an external vantage point. Roughly one in ten people report at least one OBE during their lifetime.

aliases.name: Astral projection
aliases.meaning: Paranormal framing: the soul or astral body voluntarily leaving the physical body

aliases.name: Autoscopy
aliases.meaning: Clinical term for seeing one's own body from an external vantage point

aliases.name: Bilocation
aliases.meaning: Reported experience of being in two places simultaneously

phenomena.origin: Reported across all human cultures and throughout recorded history. Cross-cultural survey data suggest approximately 10% of the global population reports at least one OBE.

phenomena.name: Owlman
phenomena.description: A winged humanoid cryptid reported around the parish church of St Mawnan and St Stephen in Cornwall, England, in 1976 and a handful of subsequent years. The case is heavily entangled with the self-described wizard and showman Tony 'Doc' Shiels, and is widely considered a hoax or folkloric construction.
phenomena.origin: Confined to the immediate vicinity of the parish church of St Mawnan and St Stephen, near Mawnan Smith on the Helford River in south Cornwall, England.

phenomena.name: Ozark Howler
phenomena.description: A regional cryptid of the Ozark Mountains of Arkansas and Missouri, described as a stocky, bear-sized animal with a shaggy black coat, glowing eyes, prominent horns, and a distinctive howling cry.

aliases.name: Hoo-Hoo
aliases.meaning: Onomatopoeic name from the creature's reported call

phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in the Ozark Mountains of northern Arkansas and southern Missouri, with occasional reports from adjacent Oklahoma and eastern Texas.

phenomena.name: Papa Bois
phenomena.description: Papa Bois ('Father of the Forest') is the protector spirit of forests and wildlife in Trinidad and Tobago and parts of the wider Lesser Antilles, depicted as an old, hairy, hooved man who guards animals from hunters and punishes those who waste or abuse the forest.
phenomena.origin: Papa Bois is principally a Trinidadian and Tobagonian folklore figure; closely related figures appear in the French/Creole-influenced islands of the Lesser Antilles, including Saint Lucia, Dominica, and Grenada.

phenomena.name: La Patasola
phenomena.description: La Patasola ('one foot') is a vampiric forest spirit of Colombian and wider Andean folklore who appears to lone men in the wilderness as a beautiful woman, then reveals her true one-legged, fanged form to feed on their blood and flesh.

aliases.name: La Mujer de Una Sola Pata

phenomena.origin: La Patasola is a creature of Colombian folklore with related traditions in Venezuela and Ecuador. She is most strongly associated with Andean Colombia and adjacent Amazonian and inter-Andean valleys.

phenomena.name: Patupaiarehe
phenomena.description: In Maori tradition, the patupaiarehe (also called turehu or pakepakeha) are pale-skinned, fair- or red-haired supernatural people of the misty forests, mountains, and high country of Aotearoa / New Zealand, regarded as he iwi atua - a 'people of the gods' rather than ordinary humans.
phenomena.origin: Patupaiarehe traditions are known across Aotearoa / New Zealand, with named locations on both the North and South Islands.

phenomena.name: Paulding Light
phenomena.description: The Paulding Light is a recurring nocturnal light visible from Robbins Pond Road (also known as Old US 45) outside Paulding, Michigan, in the Upper Peninsula. A 2010 Michigan Tech investigation identified the light as headlights from vehicles on US 45 viewed through an atmospheric inversion duct.
phenomena.origin: The phenomenon is observed from a single, well-defined viewing area on Robbins Pond Road (Old US 45) near Paulding, Michigan, in the Upper Peninsula.

phenomena.name: Phisuea Samut
phenomena.description: Phisuea Samut, often romanized 'Pee Sua Samut', is a sea ogress from the Thai epic poem Phra Aphai Mani by Sunthorn Phu, who falls in love with the prince-hero Aphai Mani, takes him to her undersea cave, and is ultimately killed by heartbreak when he escapes.

aliases.name: Sea Butterfly
aliases.meaning: Conventional gloss; the 'butterfly' element actually derives from a Thai term meaning 'ancestral ghost' rather than the insect

phenomena.origin: Phisuea Samut is a literary figure rooted in the Thai epic tradition; cultic and tourist veneration is concentrated on Ko Samet in Rayong Province, Thailand.

phenomena.name: Pegasus
phenomena.description: Pegasus is the immortal winged horse of Greek mythology, sired by Poseidon and born from the blood of the Gorgon Medusa when Perseus beheaded her; the steed of the hero Bellerophon, later the bearer of Zeus's thunderbolts and the namesake of the constellation Pegasus.

aliases.name: Pegasos
aliases.meaning: Standard Greek form of the name

phenomena.origin: As a literary and religious figure, Pegasus belongs to the Greek and wider Mediterranean mythological imagination, with a documented narrative geography centred on Corinth, Mount Helicon, Lycia, and Mount Olympus.

phenomena.name: Pelesit
phenomena.description: The pelesit is a familiar spirit of Malay folk magic, manifesting as a cricket or grasshopper (sometimes with a human head) and traditionally owned by women, who keep it in a bottle and use it to attack victims at the command of its master and its companion spirit, the polong.
phenomena.origin: The pelesit is part of Malay folk magic across Peninsular Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, and Singapore. The tradition is particularly strongly associated with Kedah in northern Peninsular Malaysia.

phenomena.name: Penanggalan
phenomena.description: The penanggalan is a vampiric female undead of Malay folklore: by day a normal-seeming woman, by night her head detaches and flies through the dark trailing her stomach, lungs, and intestines, hunting the blood of women in childbirth and newborns.
phenomena.origin: The penanggalan tradition is centred in the Malay Peninsula and the Malay Archipelago, with directly related variants attested across mainland and maritime Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Peri
phenomena.description: The peri (Persian: pari) is a winged supernatural being of immense beauty in Persian and wider Persianate folklore, originally an ambivalent or malevolent class of spirits in pre-Islamic Iranian belief and later reinterpreted as a generally benevolent fairy-like being who opposes the malevolent divs.
phenomena.origin: Peri / pari traditions span the Persianate cultural world: Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, the Kurdish regions, Pakistan, parts of India, the Caucasus, Anatolia, and Central Asia.

phenomena.name: Phantom Armies
phenomena.description: Phantom armies are large-scale collective apparitions of soldiers and battles, in which witnesses report seeing or hearing entire ghostly armies, cavalry charges, or re-enacted engagements at historical battlefields and other sites of mass military death.

aliases.name: Drosoulites
aliases.meaning: 'Dew shadows', the phantom soldiers of Frangokastello

aliases.name: Wild Hunt (related)
aliases.meaning: Spectral host of huntsmen, sometimes assimilated to phantom-army traditions

phenomena.origin: Phantom-army reports are recorded worldwide but cluster around famous battlefields in Europe, the Mediterranean, and North America.

phenomena.name: Phantom Ships
phenomena.description: Phantom ships are spectral or mysterious vessels reported by mariners throughout history, appearing as ghostly ships that materialize and vanish at sea, often considered death omens. The most famous example is the Flying Dutchman, a legendary Dutch vessel said to be cursed to sail the oceans forever.

aliases.name: Ghost Ships
aliases.meaning: Vessels with no living crew, found adrift or appearing as spectral visions at sea

aliases.name: Flying Dutchman
aliases.region: Cape of Good Hope; global maritime tradition
aliases.meaning: The archetypal legendary ghost ship cursed to sail forever

phenomena.origin: Phantom ship legends and sightings are reported globally, with the Flying Dutchman legend centered on the Cape of Good Hope and southern oceans. Real ghost ship discoveries have occurred in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans.

phenomena.name: Phi Am
phenomena.description: A nocturnal spirit in Thai folklore said to sit on a sleeper's chest, paralyzing them and causing breathing difficulty. The name is used colloquially in Thailand for the experience of sleep paralysis itself.
phenomena.origin: Thailand, with cognate traditions throughout mainland Southeast Asia. Phi Am is part of the broader Thai phi cosmology and reflects a worldwide pattern of sleep-paralysis folklore.

phenomena.name: Phi Tai Hong
phenomena.description: A vengeful ghost in Thai folklore arising from a person who died suddenly or violently — by murder, accident, drowning, suicide, or childbirth — and was unable to perform proper funeral rites, leaving the spirit angry and unwilling to depart.

aliases.name: ผีตายโหง
aliases.meaning: ghost of one who died a sudden, violent death

aliases.name: Tai Thang Klom
aliases.meaning: ghost of a pregnant woman who died with her unborn child; the most violent Phi Tai Hong variant

phenomena.origin: Thailand and culturally adjacent Tai-speaking regions of mainland Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Philadelphia Experiment
phenomena.description: An alleged 1943 U.S. Navy experiment said to have rendered the destroyer escort USS Eldridge invisible — and briefly teleported it from Philadelphia to Norfolk — based on Einstein's unified field theory. The story is widely regarded as a hoax originating with letters by Carl M. Allen in 1955–56.

aliases.name: Project Rainbow
aliases.meaning: Name used in conspiracy literature for the alleged experiment

phenomena.origin: The alleged event is associated with two real U.S. locations — the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, Pennsylvania, and Norfolk, Virginia — but the story has no verified geographic occurrence.

phenomena.name: Phoenix
phenomena.description: A long-lived bird of classical mythology that, at the end of its life, builds a nest, ignites, and is reborn from its own ashes. Frequently identified by ancient writers with the Egyptian Bennu and adopted across Roman, Christian, alchemical, and modern symbolism as an emblem of renewal.

aliases.name: φοῖνιξ (phoinix)
aliases.meaning: phoenix; possibly derived from a West Semitic word for the red dye 'madder'

aliases.name: Bennu
aliases.meaning: Egyptian solar bird associated with creation and rebirth, often identified by classical authors with the Greek phoenix

aliases.name: Fenghuang
aliases.meaning: Chinese 'phoenix' — a separate mythological bird often translated using the same English word

aliases.name: Huma
aliases.meaning: Persian mythological bird sometimes compared to the phoenix

aliases.name: Anqa / Simurgh
aliases.meaning: Other related Near Eastern mythological birds

phenomena.origin: Mythological — described in classical literature as native to Arabia, Egypt, Ethiopia, or India, depending on the author. The phoenix has no real geographic range.

phenomena.name: Phoenix Lights
phenomena.description: A widely witnessed series of unidentified aerial lights observed across Arizona and parts of Nevada on the evening of 13 March 1997. Two distinct events occurred — a high-altitude V-formation moving south, and a later set of stationary lights over the Estrella Mountains south of Phoenix — both later attributed by U.S. Air Force investigators to A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft and illumination flares from Operation Snowbird training exercises.
phenomena.origin: A single-event phenomenon localized to the southwestern United States — southern Nevada through Phoenix and surrounding Arizona to the Tucson area.

phenomena.name: Piri Reis Map
phenomena.description: A 1513 world map by the Ottoman admiral and cartographer Piri Reis, of which roughly one third survives at Topkapı Palace, Istanbul. The map gained global attention after its 1929 rediscovery and became famous in fringe-history literature for the disputed claim that it depicts an ice-free Antarctic coast.
phenomena.origin: A single physical artifact; held at the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul, Turkey.

phenomena.name: Pishacha
phenomena.description: A class of flesh-eating demons in Hindu and Buddhist tradition, often grouped with bhutas and vetalas. Said to haunt cremation grounds, possess humans, and feed on energy and corpses. Considered among the lowest, most malevolent supernatural beings in classical Indian cosmology.
phenomena.origin: Mythologically pan–South Asian, with a particular Vedic association with the northwestern frontier (Piśāca-deśa). Pishachas are referenced throughout Hindu and Buddhist literature wherever those traditions have spread, including Southeast Asia.

phenomena.name: Pocong
phenomena.description: An Indonesian and Malay ghost that takes the form of a body still wrapped in its Islamic burial shroud (kain kafan), said to arise when the shroud's knots are not untied at burial. Because the feet are bound, the pocong moves by hopping rather than walking.
phenomena.origin: Pervasive across Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, and Malay-speaking regions of Singapore and southern Thailand. Strongly associated with Javanese, Sundanese, and Malay Muslim communities.

phenomena.name: Poltergeist
phenomena.description: A pattern of paranormal disturbance — knockings, object movement, breaking glass, occasional spontaneous fires — typically centered on a specific household and frequently on a single 'agent', often an adolescent. Documented in European sources for over a millennium and theorized in modern parapsychology as Recurrent Spontaneous Psychokinesis (RSPK).

aliases.name: Recurrent Spontaneous Psychokinesis (RSPK)
aliases.meaning: William Roll's parapsychological re-naming of the phenomenon

phenomena.origin: Reported essentially worldwide; the type-cases are heavily European and North American, but extensive cases are documented in Brazil, Japan, Australia, and elsewhere.

phenomena.name: Poludnitsa
phenomena.description: A noon-time demon of Slavic folklore, said to roam the boundaries of grain fields at the height of summer heat. She tests workers with riddles, demands they dance, and afflicts those who fail with heatstroke, madness, or death. Personifies the very real danger of midday sun for agricultural labor.
phenomena.origin: Slavic folklore across Eastern, Central, and parts of Southern Europe — Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Lusatia (Sorbs), and parts of the South Slavic regions.

phenomena.name: Polybius
phenomena.description: Polybius is an urban legend about a fictional arcade game allegedly deployed in Portland, Oregon in 1981, said to cause severe psychological effects in players before being removed by government agents. No cabinet, ROM, or contemporary documentation has ever been found.

aliases.name: Sinneslöschen
aliases.meaning: Claimed name of the fictional arcade game's manufacturer; translates roughly to 'sense extinguisher' or 'sense deletion'

phenomena.origin: According to the legend, limited to Portland, Oregon arcades in 1981. As an internet legend, the story has global reach.

phenomena.name: Pontianak
phenomena.description: The Pontianak (known as Kuntilanak in Indonesia) is a vengeful female vampire spirit in Malay and Indonesian folklore, originating from women who died during pregnancy or childbirth. She appears as a beautiful woman in white to lure victims before revealing her monstrous true form.

aliases.name: Kuntilanak
aliases.meaning: Indonesian variant name; derived from the same root

aliases.name: Kunti
aliases.meaning: Colloquial abbreviation used in Indonesian popular culture

phenomena.origin: Pontianak / Kuntilanak beliefs are widespread throughout the Malay Archipelago, including Malaysia, Indonesia (especially Kalimantan, Java, and Sumatra), Singapore, and Brunei.

phenomena.name: Pope Lick Monster
phenomena.description: An urban-legend cryptid said to inhabit the Norfolk Southern railway trestle over Pope Lick Creek in the Fisherville neighborhood of Louisville, Kentucky. Described as a part-man, part-goat (and sometimes part-sheep) creature that lures trespassers onto the active trestle.

aliases.name: Goatman
aliases.meaning: Colloquial name for the part-man, part-goat figure

phenomena.origin: Strictly local urban legend confined to the Pope Lick Creek trestle in the Fisherville neighborhood of eastern Louisville, Kentucky.

phenomena.name: Popobawa
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting evil spirit of Zanzibari Swahili tradition, blamed for waves of nocturnal sexual assaults on Pemba Island, Unguja, and the Tanzanian coast. Major panics occurred in 1965, the 1970s, 1995, and 2007.
phenomena.origin: Concentrated in the Zanzibar archipelago — particularly Pemba Island and Unguja — with episodic outbreaks reaching the Tanzanian mainland (Dar es Salaam) and elsewhere on the Swahili coast.

phenomena.name: Possession
phenomena.description: Possession is the cross-cultural belief and reported experience that a human body and its functions can be controlled by an external agent — a spirit, ghost, demon, deity, or ancestor — producing dramatic changes in voice, behavior, language, and apparent identity. It is documented in 74% of 488 societies surveyed in a 1969 NIMH cross-cultural study.

aliases.name: Demonic possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a malevolent spirit, in Christian and Islamic frameworks

aliases.name: Dybbuk possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a disembodied human soul

phenomena.origin: Beliefs in and reports of possession are found in the great majority of human societies. Bourguignon's 1969 cross-cultural survey identified some form of possession belief in 74% of 488 societies, with highest prevalence in the Pacific and lowest among Native American societies.

phenomena.name: Precognition
phenomena.description: Precognition is the claimed ability to perceive or gain knowledge of future events without using known sensory channels or rational inference. Mainstream science classifies it as pseudoscience, citing the absence of replicable evidence and conflict with causality.

aliases.name: Second sight
aliases.meaning: Folk term, often for spontaneous precognition

aliases.name: Presentiment
aliases.meaning: A vague, often emotional precognitive sense

phenomena.origin: Precognition is reported across most human cultures and has been studied principally in laboratories in the United States and Western Europe.

phenomena.name: Psychic Phenomena
phenomena.description: Psychic phenomena (psi) are alleged mental abilities — telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition, and psychokinesis — that operate outside known sensory channels and physical mechanisms. The mainstream scientific community classifies the field as pseudoscience.

aliases.name: Psi
aliases.meaning: Greek letter ψ used as the field's umbrella term

aliases.name: Anomalous cognition / anomalous perturbation
aliases.meaning: Stargate-era and later technical terms for psi

phenomena.origin: Belief in psi is documented across most cultures and historical periods. Laboratory study has been concentrated in the United States, the United Kingdom, Western Europe, and the former Soviet Union.

phenomena.name: Psychometry
phenomena.description: Psychometry is the alleged paranormal ability to obtain information about an object's history — its past owners, locations, or events surrounding it — by physical contact. The term was coined by American physician Joseph Rodes Buchanan in 1842.
phenomena.origin: Practised principally in 19th- and 20th-century Anglosphere Spiritualism and 20th-century European parapsychology, though similar 'reading-from-objects' practices appear in many divinatory traditions worldwide.

phenomena.name: Púca
phenomena.description: The Púca is a shapeshifting fairy creature of Irish, Welsh, Cornish, Manx, and Scottish Gaelic folklore — most famously a black horse with luminous golden eyes. Its character is ambiguous: it can be a dangerous trickster or a beneficent helper, and is closely associated with Samhain (1 November).

aliases.name: Puck
aliases.meaning: Cognate appearing in English folklore (e.g. Robin Goodfellow / Puck in Shakespeare)

phenomena.origin: The Púca and its direct cognates are found across the Celtic fringe of the British Isles and Ireland, with the strongest tradition in Ireland (especially Munster, Leinster, and parts of Connacht), and counterparts in Wales (Pwca), Cornwall (Bucca), and the Scottish Highlands (Bòcan).

phenomena.name: Qallupilluk
phenomena.description: Qallupilluk is a water-dwelling humanoid being from Inuit folklore that lurks beneath Arctic sea ice to abduct children who wander too close to the water's edge, functioning as a cautionary tradition protecting children from the real dangers of Arctic ice.
phenomena.origin: The Qallupilluk tradition is documented in Inuit communities across Arctic Canada (especially Nunavut) and Alaska.

phenomena.name: Qarqash
phenomena.description: Qarqash (القرقش) is a malevolent desert spirit from Bedouin and Arabian Peninsula folklore, described as a terrifying entity that haunts desolate desert regions and preys upon lone travelers and children who stray from safety.

aliases.name: القرقش
aliases.meaning: The qarqash; the original Arabic-script form of the name

aliases.name: Garghash
aliases.meaning: Variant form found in Gulf Arabic tradition

phenomena.origin: The qarqash tradition is found across the Arabian Peninsula, particularly in Bedouin oral traditions of the Gulf states, Saudi Arabia, and adjacent regions.

phenomena.name: Qilin
phenomena.description: The Qilin (麒麟) is the most auspicious terrestrial creature of Chinese mythology, a chimeric divine beast whose appearance heralds the reign of a virtuous ruler or the birth of a great sage. It is said to walk so gently it does not bend a blade of grass.

aliases.name: 麒麟
aliases.meaning: The Chinese characters for qilin; qi (麒) denotes the male, lin (麟) denotes the female

aliases.name: Kirin
aliases.meaning: Japanese adaptation of the Chinese qilin

aliases.name: Girin
aliases.meaning: Korean variant; also called Giraffe in modern Korean

aliases.name: Gilen
aliases.meaning: Thai variant incorporated into Himapant forest mythology

aliases.name: Lân
aliases.meaning: Vietnamese variant; one of the four sacred creatures alongside the dragon, phoenix, and tortoise

phenomena.origin: The qilin is a mythological creature of Chinese origin, with related variants across East and Southeast Asia. As a mythological being, it has no geographic range in the literal sense; accounts of appearances are concentrated in Chinese historical texts set in China.

phenomena.name: Raiju
phenomena.description: Raiju (雷獣, 'thunder beast') is a legendary yōkai from Japanese mythology, the companion of Raijin the thunder god, whose body is composed of or wrapped in lightning. It descends during thunderstorms, becomes agitated, and may take many animal forms — most often a weasel, wolf, or cat — depending on the regional tradition.

aliases.name: Raijuu
aliases.meaning: Alternative Hepburn romanization of the same term

phenomena.origin: Raiju legends are primarily concentrated in East Japan, with notable regional variants throughout the Japanese archipelago. Most documented accounts come from the Edo period, with locations including Akita, Shinano, Echigo, Sagami, Aizu, Lake Biwa, and Akō.

phenomena.name: The Rake
phenomena.description: The Rake is an internet-born fictional entity originating from 4chan's /b/ board around 2005–2006, described as a pale, emaciated humanoid that crouches at the foot of beds or crawls on all fours. Though explicitly created as collaborative fiction, the character has since generated claimed real-world encounter reports.
phenomena.origin: As an internet-born legend, the Rake has no geographic origin. Claimed encounter reports (post-fictional-origin) come primarily from English-speaking internet communities.

phenomena.name: Rakshasa
phenomena.description: A class of powerful supernatural beings in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions, often depicted as malevolent shape-shifting demons but including morally complex and even virtuous individuals.

aliases.name: Rākṣasa
aliases.meaning: demon, fiend, that which is to be guarded against

aliases.name: Asura
aliases.meaning: broader class of power-seeking beings, sometimes overlapping

phenomena.origin: Rakshasa traditions span the entire Indic cultural sphere: South Asia (India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh), Buddhist East Asia by way of scripture, and Southeast Asia where the loanword 'raksasa' is widely used.

phenomena.name: Redcap
phenomena.description: A murderous goblin of Anglo-Scottish Border folklore who haunts ruined peel-towers and castles, dyeing his cap in the blood of travellers he kills.

aliases.name: Dunter
aliases.meaning: from the muffled dunting noise heard in the towers it haunts

aliases.name: Robin Redcap
aliases.meaning: named familiar of William de Soulis

phenomena.origin: Confined to the Anglo-Scottish Border country, with sympathetic legends in adjacent areas of northern England and southern Scotland.

phenomena.name: Remote Viewing
phenomena.description: A claimed psychic ability to perceive distant or unseen targets, studied in U.S. government-funded research programmes from 1972 to 1995 and concluded by independent review to lack reliable evidence.

aliases.name: Coordinate Remote Viewing (CRV)
aliases.meaning: Ingo Swann's structured protocol used at SRI

aliases.name: Extended Remote Viewing (ERV)
aliases.meaning: Variant developed within the U.S. Army programmes

aliases.name: Stargate Project
aliases.meaning: Umbrella name for the U.S. government remote-viewing programmes from 1991

aliases.name: Sun Streak / Center Lane / Grill Flame / Gondola Wish
