aliases.meaning: Earlier classified codenames for the same lineage of programmes

phenomena.origin: Research has been conducted primarily in the United States, with related parapsychological work in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the former Soviet Union, and elsewhere. Government interest is documented for the United States and (in declassified records) for the Soviet Union.

phenomena.name: Rendlesham Forest Incident
phenomena.description: A series of reported sightings of unexplained lights and a possible craft over three nights in late December 1980 by U.S. Air Force personnel near the twin NATO bases of RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge in Suffolk, England.

aliases.name: The Halt Incident
aliases.meaning: after Lt. Col. Charles Halt, principal U.S. military witness

phenomena.origin: Single localised incident in Rendlesham Forest, Suffolk, England, between RAF Woodbridge and RAF Bentwaters.

phenomena.name: Reptilian Conspiracy Theory
phenomena.description: A modern conspiracy theory that alleges shape-shifting reptilian humanoid beings secretly control Earth's institutions, popularised by British conspiracy author David Icke from the late 1990s onwards.

aliases.name: Draconians
aliases.meaning: alleged origin in the Alpha Draconis star system

aliases.name: Anunnaki (in some syntheses)
aliases.meaning: drawn from Zecharia Sitchin's pseudohistorical writing

phenomena.origin: As a conspiracy belief, the theory has audiences in over 40 countries, with English-language strongholds in the UK, US, Canada, Australia, and online communities globally. Belief has been measured most directly in the United States.

phenomena.name: Resurrection Mary
phenomena.description: A long-running Chicago-area vanishing-hitchhiker legend centred on Archer Avenue and Resurrection Cemetery in Justice, Illinois, in which a young blonde woman in white is said to be picked up by drivers and to vanish near the cemetery gates.
phenomena.origin: Localised to the Archer Avenue corridor between Willow Springs and Justice, Illinois, in the southwest suburbs of Chicago.

phenomena.name: Revenant
phenomena.description: A revenant is a spirit or animated corpse believed to have returned from death to haunt or harm the living, prominent in medieval European folklore from Celtic and Norse traditions through English and French accounts. Archaeologists have found revenant graves across Europe dating back 4,000 years.

aliases.name: revenant
aliases.meaning: One who returns; from revenir (to return)

aliases.name: Draugr
aliases.meaning: Again-walker; animated corpse in Norse mythology

aliases.name: Aptrgangr
aliases.meaning: After-goer; one who walks after death

aliases.name: Haugbui
aliases.meaning: Barrow-dweller; a type of Norse revenant that remains near its burial mound

phenomena.origin: Revenant beliefs are documented across Europe, with the most detailed medieval accounts from England, Wales, and France. Archaeological evidence of anti-revenant burial practices spans Europe from the Bronze Age onward.

phenomena.name: Roanoke Colony
phenomena.description: The Roanoke Colony, known as 'The Lost Colony,' was an English settlement of approximately 115–121 colonists established on Roanoke Island (present-day North Carolina) in 1587. When Governor John White returned in August 1590, the settlement was found completely abandoned, with only the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post.

aliases.name: The Lost Colony
aliases.meaning: Common name for the 1587 English colony on Roanoke Island that disappeared by 1590

phenomena.origin: Roanoke Island, present-day Dare County, North Carolina, United States. Archaeological investigation has extended to Hatteras Island (Croatoan Island) and a site 50 miles inland ('Site X' in Bertie County).

phenomena.name: Roc
phenomena.description: The Roc (Arabic: الرُخّ, al-Rukh) is a legendary giant bird of prey from Arabian and Persian mythology, most famously described in the tales of One Thousand and One Nights, capable of carrying elephants in its talons. Its egg alone was said to measure 50 paces in circumference.

aliases.name: الرُخّ
aliases.meaning: Al-Rukh; the original Arabic name for the creature

aliases.name: Ruḵḵ
aliases.meaning: Scholarly romanization of the Arabic name

aliases.name: Ruc
aliases.meaning: Medieval European transliteration used by Marco Polo and other travelers

phenomena.origin: In Arabian and Persian tradition, the roc inhabits remote islands in the Indian Ocean, particularly in the region visited by Sinbad's voyages. Marco Polo located it in the vicinity of Madagascar. As a mythological creature, it has no literal geographic range.

phenomena.name: Rokurokubi
phenomena.description: A rokurokubi is a Japanese yōkai that appears nearly human but possesses a neck that stretches to extraordinary lengths; a related subtype called nukekubi has a head that fully detaches and floats independently at night.

aliases.name: 轆轤首
aliases.meaning: pulley neck; neck that extends like a rotating mechanical device

aliases.name: ろくろ首
aliases.meaning: Hiragana form of the same name

aliases.name: Nukekubi
aliases.meaning: detachable head; a related subtype whose head fully separates from the body

regions: All regions of Japan historically; origin traditions also present in China and Southeast Asia
phenomena.origin: A creature of Japanese folklore, with analogous traditions distributed across East and Southeast Asia, suggesting shared or parallel origin traditions.

phenomena.name: Rolling Calf
phenomena.description: The Rolling Calf is one of the most feared duppies (spirits) in Jamaican folklore — a shape-shifting supernatural entity that most often appears as a large calf or bull with blazing red eyes, fire from its nostrils, and a dragging iron chain, haunting lonely roads and crossroads at night.
phenomena.origin: Primarily a Jamaican tradition, with parallel duppy beliefs across the broader Caribbean.

phenomena.name: Ropen
phenomena.description: The Ropen is a large nocturnal flying cryptid reported from Papua New Guinea, described by witnesses as a featherless, bat-winged creature with a long tail and bioluminescent glow, and interpreted by some cryptozoologists as a surviving pterosaur.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate on Umboi Island and surrounding areas of Papua New Guinea, with some claims from the broader Solomon Islands region and Indonesian Papua.

phenomena.name: Roperite
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter from American lumberjack tall tales, the Roperite is a pony-sized animal of the California Sierra foothills described as catching prey with a long, prehensile, rope-like beak that it uses as a lasso.

aliases.name: Lariat Snake
aliases.meaning: informal name in some retellings of Cox's account

phenomena.origin: Restricted in folklore to the foothills of the Sierra Nevada in California, particularly the Digger pine belt of the western slope.

phenomena.name: Roswell Incident
phenomena.description: The 1947 recovery of debris from a ranch near Corona, New Mexico, by personnel from Roswell Army Air Field, briefly described in an RAAF press release as a 'flying disc' before being officially identified as a weather balloon. From the late 1970s onward, popular UFO literature reframed the recovery as the crash of an extraterrestrial vehicle and the foundation of a long-running US government cover-up.

aliases.name: Foster Ranch Incident
aliases.meaning: After the Foster sheep ranch on which the debris was found

phenomena.origin: The debris field is on the J. B. Foster sheep ranch in Lincoln County, New Mexico, roughly 75 miles north-west of the city of Roswell. Secondary 'crash sites' and 'body recovery' sites have been claimed at multiple locations across south-central New Mexico in later literature, with no contemporaneous physical evidence.

phenomena.name: Rumtifusel
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter from American lumberjack tall tales, the Rumtifusel is a flat, mink-pelted predator that drapes itself over a stump like an abandoned fur coat to lure greedy passers-by, then drains them through suckers on its underside.

aliases.name: Fur-coat critter
aliases.meaning: informal description for the creature's lure

phenomena.origin: Within the lumberjack tall-tale tradition, the Rumtifusel is associated with the broad logging country of the northern United States and Canada — the same generic 'lumberwoods' setting that hosts most fearsome critters.

phenomena.name: Rusalka
phenomena.description: A female water spirit in East and West Slavic folklore, often understood as the restless soul of a drowned woman or unbaptized girl, who lures men into rivers and lakes during a seasonal week of activity around Pentecost.

aliases.name: Mavka
aliases.meaning: forest/water spirit, partly synonymous with rusalka

phenomena.origin: Widely attested across the East Slavic world (Russia, Ukraine, Belarus) and into Poland, Czech and Slovak lands; secondary attestations in Slovenia and parts of the Balkans.

phenomena.name: The Russian Sleep Experiment
phenomena.description: A widely-shared internet horror story, posted to the Creepypasta Wiki on 10 August 2010, framed as a declassified record of a Soviet experiment in which prisoners kept awake for 15 days by a stimulant gas descend into psychotic violence. It is fiction; investigations by Snopes and others have repeatedly confirmed there is no such Soviet experiment.

aliases.name: Orange Soda story
aliases.meaning: after the original Creepypasta Wiki author handle

phenomena.origin: Internet-native phenomenon: originated on the Creepypasta Wiki and spread through English-language forums, Reddit, YouTube and Tumblr; subsequently translated into many languages.

phenomena.name: Saci
phenomena.description: A one-legged black or dark-skinned boy from Brazilian folklore who wears a magical red cap, smokes a pipe, and travels in whirlwinds, playing pranks but rarely causing serious harm. October 31 is officially Saci Day in Brazil.

aliases.name: Saci-pererê
aliases.meaning: the canonical one-legged Black trickster form

aliases.name: Çaci
aliases.meaning: from Tupinambá 'çaci' meaning 'sick eye' or 'evil eye'

phenomena.origin: Found across Brazil; particularly strongly attested in the Southeast (São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro), the South (Paraná, Santa Catarina, Rio Grande do Sul) and the Centre-West, with regional variants throughout the country.

phenomena.name: Samjok-o
phenomena.description: A three-legged crow that lives in the sun, central to East Asian solar mythology. In Korea, the Samjok-o was a Goguryeo-era emblem of imperial authority and the sun, attested on 6th–7th-century tomb murals; cognate figures are the Chinese Sanzuwu / Jinwu and the Japanese Yatagarasu.

aliases.name: Jinwu
aliases.meaning: 'golden crow' — common variant name for the sun crow

aliases.name: Yatagarasu
aliases.meaning: 'eight-span crow' — Japanese counterpart, often three-legged in later art

regions: Goguryeo cultural sphere (Korean peninsula and southern Manchuria)
phenomena.origin: East Asian: China (Sanzuwu / Jinwu), Korea (Samjok-o, especially Goguryeo), and Japan (Yatagarasu).

phenomena.name: Sasabonsam
phenomena.description: A forest-dwelling vampiric being from Akan folklore (Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Togo), described as a hairy humanoid with iron teeth and hooked feet who sits in trees and snatches up unwary travellers. Documented ethnographically by R. S. Rattray in the 1920s.
regions: Akan-speaking parts of southeastern Côte d'Ivoire
phenomena.origin: Akan-speaking regions of southern Ghana and adjoining areas of Togo and Côte d'Ivoire; with diaspora attestations in Akan-influenced Caribbean folklore.

phenomena.name: Satori
phenomena.description: A Japanese mountain yokai shaped like an ape-like man, said to inhabit the mountains of Hida and Mino (modern Gifu Prefecture). The Satori reads a person's thoughts and speaks them aloud, but is paradoxically driven off by something genuinely unexpected.

aliases.name: 覺
aliases.meaning: 'awareness, awakening' — name used by Toriyama Sekien

aliases.name: Yamako
aliases.meaning: Chinese-origin precursor figure: an ape-man of mountain folklore

phenomena.origin: Folkloric range is the mountainous interior of central Honshu, particularly the historical provinces of Hida and Mino (modern Gifu Prefecture).

phenomena.name: Satyr
phenomena.description: Satyrs are male nature spirits from Greek mythology, depicted as hybrid humanoids combining human torsos with horse or goat features, and characterized by exuberant sexuality, love of wine and music, and mischievous behavior in the retinue of the god Dionysus.

aliases.name: Sátyros
aliases.meaning: Etymology disputed; proposed connections to thērion (wild animal), or a root meaning 'the full ones' (alluding to sexual arousal), or the root sat- (to sow)

aliases.name: Silenos / Silenus
aliases.meaning: Elder form of satyr; name of Dionysus's tutor

aliases.name: Faun
aliases.meaning: Roman counterpart; from Faunus, woodland deity

phenomena.origin: A pan-Mediterranean mythological figure, originating in ancient Greece and spreading through Hellenistic culture across the Mediterranean world and into Roman civilization.

phenomena.name: SCP Foundation
phenomena.description: A collaborative online horror-fiction project, begun on 4chan's /x/ board in 2007 and given its own wiki in 2008, in which thousands of authors document a fictional 'Foundation' that secures, contains, and protects anomalous objects and entities. All content is published under CC BY-SA.

aliases.name: Special Containment Procedures Foundation
aliases.meaning: in-fiction expansion of the acronym; sometimes glossed as 'Secure, Contain, Protect'

aliases.name: SCP Wiki
aliases.meaning: primary host site of the collaborative fiction

regions: Major translation branches across East Asia, Europe and the Americas
phenomena.origin: Global internet phenomenon. The English SCP Wiki is the primary site; substantial translation branches exist in Russian, Korean, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, German, Polish, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Thai, Czech, Vietnamese, Ukrainian and other languages.

phenomena.name: Screaming Skull
phenomena.description: A screaming skull is a haunted human skull from British folklore believed to scream, cause poltergeist phenomena, or bring misfortune when removed from its home location — most commonly a historic English manor house, farm, or castle.

aliases.name: Fetch skull
aliases.meaning: A skull believed to 'fetch' or bring disaster when disturbed

aliases.name: Guardian skull
aliases.meaning: A skull believed to guard the location it inhabits

phenomena.origin: Almost exclusively documented in England, with isolated cases in other English-speaking regions. The phenomenon is particularly concentrated in the north of England (Yorkshire, Derbyshire, Lancashire) and the south (Dorset, Somerset).

phenomena.name: Sedona Vortexes
phenomena.description: The Sedona Vortexes are specific geographic locations in Sedona, Arizona, believed by New Age practitioners to be swirling centers of earth energy conducive to healing, meditation, and spiritual transformation, drawing approximately 3 million visitors annually.

aliases.name: Sedona Vortices
aliases.meaning: Alternative plural; both 'vortexes' and 'vortices' are used

phenomena.origin: Concentrated within approximately 10 miles of central Sedona, Arizona, United States.

phenomena.name: Selkie
phenomena.description: Selkies are shapeshifting beings of Northern Isles, Faroese, Icelandic, and Irish folklore who live as seals in the sea but can shed their sealskins to take human form on land. They are best known for stories in which a human steals and hides a selkie's skin, trapping the selkie in human form.

aliases.name: Roane
aliases.meaning: seal (used for selkie-like beings in Irish folklore)

phenomena.origin: Selkie traditions cluster in the Northern Isles of Scotland (Orkney and Shetland) and along the Hebridean and northern Scottish coasts, with cognate traditions in coastal Ireland, the Faroe Islands, and Iceland. The cultural distribution corresponds closely to the historic range of Norse settlement and the grey seal's North Atlantic range.

phenomena.name: Seneca Guns
phenomena.description: The Seneca Guns are unexplained loud booming sounds, often resembling cannon fire or distant thunder, reported around Seneca and Cayuga Lakes in New York and along the coast of the Carolinas, with global cognates known as skyquakes, mistpouffers, Barisal Guns, and uminari. The booms are sometimes accompanied by ground or window-shaking but no consensus cause has been established.

aliases.name: Skyquakes
aliases.meaning: general modern term for unexplained sky-origin booms

phenomena.origin: A globally distributed family of phenomena reported on every inhabited continent. Best-known clusters in the United States are around Seneca and Cayuga Lakes (New York), the Outer Banks and coast of North Carolina, the South Carolina coast, the Florida coast, and northern Georgia. Major international cognates are reported in coastal Bangladesh and India, Japan, the Belgian and Dutch coasts, Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland, and many other regions.

phenomena.name: Shadow People
phenomena.description: Shadow people are perceived dark, human-shaped silhouettes — often glimpsed in peripheral vision, in bedrooms during sleep paralysis, or at thresholds — and frequently associated with feelings of dread. Modern folklore consolidates a recognisable 'Hat Man' variant. Mainstream research attributes the experience to sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucination, and pareidolia rather than to external entities.

aliases.name: Hat Man
aliases.meaning: shadow person variant in a wide-brimmed hat or fedora

phenomena.origin: Reported worldwide. The modern internet-era reporting cluster is heavily English-language (United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia), but accounts have been collected from every inhabited continent. The phenomenon is a domestic-interior one; it is not concentrated in particular landscapes.

phenomena.name: Shtriga
phenomena.description: The shtriga is a vampiric witch in Albanian folklore who feeds on the blood of sleeping infants. After feeding she can transform into a flying insect, and the only sure cure for her victims is a remedy obtained from the shtriga herself. Apotropaic protections include garlic, salt, the sign of the cross, and a cross of pig bone placed at a church door on Easter Sunday.

aliases.name: Strix
aliases.meaning: owl-witch; ancient ancestor of the term

phenomena.origin: Northern Albanian highlands, Kosovo, and Albanian-speaking communities of North Macedonia and Montenegro; with a wider Balkan continuum of cognate figures.

phenomena.name: Shuten-dōji
phenomena.description: Shuten-dōji ('sake-drinking lad') is a legendary oni (demon) of Japanese folklore who, set in the reign of Emperor Ichijō (986–1011), is said to have led a band of demons from a fortress on Mount Ōe and abducted nobles of the capital. He was defeated by the warrior Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō) and his Four Heavenly Kings, who infiltrated his stronghold disguised as yamabushi and gave him a poisoned sake.

aliases.name: Ibukidōji
aliases.meaning: Mount Ibuki version of the legend

phenomena.origin: Mountain regions north and northwest of the Heian capital (Kyoto): Mount Ōe (Ōeyama) on the border of Tango and Tamba provinces; Mount Ibuki on the Ōmi–Mino border; and the southern Ōe area near Kameoka in modern Kyoto Prefecture.

phenomena.name: Sidehill Gouger
phenomena.description: The Sidehill Gouger is a fearsome critter of American lumberjack folklore: a hoofed, hill-dwelling beast with legs shorter on one side than the other, perfectly adapted to walk a steep slope but only in one direction around a hill. It belongs to the humorous tall-tale tradition of the North American logging camps and is not a creature anyone was ever expected to believe in.
phenomena.origin: Reported in tall-tale tradition across the lumberwoods of the northern and western United States and adjacent Canada, particularly New England, the Adirondacks and Appalachians, the Great Lakes states, the Driftless Area of Wisconsin, the northern Rockies, and the Pacific Northwest.

phenomena.name: La Siguanaba
phenomena.description: La Siguanaba is a shapeshifting female spirit of Central American folklore who appears to lone travellers — typically unfaithful or wayward men — as a beautiful long-haired woman seen from behind, then turns to reveal a horrifying face (a horse skull or a death's head). She lures her victims to ravines or rivers, where they may be driven mad or killed.

aliases.name: Sihuehuet
aliases.meaning: 'beautiful woman' — her original name in Salvadoran Cuscatleca tradition

phenomena.origin: Central American folklore from southern Mexico to Costa Rica, with regional variants in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica.

phenomena.name: Simurgh
phenomena.description: The Simurgh is a benevolent mythical bird of Iranian tradition — wise, ancient, and immense — said to nest atop the Alborz Mountains. It is most famous for raising the hero Zal in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and for serving in Attar of Nishapur's Sufi poem 'Conference of the Birds' as the goal of a spiritual journey whose surprise is the discovery that the seekers themselves (sī murğ, 'thirty birds') are the Simurgh.

aliases.name: Sī murğ
aliases.meaning: 'thirty birds' — a Persian pun central to Attar's poem

aliases.name: Anqa
aliases.meaning: in some Islamic contexts conflated with the Simurgh

phenomena.origin: Iranian cultural zone, including modern Iran, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Iraqi Kurdistan, and the broader Persianate world (Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Indian subcontinent under Mughal influence, and the Ottoman world).

phenomena.name: Siren
phenomena.description: Sirens are mythological singers of Greek tradition, originally depicted as bird-women whose irresistible song lures sailors to their deaths on rocky islands of the western Mediterranean. From the early medieval period the figure was progressively conflated with the fish-tailed mermaid; modern usage encompasses both forms.

aliases.name: Parthenope
aliases.meaning: named siren whose tomb was the legendary foundation of Naples

phenomena.origin: Greek and Roman literary geography places the sirens in the western Mediterranean, principally off the Tyrrhenian and Campanian coasts of Italy. The medieval mermaid-siren is much more widely distributed across European bestiary geography.

phenomena.name: Siren Head
phenomena.description: Siren Head is a fictional horror entity created by Canadian artist Trevor Henderson in 2018 — a skeletal 40-foot-tall humanoid with two mechanical sirens in place of a head — that spread virally through internet horror communities and inspired games, videos, and fan works before being misidentified by some users as a real cryptid.

aliases.name: Sirenhead
aliases.meaning: Common one-word spelling used by fans and media

phenomena.origin: A fictional entity with no real-world geographic range. In its fictional framing, depicted in rural North American settings.

phenomena.name: Skinned Tom
phenomena.description: Skinned Tom is a Southern American urban legend and cautionary tale about a man flayed alive after an adulterous affair, whose skinless, knife-carrying spirit now haunts lovers' lanes and remote roads as a warning against infidelity.
phenomena.origin: The American South, with documented oral tradition in Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, and parts of Georgia.

phenomena.name: Skinwalker Ranch
phenomena.description: Skinwalker Ranch is a 512-acre property in Uintah County, Utah, that has been the subject of claims of extensive paranormal activity including UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, poltergeist phenomena, and cryptid encounters, and which was investigated by Robert Bigelow's NIDS organization and a $22 million Pentagon study.

aliases.name: Sherman Ranch
aliases.meaning: Name during the Sherman family's ownership (1994–1996)

aliases.name: UFO Ranch
aliases.meaning: Informal name based on the UFO sighting claims

phenomena.origin: A single specific property in Uintah County, Utah.

phenomena.name: Skinwalker (Yee Naaldlooshii)
phenomena.description: In some Indigenous American legends, a skinwalker (Navajo: yee naaldlooshii) is a harmful witch with the power to disguise itself as, transform into, or possess an animal. The figure is deeply embedded in Navajo tradition and is rarely discussed with outsiders.

aliases.name: Yee Naaldlooshii
aliases.meaning: 'By means of it, it goes on all fours'

aliases.name: 'Ánti'įhnii
aliases.meaning: Witch / one who practices witchcraft (broader category)

phenomena.origin: Yee naaldlooshii belief is specific to Navajo (Diné) communities of the Four Corners region of the southwestern United States. Outside that cultural context, an English-language 'skinwalker' folklore — often substantially altered from the Navajo tradition — circulates broadly across North American popular culture and the internet.

phenomena.name: Skunk Ape
phenomena.description: The Skunk Ape is a bipedal, ape-like cryptid reported primarily in the swamps and forests of Florida and the wider southeastern United States, named for the strong, foul odor associated with its reported encounters.
phenomena.origin: Reports concentrate in central and southern Florida, with secondary clusters across Georgia, Alabama, and the wider southeastern coastal plain. According to coverage cited on the English Wikipedia article, sightings have been reported from 48 of Florida's 67 counties since 2010.

phenomena.name: Skvader
phenomena.description: The skvader is a Swedish fictional taxidermy creature combining the front half of a European hare with the back, wings, and tail of a female western capercaillie (wood grouse). It originated in a tall tale by Håkan Dahlmark and was constructed by taxidermist Rudolf Granberg in 1918.

aliases.name: Tetrao lepus pseudo-hybridus rarissimus
aliases.meaning: Mock scientific name given to the taxidermy specimen

phenomena.origin: The skvader is a place-bound cultural artefact of the Medelpad province in central Sweden, with the original specimen on permanent display at the Norra Berget museum in Sundsvall.

phenomena.name: Skyquakes
phenomena.description: Skyquakes are unexplained loud booming sounds, often resembling cannon fire or thunder, reported around the world — typically in clear weather, with no obvious source, and frequently along coastlines and large bodies of water.

aliases.name: Seneca Guns
aliases.region: Seneca Lake, New York and the Carolinas, USA

aliases.name: Bombes de mer / Canons de mer

phenomena.origin: Reported globally on all inhabited continents, with notable historical clusters along the North Sea, the Ganges Delta of Bangladesh, the Finger Lakes and U.S. East Coast, coastal Japan, and parts of Italy and Indonesia.

phenomena.name: Sleipnir
phenomena.description: In Norse mythology, Sleipnir is the eight-legged grey horse of Odin, son of the trickster god Loki and the stallion Svaðilfari. He is described as the best of horses and is attested in both the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda.
phenomena.origin: As a mythological figure, Sleipnir 'inhabits' the cosmological geography of Old Norse religion. The textual and material attestations are concentrated in medieval Iceland and in Viking-Age Scandinavia (especially Gotland).

phenomena.name: Slender Man
phenomena.description: Slender Man is a fictional supernatural character created by Eric Knudsen ('Victor Surge') on the Something Awful forums on June 10, 2009. He is depicted as an unnaturally tall, thin, faceless figure in a black suit and is one of the foundational figures of digital folklore.

aliases.name: Der Großmann
aliases.meaning: 'The Tall Man' — fictional German backstory invented by users

phenomena.origin: As an internet-native fictional entity, Slender Man's 'distribution' is global wherever the anglophone internet reaches. The originating community is North American, but the character has become a globally recognised piece of digital folklore.

phenomena.name: Slide-Rock Bolter
phenomena.description: The Slide-Rock Bolter is a fearsome critter of American lumberjack folklore from Colorado's Rocky Mountains. Documented by Minnesota State Forester William T. Cox in 'Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods' (1910), the creature is described as an enormous fish-like beast that anchors itself by hooked tail to a mountain ridge and slides down on its prey.

aliases.name: Macrostoma saxiperrumptus
aliases.meaning: Mock scientific name given by William T. Cox (1910)

phenomena.origin: Restricted in the lumberjack tradition to the high Rocky Mountains of Colorado, especially on slopes steeper than 45°. Cox specifically associates the creature with the country between Ophir Peaks and Lizard Head Peak in San Miguel and Dolores counties.

phenomena.name: Smile Dog
phenomena.description: Smile Dog (also written Smile.jpg) is an image-based creepypasta about an allegedly cursed photograph of a husky-like dog with human-style teeth. The accompanying short story is most often attributed to Michael Lutz, who posted a canonical version to the Creepypasta Wiki in August 2010.
phenomena.origin: An internet-native fiction: distribution is anywhere the anglophone internet reaches. The originating community is North American imageboard culture (4chan) and the wider Creepypasta Wiki community.

phenomena.name: Snallygaster
phenomena.description: The Snallygaster is a dragon-like creature of central-Maryland folklore — particularly Frederick County and the South Mountain area — whose name derives from the Pennsylvania German 'schneller geist' ('quick spirit'). The creature became a newspaper sensation in 1909 when the Middletown Valley Register published a series of sensational reports.
phenomena.origin: Concentrated in central and western Maryland (especially Frederick County), with secondary reports in the Washington, D.C. metro area and Berkeley County, West Virginia.

phenomena.name: Soucouyant
phenomena.description: The soucouyant is a figure of Caribbean folklore: an old woman by day who at night sheds her skin, transforms into a ball of fire, and flies in search of victims whose blood she drains. She is defeated by finding her shed skin and salting it so she cannot return to human form before sunrise.

aliases.name: Ole Higue / Ol' Higue / Ole Haig

phenomena.origin: Across the Caribbean, including Anglophone, Francophone, and Dutch-speaking territories, with diaspora reach into the United States (notably Louisiana) and Canada.

phenomena.name: Sphinx
phenomena.description: The sphinx is a mythological composite creature — combining human and animal features, primarily a human head and lion body — that appears in both ancient Egyptian and ancient Greek traditions with distinct roles: guardian and royal symbol in Egypt, riddle-posing deadly monster in Greece.

aliases.name: Andro-sphinx
aliases.meaning: Male-headed sphinx (Egyptian type); from Greek andros (male)

aliases.name: Σφίγξ
aliases.meaning: Sphinx; possibly from sphingein (to squeeze/strangle), referring to the lion's killing method

aliases.name: Shesep-ankh
aliases.meaning: 'Living image'; proposed Egyptian origin of the word sphinx

phenomena.origin: Ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, and subsequently throughout the Mediterranean world and into South and Southeast Asia through cultural diffusion. Physical sphinx statues survive primarily in Egypt and in museums worldwide.

phenomena.name: Splintercat
phenomena.description: The Splintercat is a fearsome critter from American lumberjack and woodcraft folklore — a nocturnal flying feline creature with an impossibly hard forehead that hunts by flying headfirst into trees at tremendous speed, smashing them to splinters to expose raccoons and bee hives for food.

aliases.name: Splinter Cat
aliases.meaning: Two-word alternate spelling used in some sources

phenomena.origin: A creature of American lumberjack folklore distributed wherever the tradition was carried — primarily the Pacific Northwest, Great Lakes region, and northeastern United States and Canada. A Nova Scotia variant is documented. Splintercat Creek in Oregon's northern Cascade Range is named for the creature.

phenomena.name: Spontaneous Human Combustion
phenomena.description: Reported deaths in which a human body is severely burned, often reduced to ash, with little damage to the surroundings and no obvious external ignition source. Modern forensic science treats these cases as conventional fires propagated by the 'wick effect'.
phenomena.origin: Reported cases cluster in Europe (especially Britain, Ireland, France, Italy, Germany) and North America from the 17th century onward; isolated cases elsewhere.

phenomena.name: Spring-Heeled Jack
phenomena.description: A leaping, claw-handed, sometimes flame-breathing figure reported in England from the late 1830s through the early 20th century. Initially a panic in suburban London, Spring-Heeled Jack became one of the foundational characters of Victorian urban legend and penny dreadful fiction.
phenomena.origin: Concentrated initially in the suburbs of London (1837–1843), then in scattered reports across the English Midlands, the Home Counties, Lincolnshire, Hampshire (Aldershot Garrison, 1877), and northern England (Liverpool, 1888 and 1904).

phenomena.name: Squonk
phenomena.description: A 'fearsome critter' of North American lumberjack folklore, said to inhabit the hemlock forests of northern Pennsylvania. The squonk is famously ugly, weeps continuously, and is said to dissolve into its own tears when cornered.

aliases.name: Lacrimacorpus dissolvens
aliases.meaning: 'Tear-body that dissolves itself'; coined by William T. Cox (1910)

phenomena.origin: Confined in lumberjack folklore to the hemlock forests of northern Pennsylvania, USA. Cox notes a possible secondary range in adjacent forested mountain country.

phenomena.name: St. Elmo's Fire
phenomena.description: A bright blue or violet glow appearing as a brushlike or pointed flame on tall, sharp objects (ship masts, aircraft, lightning rods, mountain peaks) during strong atmospheric electric fields. Long mistaken for a supernatural sign, it is now understood as a corona discharge of ionized air.

aliases.name: Castor and Pollux
aliases.meaning: Twin flames, the Dioscuri; classical name when seen in pairs

aliases.name: Helena's fire
aliases.meaning: Single flame considered an ill omen in classical sources

phenomena.origin: Global. Anywhere strong atmospheric electric fields develop near pointed grounded conductors — open ocean storms, thunderstorm cells over land, volcanic plumes, and high-altitude flight.

phenomena.name: Stick Indian
phenomena.description: A category of forest beings in the traditions of many Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples (Salish, Yakama, Klickitat, Cayuse, Nez Perce, and others). Variously described as tall hairy giants or as small forest dwarves, they are most commonly known for whistling at travellers, leading people astray, and punishing those who disrespect the forest.
phenomena.origin: Traditional homelands of Pacific Northwest peoples whose oral traditions include Stick Indian / tsiatko / seeahtik beings — including the Coast Salish region of present-day Washington and southwestern British Columbia, the Plateau (Yakama, Klickitat, Cayuse, Nez Perce, Wenatchi, Colville, Spokane), and the Olympic Peninsula.

phenomena.name: Stone Tape Theory
phenomena.description: A pseudoscientific hypothesis that strong emotional or traumatic events are 'recorded' onto the surrounding stone, masonry, or other materials of a location, and replayed under suitable conditions as a haunting. Popularised by Nigel Kneale's 1972 BBC television play The Stone Tape; the underlying idea has older roots in 19th- and 20th-century parapsychology.

aliases.name: Residual haunting hypothesis
aliases.meaning: Modern parapsychological term for the same idea

aliases.name: Place memory
aliases.meaning: T. C. Lethbridge's term for emotional energy stored in the landscape

phenomena.origin: As an interpretive framework rather than a localised phenomenon, the theory is invoked worldwide. Its strongest cultural footprint is in the United Kingdom, where it originated, and in English-language paranormal media generally.

phenomena.name: Stonehenge
phenomena.description: A prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, built in stages between roughly 3100 and 1600 BC. A UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986) of central importance to British archaeology, it is also a focus of folklore and modern pagan and druidic ceremony.

aliases.name: Stanenges / Stanhenges
aliases.meaning: Possibly 'hanging stones'; recorded by 11th-12th century writers

phenomena.origin: A single monument on Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, England.

phenomena.name: Strigoi
phenomena.description: Vampiric undead of Romanian folklore, distinguished from many other European vampire traditions by an active 'living' form (strigoi viu, a sorcerer or witch) and a 'dead' form (strigoi mort) that rises from the grave to torment family members.

aliases.name: Strigoi viu
aliases.meaning: 'Living strigoi' — sorcerer or witch with strigoi powers

aliases.name: Pricolici
aliases.meaning: Werewolf-strigoi crossover; undead transforming into a wolf

phenomena.origin: Folk traditions of Romania, especially rural Wallachia, Moldavia, Transylvania, and Oltenia. Cognate beliefs extend across the Balkans and into the Slavic world.

phenomena.name: Strzyga
phenomena.description: The strzyga is a usually female demon from Polish Slavic folklore — a dual-souled being born with two hearts and two rows of teeth, whose demonic soul leaves the body after death to prey on the living by drinking blood and consuming organs.

aliases.name: Strzygoń
aliases.meaning: Masculine form used in some regional traditions

aliases.name: Striga
aliases.meaning: Latin root; a screech-owl or blood-drinking demon; source of the Polish term

aliases.name: Strigă
aliases.meaning: Romanian cognate; related but distinct vampire tradition

regions: Broadly: Eastern Europe and former Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth territories
phenomena.origin: Primarily Polish folklore, with cognate traditions in Romanian, Albanian, and Hungarian folk belief. The broader strix tradition extends throughout the ancient and medieval Mediterranean and Eastern European world.

phenomena.name: Succubus / Incubus
phenomena.description: In medieval Christian demonology, the succubus (female) and incubus (male) are demons that seduce humans during sleep through sexual encounters, draining their life force; the tradition appears globally under various names and is now understood to be closely associated with sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

aliases.name: Lilith
aliases.meaning: night demon associated with sexual predation

aliases.name: Mara
aliases.meaning: nightmare spirit that rides sleeping persons

aliases.name: Cambion
aliases.meaning: offspring of a demon and human

phenomena.origin: The succubus/incubus tradition is found throughout medieval Europe and has functional analogues in cultures worldwide. The specific Christian demonological framework is primarily European (especially Western and Central Europe), but similar nocturnal sexual demon traditions appear across the Middle East, Africa, and Asia.

phenomena.name: Sundel Bolong
phenomena.description: The Sundel Bolong is a female ghost from Indonesian (primarily Javanese) folklore, defined by a large hole in her back; she is the spirit of a woman who died pregnant or in childbirth under shameful circumstances and takes revenge on men and abducts infants.
phenomena.origin: Indonesian folklore, centered in Java but present throughout the archipelago including Sumatra, Kalimantan, and other islands.

phenomena.name: Supay
phenomena.description: Supay is a significant deity in Andean (Inca/Quechua) mythology who rules the underworld realm Ukhu Pacha; originally an ambivalent god of death, he was recast by Spanish colonial missionaries as equivalent to the Christian devil, a syncretic transformation that persists in modern Andean culture.

aliases.name: Çupay
aliases.meaning: early colonial spelling used by Spanish chroniclers

aliases.name: El Tío
aliases.meaning: The Uncle — syncretic mining deity identified with Supay

aliases.name: China Supay
aliases.meaning: Female Supay; she-devil in the Diablada dance

phenomena.origin: The Andean region of South America, encompassing the territories of the pre-Columbian Inca Empire. Strongest contemporary presence in mining communities of Bolivia and Peru.

phenomena.name: Superstition Mountains
phenomena.description: A rugged volcanic mountain range east of Phoenix, Arizona, famous for the Lost Dutchman's Gold Mine legend and a long sequence of disappearances and unexplained deaths within its wilderness.
phenomena.origin: Volcanic mountain range east of Phoenix, Arizona, spanning Maricopa, Pinal, and Gila counties.

phenomena.name: Swan Maiden
phenomena.description: A widespread folktale motif in which a supernatural woman able to transform into a swan (or other bird) is captured by a man who steals her feather-cloak, forced into marriage, and eventually escapes when she recovers it.

aliases.name: Bird Maiden
aliases.meaning: Generic English term for shapeshifting bird-women across folklore

aliases.name: Apsara (related)
aliases.meaning: Celestial maidens often involved in similar 'stolen garment' tales

aliases.name: Selkie (analogous)
aliases.meaning: Seal-skin counterpart of the swan-feather motif

phenomena.origin: The swan-maiden motif is one of the most widely distributed folktale types in Eurasia and adjacent regions, with attested variants from Western Europe through Siberia, East Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and into Indigenous North America.

phenomena.name: Tailypo
phenomena.description: An Appalachian folktale creature, dog- or cat-like with a long tail, that returns night after night to a hunter who cut off and ate its tail, demanding its return and ultimately killing him.
phenomena.origin: Folktale concentrated in the Appalachian region and the broader American South. The tale also appears, with variations, in African-American Southern oral tradition and in 20th-century children's-literature retellings.

phenomena.name: Tamamo-no-Mae
phenomena.description: A legendary Japanese nine-tailed fox spirit who, disguised as a beautiful court lady, infiltrated the Heian Imperial court and bewitched the Emperor before being exposed and slain on the Nasu plain.

aliases.name: Hakumen Konmō Kyūbi no Kitsune
aliases.meaning: 'White-Faced Golden-Haired Nine-Tailed Fox' — title used in some otogizōshi

phenomena.origin: The legend is centered in Japan, with the climactic events on the Nasu plain in modern Tochigi prefecture. Earlier 'lives' of the fox spirit are set in China (Shang court) and India.

phenomena.name: Taniwha
phenomena.description: Supernatural beings in Māori tradition that inhabit deep pools, rivers, harbours, caves, and dangerous coastal waters of Aotearoa (New Zealand), acting as both guardians (kaitiaki) and monstrous threats.

aliases.name: *tanifa
aliases.meaning: reconstructed ancestor of the word, referring to a dangerous shark species

aliases.name: Tanifa / Tanifoa
aliases.meaning: cognate terms for large or dangerous sharks

phenomena.origin: Taniwha are particular to Aotearoa (New Zealand), with cognate water beings throughout Polynesia.

phenomena.name: The Taos Hum
phenomena.description: A persistent low-frequency hum reported by a small minority of residents around Taos, New Mexico from the early 1990s onward, investigated by a 1993 university-led panel without identifying a specific source.
phenomena.origin: Reports center on Taos and surrounding Taos County in northern New Mexico, with one early hearer reporting a perceived range of approximately 30 miles (48 km).

phenomena.name: Tatzelwurm
phenomena.description: An alpine lizard-like cryptid reported in Switzerland, Austria, Bavaria, and adjacent French and Italian Alps from the 17th century onwards, with stubby body, cat-like face, and reduced limbs.
phenomena.origin: Reports cluster in the Alps of Switzerland, Austria, Bavaria, the French Alps, and northern Italy, with cognate creatures reported in southern Sweden.

phenomena.name: Teakettler
phenomena.description: A small, behaviorally defined fearsome critter of North American lumberjack folklore that produces a teakettle-like whistling sound. First catalogued in William T. Cox's 1910 'Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods'.
phenomena.origin: Folklore current in the lumber-camp belt of the northern United States and Canada in the late 19th and early 20th century.

phenomena.name: Teke Teke
phenomena.description: A Japanese urban-legend onryō: the spirit of a young woman or schoolgirl bisected by a train who travels on her hands or elbows, making a 'teke-teke' scratching sound, and bisects those she catches.

aliases.name: テケテケ
aliases.meaning: Onomatopoeic 'teke teke' for the scratching/scuttling sound she makes

aliases.name: Kashima Reiko
aliases.meaning: Closely related Japanese urban-legend figure of a girl whose legs were severed by a train, often treated as a precursor to the Teke Teke legend

phenomena.origin: Originally a Japanese schoolyard / tabloid urban legend; widely diffused since the 2000s through Japanese horror media and English-language internet culture.

phenomena.name: Telepathy
phenomena.description: The purported direct transmission of information from one mind to another without using any known sensory channel. Coined as a scientific term by Frederic W. H. Myers in 1882; treated by mainstream science as not demonstrated.

aliases.name: Mind reading
aliases.meaning: Popular term for purported direct mind-to-mind communication

aliases.name: Thought transference
aliases.meaning: Earlier 19th-century term used by SPR researchers before Myers coined 'telepathy'

aliases.name: Mental Radio
aliases.meaning: Title of Upton Sinclair's 1930 book; popular nickname for telepathy in the 1930s–40s

phenomena.origin: Telepathy is reported and researched globally; experimental and theoretical work has been concentrated in the UK, USA, USSR/Russia, and continental Europe.

phenomena.name: Tengu
phenomena.description: Japanese mountain spirits, classed as both yōkai and kami, ranging from lesser bird-like kotengu to high-ranking long-nosed daitengu, originally portrayed as Buddhist demons but later re-imagined as protective mountain guardians and martial-arts mentors.
regions: Kansai (Mount Kurama, Mount Atago, Mount Hiei)
phenomena.origin: Tengu are exclusively associated with Japan and concentrated in the country's mountainous interior, especially central Honshu.

phenomena.name: Teotihuacan
phenomena.description: Teotihuacan is a vast pre-Columbian city in the Valley of Mexico, approximately 40 km northeast of Mexico City, that was one of the largest cities in the ancient world at its peak (c. 100,000–200,000 inhabitants around 400–500 CE); its builders remain unknown, and the city features extraordinary astronomical alignments, a 100-meter ritual tunnel sealed for 2,000 years, and evidence of collective governance unlike other ancient civilizations.

aliases.name: Teohuacan
aliases.meaning: proposed alternate original name meaning 'City of the Sun' (scholarly debate, 2018)

aliases.name: Puh
aliases.meaning: Place of Reeds — Maya designation for the city found in Maya texts

aliases.name: Teōtīhuacān
aliases.meaning: Birthplace of the gods — name given by the Aztecs who arrived after the city's abandonment

regions: State of Mexico (municipio de San Juan Teotihuacan)
phenomena.origin: Single location in the Valley of Mexico, but cultural influence extended across Mesoamerica during the city's peak period (1–650 CE).

phenomena.name: Thunderbird
phenomena.description: A massive bird-spirit central to many Indigenous North American traditions, paired in modern cryptozoology with reports of enormous unidentified birds with wingspans far exceeding any known living species.
phenomena.origin: Thunderbird traditions are recorded across the Pacific Northwest Coast, Great Lakes, Great Plains, American Southwest, and US East Coast. Modern cryptozoological 'giant bird' reports cluster in Illinois, Pennsylvania, the Ozarks, and Alaska.

phenomena.name: Tikbalang
phenomena.description: A creature of Philippine folklore depicted as a tall, gaunt humanoid with the head and hooves of a horse, known for leading travelers astray in remote forested or rural areas.

aliases.name: Multo / bibit
aliases.meaning: Earlier Spanish colonial terms ('ghost', 'spirit') used for the same forest phantom

phenomena.origin: Reported throughout the Philippine archipelago, particularly in mountainous and forested provinces of Luzon and the Visayas.

phenomena.name: Time Slips
phenomena.description: An anomalous experience in which a percipient apparently perceives, or briefly enters, a different time period (most often the past) before returning to the present without the passage of normal time.

aliases.name: Retrocognition
aliases.meaning: Apparent perception of a past event

phenomena.origin: Reported worldwide; the largest published clusters are in the United Kingdom (Versailles in France, Liverpool, Wiltshire, Norfolk) and the United States.

phenomena.name: John Titor
phenomena.description: An anonymous online persona who, between 1998 and 2001, claimed to be an American soldier from the year 2036 sent back to 1975 to retrieve an IBM 5100 computer. Widely regarded as one of the most elaborate early-internet hoaxes.

aliases.name: TimeTravel_0
aliases.meaning: Username used on the Time Travel Institute forum, late 2000

aliases.name: John Titor
aliases.meaning: Username used on the Art Bell BBS forum, 2001

phenomena.origin: Posts originated through online forums based primarily in the United States.

phenomena.name: Tokoloshe
phenomena.description: A dwarf-like water spirit of Nguni (Zulu, Xhosa) folklore in Southern Africa, traditionally summoned by witch doctors to harm enemies. Known for invisibility, biting sleeping victims, and aggressive nocturnal behavior.
phenomena.origin: Reported throughout Southern Africa, especially among Nguni-speaking peoples (Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Ndebele) and into neighboring states.

phenomena.name: Tommyknockers
phenomena.description: An American mining spirit of Cornish origin, brought to the United States by Welsh and Cornish immigrant miners in the 19th century. Described as a small, bearded, mining-clothed figure whose knocking on mine walls warns miners of collapse or guides them to ore.
phenomena.origin: Original tradition in Cornwall and Devon, England, and Wales; carried by Cornish and Welsh immigrant miners to the eastern United States from the 1820s and to the American West following gold and silver rushes.

phenomena.name: Tote-Road Shagamaw
phenomena.description: A 'fearsome critter' of North American lumberjack folklore, first described in William T. Cox's 1910 Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods. The Shagamaw has the front quarters of a bear and the hindquarters of a moose, and supposedly walks on its forelegs for exactly a quarter of a mile before switching to its hind legs.
phenomena.origin: Cox locates the Shagamaw in the Maine lumberwoods, with Aroostook County mentioned in his account.

phenomena.name: Tower of London
phenomena.description: A historic royal castle on the north bank of the Thames in London, founded in 1066 by William the Conqueror. With a millennium of executions, imprisonments, and political violence, it is among the most-reported haunted sites in the United Kingdom.

aliases.name: His Majesty's Royal Palace and Fortress of the Tower of London
White Tower
aliases.meaning: Original Norman keep at the centre of the complex

phenomena.origin: A single fixed historic site of approximately 12 acres on the north bank of the Thames, central London.

phenomena.name: Toyol
phenomena.description: An undead infant familiar in Malay and Indonesian folklore, kept by a shaman or owner to steal money and small valuables for its master. Belief remains widespread across the Malay Archipelago.

aliases.name: Kuman Thong (cf.)
aliases.meaning: Related Thai child-spirit familiar; not identical

phenomena.origin: Belief is found throughout the Malay Archipelago and the Malay-Chinese diaspora, including Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, and southern Thailand.

phenomena.name: Tripodero
phenomena.description: A fearsome critter of North American lumberjack folklore, native to the Californian chaparral. First described by William T. Cox in 1910 as a small, kangaroo-tailed creature with two telescopic legs and a blowgun-like snout that fires mud pellets at prey.
phenomena.origin: Cox locates the Tripodero in the Californian chaparral and the foothills of the Sierra Nevada.

phenomena.name: Trolls
phenomena.description: Trolls are supernatural beings from Scandinavian and Norse folklore, typically described as large, old, strong, dim-witted humanoids dwelling in isolated mountains and caves; their defining characteristic is vulnerability to sunlight, which turns them to stone.

aliases.name: Trǫll
aliases.meaning: archaic form; fiend or supernatural being

aliases.name: Trow
aliases.meaning: smaller supernatural beings; from Norse troll

aliases.name: Tusser
aliases.meaning: smaller Norwegian trolls; sometimes distinguished from mountain trolls

phenomena.origin: Scandinavian and Norse cultural sphere. Most deeply embedded in Norwegian, Swedish, and Danish folklore. Also present in Icelandic tradition and in Norse-influenced areas including Orkney and Shetland (as 'trows').

phenomena.name: Tsukumogami
phenomena.description: Tsukumogami (付喪神) are a class of Japanese yokai in which household items and tools gain sentience and spiritual essence after approximately 100 years of existence; rooted in Shinto animism and Buddhist teachings, they can range from benign pranksters to vengeful spirits if discarded carelessly.

aliases.name: 付喪神
aliases.meaning: The kanji form: attached/grieving spirit of an object; read tsukumogami

aliases.name: 九十九神
aliases.meaning: Alternate kanji: ninety-nine spirits; emphasizes great age (100 years) as the threshold for animation

regions: Particularly associated with the Heian-period (794–1185 CE) court culture where many of the originating texts were composed
phenomena.origin: Japan; the tsukumogami concept is specific to Japanese culture and is rooted in Shinto animism and Japanese Buddhist traditions.

phenomena.name: La Tunda
phenomena.description: A shapeshifting female forest entity from the Afro-Colombian and Afro-Ecuadorian Pacific coast who lures victims, especially children and disobedient men, into the forest by impersonating their loved ones.

aliases.name: Tunda
aliases.region: Pacific coast of Colombia and Ecuador

aliases.name: Entundado / Entundada
aliases.meaning: a person bewitched or held under La Tunda's spell

aliases.name: Entundamiento
aliases.meaning: the deceptive trance La Tunda induces in her victims

phenomena.origin: La Tunda is a regional Pacific-coast spirit of Colombia and Ecuador, especially associated with Afro-descendant communities living in dense tropical rainforest, riverine, and mangrove environments.

phenomena.name: Tunguska Event
phenomena.description: A large atmospheric explosion over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, Siberia, on 30 June 1908 — the largest impact event in recorded history, now widely attributed to the airburst of a small asteroid 5–10 km above the surface.
phenomena.origin: Localized event with effects concentrated in central Siberia, but atmospheric and luminous effects observed across Eurasia.

phenomena.name: Tylwyth Teg
phenomena.description: The Tylwyth Teg ('Fair Family') are the principal fairy folk of Welsh folklore, parallel to the Aos Sí of Ireland and the fairies of English and Continental tradition.

aliases.name: Gwragedd Annwn
aliases.meaning: Wives of the Otherworld; lake fairies

phenomena.origin: Tylwyth Teg traditions are found across Wales, with regional variations in name and emphasis. They are part of the broader Brythonic Celtic fairy tradition shared with Cornwall and Brittany.

phenomena.name: Ubume
phenomena.description: A Japanese yōkai of a woman who died in or shortly after childbirth, who appears at night carrying a baby and tries to pass it to a passerby; the bundle then turns to leaves, stones, or grows unbearably heavy.
phenomena.origin: Found across Japan with regional variants and overlaps with Chinese-derived bird-spirit traditions.

phenomena.name: Unicorn
phenomena.description: A legendary single-horned quadruped most familiar in Europe as a horse-like creature symbolizing purity, but with deep roots in Greco-Roman natural history, biblical translation, and global one-horned-creature traditions.

aliases.name: Re'em
aliases.meaning: horned wild ox; rendered as 'unicorn' in the Septuagint and KJV

aliases.name: Qilin / Kirin
aliases.meaning: an East Asian one- or two-horned chimerical creature, often called the 'Chinese unicorn' though distinct in tradition

aliases.name: Karkadann
aliases.meaning: single-horned creature of Persian and Arabic literature, often associated with the rhinoceros

phenomena.origin: Unicorn-type traditions are global and pre-modern; the European unicorn is most closely associated with India and the imagined East in classical sources, and with European forests in medieval bestiaries.

phenomena.name: Upyr
phenomena.description: The upyr is the Slavic revenant or blood-drinking undead from which the modern Western 'vampire' concept is descended; a corpse that rises from the grave to attack family, livestock, and community.
phenomena.origin: Upyr traditions are found across the Slavic world and adjacent regions, from East Slavic (Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian) through West Slavic (Polish, Czech, Slovak, Sorbian) to South Slavic (Serbian, Bulgarian, Macedonian) cultures. Closely related traditions exist among Romanians (strigoi), Greeks (vrykolakas), Albanians (shtriga), and Turkic-speaking peoples (ubir).

phenomena.name: Urban Legends
phenomena.description: A genre of contemporary folklore consisting of unusual, frightening, or humorous narratives told as true accounts about everyday life, typically attributed to a 'friend of a friend' and rarely verifiable.

aliases.name: Contemporary legend
aliases.meaning: academic preferred term in folklore studies

aliases.name: FOAFtale
aliases.meaning: 'friend-of-a-friend' tale; coined by folklorists for the genre's signature attribution

phenomena.origin: Urban legends are a global phenomenon, with active traditions documented across the United States, the United Kingdom, continental Europe, Latin America, East and South Asia, Africa, and Oceania.

phenomena.name: Ushi-oni
phenomena.description: The Ushi-oni (牛鬼, also read gyūki) is a fearsome yokai from Japanese folklore combining the head of an ox with a monstrous body; it inhabits coastal and waterside areas in western Japan and is known for savage attacks on humans.

aliases.name: 牛鬼
aliases.meaning: Ox-demon; the kanji form read as ushi-oni

aliases.name: Gyūki
aliases.meaning: Alternative reading of the same kanji 牛鬼; ox-demon

regions: Coastal areas of western Japan generally
phenomena.origin: Western Japan, particularly coastal areas of Ehime, Wakayama, Shimane, and other prefectures along the Seto Inland Sea and Sea of Japan coastlines.

phenomena.name: Valkyrie
phenomena.description: Valkyries are female figures in Norse mythology who serve Odin, choosing which warriors die in battle and escorting the chosen slain (einherjar) to Valhalla; their name derives from Old Norse valkyrja meaning 'chooser of the slain.'

aliases.name: Valkyrjur
aliases.meaning: Plural form: choosers of the slain

aliases.name: Wælcyrge
aliases.meaning: Old English cognate; slaughter-chooser or battle-spirit

aliases.name: Walküre
aliases.meaning: German form; most familiar through Wagner's opera Die Walküre (1870)

aliases.name: Skjaldmær
aliases.meaning: Shield-maiden; related but distinct category of mortal female warrior sometimes conflated with valkyries

phenomena.origin: Norse and Germanic mythology across Scandinavia and the broader Germanic cultural sphere. Primary textual sources are Old Norse (Iceland, Norway); Old English cognates appear in Anglo-Saxon manuscripts.

phenomena.name: Vampires
phenomena.description: Vampires are undead or supernatural beings from predominantly Eastern European folklore that survive by feeding on the blood of the living; the modern concept emerged primarily from 18th-century Slavic vampire panics and was transformed into the aristocratic Gothic figure through 19th-century literature.

aliases.name: Vampir
aliases.meaning: vampire; possibly from Old Slavic onpyr

aliases.name: Strigoi
aliases.meaning: Romanian vampire/undead; from Latin strix (owl/night bird)

aliases.name: Nosferatu
aliases.meaning: Possibly 'not dead' or 'plague-carrier'; popularized by the 1922 film

aliases.name: Penanggalan
aliases.meaning: Malay vampire variant; a detached flying female head with dangling organs

phenomena.origin: The vampire tradition is most strongly associated with Eastern and Southeastern Europe (Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Poland, Russia), but blood-drinking supernatural beings appear in folklore worldwide.

phenomena.name: Van Meter Visitor
phenomena.description: The Van Meter Visitor is a winged creature reported by multiple witnesses in Van Meter, Iowa over five consecutive nights in late September to early October 1903; witnesses described a large, dark, winged humanoid with a bioluminescent horn projecting from its forehead and a powerful offensive odor.

aliases.name: Van Meter Monster
aliases.meaning: Common alternate name used in local and cryptozoological sources

phenomena.origin: Single location: Van Meter, Iowa, USA. No other sightings documented in the area before or after the 1903 incidents.

phenomena.name: Vanishing Hitchhiker
phenomena.description: The Vanishing Hitchhiker is one of the world's most widespread urban legends, in which a driver picks up a hitchhiker who subsequently disappears from the moving vehicle; the driver later learns the hitchhiker died years earlier, often at or near the pickup location.

aliases.name: Phantom Hitchhiker
aliases.meaning: Ghost or apparition encountered hitchhiking on a road

aliases.name: Resurrection Mary
aliases.meaning: Most famous named American vanishing hitchhiker — a young blonde woman reportedly seen near Resurrection Cemetery, Justice, Illinois

regions: Chicago area (Resurrection Mary — most famous American version)
phenomena.origin: Worldwide — one of the most geographically widespread urban legends documented by folklorists. Versions have been recorded across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and among diaspora communities worldwide.

phenomena.name: Vetala
phenomena.description: A class of spirit-beings in Hindu mythology that inhabits and animates corpses, traditionally associated with cremation grounds, fortune-telling, and the riddle-cycle of Vikramaditya in the Vetala Panchavimshati.
phenomena.origin: The vetala is a feature of Hindu mythology and South Asian folklore, with the strongest literary and cultic tradition in India and Nepal. Regional veneration of Vetoba/Betal is concentrated in the Konkan coastal region of western India.

phenomena.name: Vila
phenomena.description: Female nature-spirits of Slavic, especially South Slavic, folklore, often described as beautiful long-haired women in white who dance in mountain meadows and possess powers over weather, healing, and prophecy.
phenomena.origin: Strongest attestation in South Slavic folklore (Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Montenegro), with regional variants in Czech, Slovak, and Polish tradition. Russian attestation is disputed in scholarship.

phenomena.name: Vodyanoy
phenomena.description: A male water spirit of Slavic folklore, especially Russian, Czech, and Slovak traditions, said to inhabit rivers, lakes, mill-pools, and marshes; capricious, sometimes drowning humans and livestock, sometimes blessing fishermen and millers in return for offerings.
phenomena.origin: Vodyanoy and his counterparts are attested across the Slavic-speaking world: Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, and parts of the Balkans.

phenomena.name: Voynich Manuscript
phenomena.description: An illustrated 15th-century codex written in an unidentified script and held since 1969 at Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library as MS 408; its language and meaning have not been deciphered despite more than a century of expert study.

aliases.name: Voynichese
aliases.meaning: Informal name for the manuscript's unidentified script and language

phenomena.origin: A single physical artifact whose ownership and physical location have moved across central Europe and the United States; the surrounding research community is global.

phenomena.name: Vrykolakas
phenomena.description: A revenant of Greek folk belief — an undead, often swollen and bloated corpse held to leave the grave at night and afflict the living, with strong continuity to wider Balkan vampire traditions.
phenomena.origin: Strongest in the Greek-speaking world: mainland Greece, the Aegean islands (especially Mykonos, Santorini, Crete, and Chios), and historically Greek communities of Anatolia, Cyprus, and the southern Balkans.

phenomena.name: Wampus Cat
phenomena.description: A panther-like cryptid of Appalachian folklore with roots in Cherokee mythology, often described as a large, dark cat — sometimes with extra legs, glowing eyes, and shapeshifting powers — said to roam the southeastern United States.

aliases.name: Catawampus
aliases.meaning: regional adjective sometimes used for the creature

phenomena.origin: Reports and folklore concentrate in the southern Appalachian Mountains (Tennessee, North Carolina, Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, northern Georgia and Alabama) and the Ozarks (Arkansas, Missouri).

phenomena.name: Wanyūdō
phenomena.description: A Japanese yōkai depicted as a flaming oxcart wheel with a tormented man's face at its hub, said to roll along roads at night, steal souls, and punish the curious in Edo-period folklore.

aliases.name: Katawaguruma
aliases.meaning: one-wheeled cart; closely related yokai often discussed alongside wanyūdō

phenomena.origin: Edo-period Japan, with strongest folk associations to Kyoto and the wider Kinai region; subsequently transmitted across Japan through kaidan literature and yōkai art.

phenomena.name: Waverly Hills Sanatorium
phenomena.description: A former tuberculosis sanatorium in Louisville, Kentucky (opened 1910, expanded 1926, closed 1961) widely reputed to be haunted; among the most heavily investigated 'haunted hospital' locations in the United States.
phenomena.origin: A single fixed location: the Waverly Hills Sanatorium complex on Paralee Drive, Louisville, Kentucky.

phenomena.name: Wendigo
phenomena.description: A malevolent spirit-being central to the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples of northern North America, embodying winter, famine, greed, and the gravest taboo of cannibalism; humans who break that taboo are said to risk transformation into a wendigo.
phenomena.origin: Pan-Algonquian, with strongest presence in the boreal-forest territories of the Ojibwe, Cree, Innu, Algonquin, and Saulteaux peoples across central and eastern Canada and the upper Midwest of the United States.

phenomena.name: Wendigo (Cree)
phenomena.description: The Wendigo (Cree: Wīhtikōw; Ojibwe: Wiindigoo) is a supernatural being in Cree, Ojibwe, and related Algonquian traditions that embodies the ultimate transgression — cannibalism driven by greed — and the spiritual and physical transformation that results; associated with winter, cold, and insatiable hunger.

aliases.name: Wīhtikōw
aliases.meaning: The Cree-language name for the wendigo; the primary indigenous term

aliases.name: Wiindigoo
aliases.meaning: The Ojibwe-language name; source of the English 'wendigo'

aliases.name: Wetiko
aliases.meaning: Variant spelling of the Cree term; used in contemporary indigenous scholarship as a metaphor for colonial and capitalist exploitation

aliases.name: Windigo
aliases.meaning: Alternate English spelling; used in ICD-10 for the culture-bound syndrome

regions: Boreal forest regions of Canada generally
phenomena.origin: The boreal forest regions of Canada and the northern United States, corresponding to the traditional territories of Algonquian-speaking peoples. Strongest tradition among the Cree, Ojibwe, Saulteaux, Naskapi, and Innu peoples.

phenomena.name: Werewolf
phenomena.description: A human capable of transforming into a wolf or wolf-human hybrid, featuring in the folklore and mythology of many cultures, with the most developed European tradition producing historical trials and executions between the 1500s and 1700s.

aliases.name: Loup-garou
aliases.meaning: Wolf-werewolf; redundant compound from Old French

phenomena.origin: Werewolf traditions are documented across Europe (with especially dense legal and trial records in France, Germany, Switzerland, and the Low Countries), Slavic Europe, the Caucasus, and, through colonial transmission, the Americas (particularly French Canada, Louisiana, and Haiti).

phenomena.name: Wewe Gombel
phenomena.description: A Javanese ghost figure — the spirit of a tragically wronged woman — who abducts neglected or mistreated children, caring for them protectively until their parents repent. She is a cautionary figure in Javanese child-rearing tradition, originating from the Bukit Gombel area of Semarang, Central Java.

aliases.name: Wewegombel
aliases.meaning: Compound of wewe (woman/widow) and Gombel (a scrubby hill in Semarang)

phenomena.origin: Central Java, Indonesia; the legend is most strongly associated with Semarang and the surrounding Bukit Gombel area, though it is known across Javanese-speaking communities in Central and East Java.

phenomena.name: Whirling Whimpus
phenomena.description: A 'fearsome critter' of North American lumberjack tall tales: a gorilla-shaped beast that spins so fast it becomes invisible, mistaken for a small dust devil or whirlwind, and crushes anything that strays into its path.
phenomena.origin: A tall-tale beast of the North American lumberwoods, particularly the Appalachian Mountains and the Great Lakes / eastern logging regions in which the fearsome-critters tradition flourished c.1880–1940. Often associated specifically with Tennessee and the southern Appalachians.

phenomena.name: White Lady
phenomena.description: A globally recurring ghost archetype: a female apparition in white clothing tied to a specific location and a story of tragic, often violent death — most commonly suicide, murder, accident, or death in childbirth.

aliases.name: Witte Wieven
aliases.region: Netherlands and surrounding Low Saxon area

aliases.name: Lady of the Lake (Rochester)
aliases.region: Durand-Eastman Park, Rochester, New York, USA

aliases.name: La Llorona (related)
aliases.meaning: The Weeping Woman; a related but distinct white-clad female-ghost archetype

phenomena.origin: The White Lady is a globally distributed archetype with attested local traditions across Europe (Germany, Czech Republic, England, Wales, Ireland, Netherlands, Switzerland, Hungary, Estonia, Russia, Serbia), the Americas (United States, Brazil), and parts of Asia (Philippines, Thailand).

phenomena.name: Wild Hunt
phenomena.description: A widespread northern and central European folk motif of a spectral troop of hunters, hounds, and horses tearing through the night sky or wild lands, led by a mythological or legendary figure and often regarded as an omen of war, plague, or death.

aliases.name: Cŵn Annwn
aliases.meaning: Hounds of Annwn — the Welsh hellhound counterpart

phenomena.origin: The Wild Hunt motif spans most of northern, central, and parts of southern Europe, with distinct regional families in Germanic-speaking lands, Scandinavia, the British Isles, France, and Iberia.

phenomena.name: Will-o'-the-Wisp
phenomena.description: A faint, drifting nocturnal light reported above bogs, marshes, and graveyards. Long woven into folklore as fairy lights, ghost candles, or treasure markers, and chiefly explained by modern science as the spontaneous combustion of swamp gases (methane, phosphine, diphosphane).
phenomena.origin: Reported worldwide wherever organic-rich wetlands or bogs occur, with strong concentrations in the British Isles, north-western Europe, North America, the Indian subcontinent, and Australia.

phenomena.name: Windigo
phenomena.description: A spirit-being of Algonquian-language traditions — Ojibwe wiindigoo, Cree wīhtikōw — embodying the moral horror of cannibalism, of insatiable greed, and of the heart turned to ice. Both a being met in story and a name for a culturally specific psychological transformation.

aliases.name: Wendigo
aliases.meaning: Anglicised form popularised by Algernon Blackwood (1910)

aliases.name: Wechuge
aliases.meaning: Closely related but distinct cannibal-spirit figure

phenomena.origin: The Windigo is a being of the boreal forest of northern North America, associated specifically with the territories of Algonquian-speaking peoples — Ojibwe / Anishinaabe, Cree, Innu, Naskapi, Atikamekw, Saulteaux — across present-day Canada and the northern United States.

phenomena.name: Wolpertinger
phenomena.description: A mythical hybrid creature of southern Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg: a small mammal — typically a rabbit or hare — fitted with antlers, fangs, wings, and other animal parts, popularised through 19th- and 20th-century 'gaff' taxidermy mounts displayed in inns and museums.

aliases.name: Jackalope
aliases.region: United States (Wyoming and the American West)

phenomena.origin: Folkloric range is the alpine and pre-alpine forests of southern Germany, particularly Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, with extensions into the broader Alpine region.

phenomena.name: Xtabay
phenomena.description: A Yucatec Maya female spirit said to lurk near ceiba trees at night, appearing as a beautiful woman with very long black hair and luring unfaithful or drunken men to madness, injury, or death deep in the forest.
phenomena.origin: Yucatec Maya cultural area: the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico (states of Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche) with extensions into northern Belize and the Petén region of Guatemala.

phenomena.name: Yacuruna
phenomena.description: Powerful water spirits in the mythology of various Indigenous peoples of the Amazon basin, particularly Quechua-speaking and riverine cultures. The Yacuruna inhabit underwater cities beneath Amazonian rivers and lakes, riding black crocodiles by night and shapeshifting into Amazon river dolphins to interact with humans.
phenomena.origin: The Yacuruna tradition is documented across the Amazonian basin, particularly among Quechua-speaking peoples of Peru and adjacent riverine cultures (Cocama, and others). The belief complex extends across the broader Amazonian cultural area where the boto (Amazon river dolphin) is ecologically present.

phenomena.name: Yama-no-kami
phenomena.description: A Shinto kami (divine spirit) of the mountains revered across Japan, who rules over mountains and forests in winter and descends to become Ta-no-kami (rice-field god) in spring. Worshipped by hunters, woodcutters, and farmers, Yama-no-kami is accompanied by strict taboos and is generally depicted as a female deity.

aliases.name: 山の神
aliases.meaning: Mountain kami; the standard kanji rendering

aliases.name: Yamagami
aliases.meaning: Alternative reading of the characters 山神; mountain god/spirit

aliases.name: Ta-no-kami
aliases.meaning: Rice-field god; the seasonal alter ego of Yama-no-kami, who descends from the mountain in spring

aliases.name: Sansin
aliases.meaning: Mountain spirit; East Asian cognate deity

regions: Significant tradition on Mount Hiei (Oyamakui no Kami)
Mount Fuji associated with Ōyamatsumi worship
phenomena.origin: Worshipped throughout Japan, with active shrines in all mountainous regions. The tradition is most prominent in rural agricultural and forestry communities. Cognate traditions extend across East Asia (Korea's Sansin, China's Shanshen, Vietnam's Son than).

phenomena.name: Yama-oroshi
phenomena.description: A Japanese yokai (tsukumogami) born from a neglected grater that has become too dull to function. The yama-oroshi grows a body, and its dull, worn slicers protrude like wild spines. Its name is a triple pun: on oroshi (grater), yamaarashi (porcupine), and the strong mountain wind (yama-oroshi) blowing down from peaks. The creature's breath is said to be ten thousand times stronger than a human's, explaining mysterious mountain winds.

aliases.name: 山颪
aliases.meaning: Mountain wind; the primary kanji rendering, punning on both 'grater' and 'wind blowing down from mountains'

aliases.name: やまおろし
aliases.meaning: Hiragana form; reads as both 'mountain wind' and 'mountain grater'

phenomena.origin: Japanese folklore tradition; documented as part of the broader tsukumogami and yokai tradition of Japan. The creature is associated with mountain environments across Japan.

phenomena.name: Yamauba
phenomena.description: A morally ambivalent yokai in Japanese folklore — an elderly mountain woman who may shelter and aid travelers or devour them. She is most famous as the mother of the folk hero Kintaro and is a major subject of Noh theater. She embodies the dual nature of the wild mountain: nurturing yet consuming, maternal yet dangerous.

aliases.name: Yama-uba
aliases.meaning: Mountain hag / mountain old woman; from yama (mountain) + uba (old woman, wet nurse)

aliases.name: 山姥
aliases.meaning: Primary kanji rendering: mountain (山) + hag/old woman (姥)

aliases.name: Yamahime
aliases.meaning: Mountain princess; a regional variant name for a related mountain woman figure

phenomena.origin: Found throughout Japanese folklore, with documented regional variants across Honshu, Hokkaido, Shikoku, and Kyushu. Particularly associated with the mountainous interior of Japan and mountain-pass routes historically traveled by merchants and ox-drivers.

phenomena.name: Yamata no Orochi
phenomena.description: An eight-headed, eight-tailed giant serpent of Japanese mythology, slain by the storm god Susanoo no Mikoto in the Hi River valley of Izumo Province. The creature's defeat yielded the Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi sword, one of Japan's three Imperial Regalia, making the Orochi myth one of the most consequential narratives in Japanese culture.

aliases.name: 八岐大蛇
aliases.meaning: Eight-branching great serpent; the kanji rendering combining eight (八), branch/fork (岐), great (大), serpent (蛇)

aliases.name: 八俣遠呂知
aliases.meaning: Alternative archaic kanji rendering found in the Kojiki

aliases.name: Orochi
aliases.meaning: Great serpent; the short form used independently in later tradition

phenomena.origin: The myth is geographically anchored to the Hi River (now the Hii River) in Izumo Province (modern Shimane Prefecture), western Honshu, Japan. The narrative is national in significance but locally specific in setting.

phenomena.name: Yara-ma-yha-who
